Tiisetsoâs view
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa acquired some useful new friends in Washington this week. Unfortunately for him, they cannot solve either of his immediate problems.
The first is at home. The African National Congress, the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela, is taking a drubbing in the local government elections, threatening Ramaphosa as the ANCâs 2027 leadership contest approaches.
With more than two-thirds of the vote counted, a respected election modeling outfit projects the ANC at around 32%. This puts it on course for its worst-ever municipal performance and emboldens those arguing that the centrist political formula of Ramaphosaâs presidency is not winning over voters.
His second problem sits in the White House, where US President Donald Trump has waged a campaign against Pretoria over everything from race policies to its foreign policy choices, and has now put a preferential trade program, the African Growth and Opportunity Act, on the chopping block.
That said, Ramaphosa sees an opening, saying he predicted a ânew era in world relations,â after Democrats captured both houses of Congress. Richard Neal, a top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, slammed the ejection of South Africa from AGOA as âgrounded in grievance,â while Gregory Meeks and Jeanne Shaheen, the partyâs senior voices on foreign policy in the House, warned the move could hand China a strategic advantage.
The catch is that a weakened Trump may be a Trump more inclined to target South Africa â a distant country whose post-apartheid racial politics can be repackaged to fit Americaâs own culture wars just as Ramaphosaâs political authority is shrinking at home.

Wall Street wants a price for AI compute. Washington may not.
Exchange operators are racing to make GPU compute a tradable commodity like oil or wheat. But that effort is complicated by the fact that the biggest buyers, AI hyperscalers, pay under secret contracts, leaving most of the public data on how much people are paying for compute coming from the spotty offerings from neoclouds.
Intercontinental Exchange CEO Jeff Sprecher told me when I interviewed him this week at the futures industryâs annual confab in Chicago that he was âbullish but cautious.â Futures normally follow an established spot market, and compute doesnât really have one (see this robust X debate). âWeâre kind of [working] backwards,â Sprecher said.
The AI debt boom might just bring the push the markets need. Sprecher said lenders that are increasingly nervous about financing data centers could start demanding that companies lock in their GPU prices for as long as theyâre asking to borrow. âIt may be that the capital markets require that, given how much money is being lent,â he said. âAnd then Zuckerberg comes over and says, âI need to do a big trade,ââ he added with a smile.
The bigger wild card is Washington. Pressure from the Trump administration forced Kalshi to scrap one of its GPU price trackers in September, Semafor reported, which Sprecher chalked up to concerns that transparent pricing for AI could disadvantage the US in its competition with China. âThe United States is a free market and that has always advantaged us vis-Ã -vis China, so I suspect thatâs where theyâll come out. But weâre all waiting with bated breath.â

effdb9c4e032.text:
Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.
Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.
G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.
Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.
It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.
For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.
Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.
The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.
G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.
There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

As the US midterm election results rolled in, long-held Israeli assumptions about the transatlantic alliance began to shatter.
"For us in Israel, this will be a generational sea change," wrote one prominent journalist in Israel's biggest-selling newspaper, right-leaning Yedioth Ahronoth. "The [prime minister, Benjamin] Netanyahu government sowed the wind and reaped the tsunami."
Israel's opposition leaders have lined up to blame their prime minister, with one saying the US results showed "just how toxic Netanyahu has become" among both Democrats and Republicans.
The prime minister himself has so far remained silent.
"Israel's political establishment understood intellectually that things have been shifting. They have not understood how much and how quickly," one US official with knowledge of the situation told me.
Israel's relationship with the US was a campaign issue in races across America.
Many Democratic candidates were sharply critical of Israel's actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, and the costs of the joint US-Israeli war on Iran was a key issue for many voters.
The US president himself blamed the Iran War for the Republican rout â a war that Israel's leader is widely seen as having promoted to him.
And US Vice-President JD Vance cited the US relationship to Israel as one of four key reasons voters had deserted the party, hammering home the message that the relationship is now seen as a political problem by its key ally.
"That might be even worse than what happened in the midterms," Israeli political and security analyst Yaakov Katz told me. "Because the Democrats we knew about, now [Vance] is pointing the finger and saying: 'Our voters want us to change our position on Israel' â and Israelis don't fully understand where this is going."
The question plaguing Israelis now is what this means for Israel's security and influence.
The sense of staunch US military and diplomatic support had remained unshaken in Israel despite growing anger among US voters, President Donald Trump's public insults to Netanyahu, and differences over Israel's actions in Iran and Lebanon.
Israel's prime minister continually boasted of his closeness to Trump, describing his "true friendship" and "unwavering support".
And just nine months ago, Israelis watched their armed forces wage war on Iran hand in hand with the US military, as the "unprecedented" coordination of the two allies became a daily mantra among military spokespeople and politicians.
So Trump's unexpected statement during a Fox News interview this week that he would stop $3.8bn (3.4bn euros; Â£2.8bn) in US military aid to Israel two years earlier than planned, caused shock here â not so much for the loss of aid as for what the move said about Israel's status as a diplomatic partner.
Israel's president said the announcement came as "a bolt from the blue".
"Nobody knows anything," was the headline in a report by Yedioth Ahronoth, adding that officials were still struggling to understand whether Trump's remark was serious, two days on.
The Israeli prime minister's office responded to the news several days later, saying that the shift from US aid to partnership showed "the strength and sophistication" of the bilateral relationship.
US military aid is less than 10% of Israel's annual military budget. But Yaakov Katz, author of several books about Israel's defence and security, said Trump's announcement was the tip of a much larger question around future funding, arms sales and joint military projects with Israel. All of this could be slowed or stalled by a Democrat-controlled Congress, even without the two-thirds majority it would need to overrule Trump.
"Everything that Israel used to get in a simpler, easier process will now potentially be much more complicated, and Israel has to be prepared that this is a new reality," he told me.
"Our entire Air Force is American-made military planes, we're dependent on American spare parts and American weapons. The last three years have shown us how dependent we are on American missile-defence systems. [If] those don't show up at the same pace, that's a real difference â that changes your calculation of what you're able to withstand if you go to war."
Katz believes the midterms could also translate into tougher demands on Israel over its actions in Gaza and Lebanon, and a requirement not to undermine an agreement with Iran.
"Something will change in the US-Israeli relationship, but it's a question of scale," said the US official I spoke to, who was not authorized to speak on the record. "It means shifting to [being] willing to criticise Israel when it's warranted, but the bedrock fundamental relationship will still be there."
In an interview on Israeli television, the US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee signalled little shift so far in core American positions, including on Israel's occupation of the West Bank, describing the sanctions imposed by other countries as "irrational" and counterproductive.
Israel's ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, told another Israeli channel that Trump would be in the White House for the next two years, and that Israel could "feel good" about the US veto in the UN Security Council â something Washington has repeatedly used in the past to block resolutions that target Israel.
"But we have to pay attention to the voices â not only in the Democratic Party but also the Republican Party â criticising Israel," he said. "It will be harder for us."
Questions over its key alliance have come at a particularly sensitive time for Israel, less than two weeks after its own parliamentary elections left neither government nor opposition with a clear majority. Discussions are now taking place with the country's president, who will decide whether Netanyahu or his centrist rival, Gadi Eisenkot, will get the first chance to form a governing coalition.

4b96f8acc113.text:
The News
Bankers and advisers were âshockedâ when OPay abruptly pulled its $304 million US IPO just hours after pricing on Oct. 30, after a Chinese regulatory inquiry forced the Nigeria-focused fintech to abandon its planned New York Stock Exchange debut, people close to the transaction told Semafor.
Speaking on condition of anonymity, they said the advisers were caught off guard by the intervention, with one calling the outcome âa disaster for everyone.â The inquiry was unexpected because OPay, headquartered in Singapore, generates 90% of its revenue in Nigeria and has no operating business or revenue in mainland China. But its founder, Chinese billionaire Zhou Yahui, remains a key figure in its ownership.
OPay, its advisers, and the banks involved have declined to comment further on the transaction.
Know More
In its prospectus filing, the company advised investors of the risk with Chinese regulators even though it does not operate there. OPay acknowledged that there were uncertainties over whether it might need approval from the authorities in Beijing to list in the US. However, citing advice from its Chinese legal counsel, the company said it did not believe it was required to obtain approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission .
The dealâs earlier documentation also listed China International Capital Corporationâs Hong Kong securities business among the transactionâs bankers, alongside Citigroup, Deutsche Bank, and South Africaâs Standard Bank. CICC was subsequently absent from the list of underwriters accompanying Fridayâs announcement, a detail that may have been an early indication of complications.
Those close to the deal also pushed back against suggestions that the IPO had been priced too aggressively. OPay set 16 million American depositary shares at $19 each, the bottom of its $19-$21 target range. The shares were subsequently indicated to open below the offering price, but the company withdrew before trading began.
Step Back
OPay said in its announcement that the inquiry concerned a jurisdiction âimmaterial to the Companyâs core business operationsâ and that it expected the matter to be resolved satisfactorily in the near future. It has not announced a revised timetable for a listing.
For African investors and technology founders, the hope will be that OPayâs setback proves an isolated complication rather than another obstacle to attracting international public-market capital. After years of difficult fundraising conditions, the continentâs venture industry needs successful exits and public listings to persuade investors that its technology businesses can deliver returns at scale.

- Published
The "Male State", an extremist misogynistic group named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, has denied any link to the false warnings causing flight disruption across Europe.
The comments to the BBC came as reports of more bomb scares to airlines began appearing, including on a Ryanair flight from Rome to Lisbon and a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome which was diverted to Venice.
Bomb threats were also reported to a number of high-profile Irish media organisations on Friday, prompting evacuations and a statement from the Irish government suggesting a "co-ordinated campaign of disruption".
Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats.
"What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"
The group was banned in Russia in 2021 and Pozdnyakov is now thought to live abroad. It has since renamed itself in some places as "Male Legion".
The initial hoax email, seen by the BBC, was sent on Thursday at 07:21 with the subject title: warning of a threat.
It was addressed to several offices and individuals at Aeroporti di Roma (ADR), the airport managing company in Rome, as well as accounts at the city's Fiumicino airport itself. The originating email address seems to be linked to the state health services in Bogota, Colombia.
It's not clear whether other countries' airports or airlines received the same or similar threat. At least one warning made on Friday appears to have come by phone, not email.
Written in word perfect Italian, the bizarre text sent to Rome on Thursday claimed that "fighters" of the "Male State" had planted explosives on two incoming flights in an attack on Italy's "feminist regime" that would be "remembered forever".
One flight was diverted as a result - ordered to land in France â another was escorted into Rome by Italian air force jets, scrambled for the second time this week. No explosives were found on either plane, or any other that reported receiving bomb threats.
Asked why this particular email was taken so seriously, a source at ADR in Rome told the BBC that such warnings were extremely unusual. They didn't remember anything similar in recent years.
Despite the Russian group's denial, Italy's La Stampa newspaper appears in no doubt that "Male State" was behind the threats, asking in an article whether it is acting as "the regime's armed wing".
"Attacking, and being able to deny the attacks...is part of the Russian game plan," the paper writes, external.
One Telegram channel linked to Pozdnyakov is mainly filled with virulently pro-Russian messaging about the war on Ukraine and other posts highlighting problems and tensions in Europe, including recent youth protests.
The online investigation team at Bellingcat, who studied the group back in 2022, called it then a "vocal and vile online booster" of the Russian invasion, with a clear extremist far-right ideology.
As the Europe-wide hunt continues for who is behind the spate of hoax mails, and whether they are being co-ordinated - or could be the work of copycats - Italy's defence minister has warned of a "strategy to increase chaos".
Guido Crosetto noted that he had been talking of the "hybrid threat" to Europe for some years.
"It seems to me that, day after day, from incidents involving refrigerators to the blood supply in France and now these false alarms, there are those who have an interest in fuelling tensions," the minister said on Thursday, referring to a spate of recent cyber attacks that boosted supermarket fridge temperatures, destroying mountains of produce.
"Our interest is to do the opposite and ensure the country's security," Crosetto said.
Additional reporting by Davide Ghiglione

A rockets manufacturer says the mothballed Sutherland Spaceport could become its first launch site outside the US.
Colorado-based Leap has agreed to work with Highlands and Islands Enterprise (HIE), which owns the area of peatland near Tongue, to develop the plans.
Little work has been done at the site after Moray-headquartered rockets firm Orbex put construction on hold in 2024. The company later collapsed and its assets were sold off.
Leap said the spaceport could potentially be used for launching small satellites for customers in the UK and mainland Europe.
Leap is designing rockets that could be mass produced in factories.
Chief executive Chris Beckman said: "We're not just building a rocket. We're building a global logistics network, and a network needs launch sites wherever customers require them.
"Sutherland is an ideal starting point for a network that begins in Europe, and HIE shares our ambition to make recurring spaceflight from Scotland real."
HIE and Economy Secretary Stephen Flynn have welcomed the agreement.
The site is on Melness Crofters Estate, an area of small-scale farms on the A' Mhoine Peninsula in Sutherland in the north-west Highlands.
Chairwoman Dorothy Pritchard said the estate was delighted to welcome Leap as a potential launch operator.
She said: "We believe their presence here will be an important step towards establishing a thriving and sustainable spaceport that can bring long-term benefits to Sutherland and the UK's growing space industry.
"Alongside other UK launch sites, both developed and emerging, an operational Sutherland Spaceport will become an integral part of a resilient and diverse UK launch ecosystem, securing the UK position within the global space economy, something we welcome and support.
"Melness Crofters Estate looks forward to seeing the spaceport become a driver of economic opportunity."
Last month, the UK and German governments said they planned to use another Scottish spaceport - SaxaVord in Shetland - as part of increased co-operation between the two countries.
The agreement followed a meeting between Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin last week.
In a joint statement, the two governments said they would deepen strategic co-operation on civil, commercial, security and defence interests in space.
SaxaVord in Unst is the UK's first fully-licensed spaceport and has regulatory approval for up to 30 rocket launches a year.

fcd6b5197447.text: Refrigerator hacks. $6.3 billion crypto heists . 14-country espionage campaigns carried out in just 11 days. All in the span of a week. Why it matters: State-backed hackers are finding new ways to launch cyberattacks at remarkable speed and scale, with AI and automation threatening to widen the gap between attackers and defenders. Driving the news: Hackers tampered with refrigeration systems at dozens of European grocery stores in one night earlier this week — raising temperatures and spoiling food in a sweeping attack some linked to Russia. "It's hard to imagine this is not the work of a nation state pretending to be a criminal actor," Cynthia Kaiser, former deputy director of the FBI's cyber division, told Axios. "Given the concentration around Europe, Russia is a reasonable first suspect." French blood banks were also affected in the attacks on European refrigeration systems, authorities said Wednesday. SentinelOne researchers reported Tuesday that Russian-aligned hackers have previously claimed attacks on European refrigeration systems. Meanwhile, the Pentagon has also been investigating a series of suspected hacks of refrigeration systems on its military bases over the summer. Nextgov reported that investigators suspect Iran was behind those attacks. Others have suggested potential Iran ties in Europe as well. The big picture: No clear evidence has yet linked the attack on food supply through smart refrigeration to AI or automation, but nation-state hackers have used those tools in other breaches to speed up their operations. Google researchers said last week that multiple hacking groups have used automated security testing tools in recent attacks. One China-linked group gained deep access to a victim's network in as little as 15 minutes. North Korean hackers behind last week's record-setting Binance heist also likely used automation to move stolen cryptocurrency and cover their tracks, according to Chainalysis. Case in point: China-linked hackers used an AI-powered tool called Artex to target more than 200 organizations across 14 countries in just 11 days last month, CrowdStrike found . The group, known as Vapor Panda, targeted government agencies across Latin America, the Middle East and Europe, along with U.S. organizations and telecommunications providers in several countries. The hackers paired Artex with DeepSeek and a commercial AI model to run agents that automated much of the operation. Between the lines: Artex is one of several AI-powered tools automating tasks once handled by skilled human hackers. Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's senior vice president of counter adversary operations, told Axios he tested Artex himself and found it could probe websites for weaknesses far faster than a human. "It was doing the stuff that you, as a pen tester, would do," Meyers said. "But it does it really at a scale and a speed that I think a human would not be able to do." Other AI-powered security testing tools, including Cairn and Strix, could be repurposed for similar attacks, Meyers said. Reality check: The refrigeration attacks also raise questions about overlooked security gaps that hackers can exploit without sophisticated AI tools. "I see these attacks the same way I saw the attacks on U.S. water systems this summer: Nobody looked until it made the news," Mike Searight, a former public-sector CIO and executive advisor to Elisity, told Axios. AI-powered hacking tools still need weaknesses to exploit. "It's not magic," Meyers said. What to watch: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre warned Tuesday that AI could accelerate existing hacking tactics, leaving organizations with weaker defenses and outdated technology especially vulnerable. Go deeper : AI is supercharging hacks of everyday utilities

The German government has launched an international initiative to curb emissions of sulfur hexafluoride, an exceptionally potent greenhouse gas that it says has long been overlooked in efforts to address climate change.
Announced this week at a United Nations Environment Program meeting in Kigali, Rwanda, the “Global SF6 Pledge” urges countries to commit to monitoring, reporting and reducing emissions of the synthetic gas from the electric power sector, where it is used as an insulator in high-voltage equipment.
Pound for pound, SF6 is 24,300 times more effective at warming Earth’s atmosphere than carbon dioxide and remains in the atmosphere for 1,000 years. Although the United Nations identified it as one of six key greenhouse gases in the 1990s, it has received relatively little attention from policymakers.
“It’s a gap,” said Philippe Lempp of Germany’s international development agency, which is implementing the pledge. “We need to take care of this one because it’s something that we cannot rely on countries to do themselves.”
More than half of all sulfur hexafluoride emitted globally comes from China, a country that is rapidly expanding its electric grid. The country’s state-owned electric power companies recycle only about 30 percent of the gas they discard each year, with the remainder likely released into the atmosphere, a recent Inside Climate News analysis concluded.
“The pledge finally turns the spotlight on SF6, but until the world’s largest grid builder matches that ambition, we’re only treating half the leak,” said Richard Ferris, senior counsel at the Institute for Governance and Sustainable Development, a Washington, D.C.-based environmental research and advocacy organization.
China’s central government released its National Climate Change Response Plan in July, which called for an SF6 management plan to reduce emissions of the pollutant. The pledge and the attention it brings could hasten China’s efforts, Ferris said.
“China will continue to work with all countries to strengthen international cooperation on climate change, contributing to a green transition and the sustainable development of humanity,” Liu Chang, spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, D.C., said in a written statement. Liu did not directly respond to a question about whether China intends to sign the pledge.
Countries that sign the SF6 Pledge commit to strengthening monitoring and reporting of SF6 emissions while supporting efforts to reduce releases of the pollutant. SF6 emissions can be cut by recycling rather than venting used gas, reducing leaks from high-voltage equipment and using alternative gases or technologies as electrical insulators.
The European Union and the United Kingdom are the first to endorse the pledge, which officially launches this month at the United Nations’ global climate conference in Antalya, Turkey. The U.S. State Department declined to comment.
The United States released 328 metric tons of sulfur hexafluoride in 2023, primarily from the electric power sector, the most recent year for which data are available, according to U.S. Environmental Protection Agency data. This equals the annual climate pollution of 1.9 million automobiles, based on the agency’s greenhouse gas equivalency calculator.
The EPA has repeatedly extended the deadline for large greenhouse gas emitters—including those that release SF6—to report their climate pollution, as the agency considers scrapping reporting requirements entirely under an executive order by President Trump.
The pledge joins a growing list of voluntary initiatives, such as the Global Cooling Pledge and the Global Methane Pledge, that aim to reduce climate pollution. More than 150 countries have signed the methane pledge.
The SF6 pledge would provide a valuable platform for international cooperation, but “voluntary commitments must be backed by national regulations and accountability,” said Avipsa Mahapatra, climate campaign director for the Environmental Investigation Agency US, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit organization, in a written statement. “Success should not be measured by how many countries sign the pledge, but by how quickly countries stop installing new SF6-dependent equipment where alternatives are available, reduce emissions from existing equipment, and establish credible pathways toward eliminating SF6 emissions.”
Efforts should also target other industries that use and emit SF6, including semiconductor manufacturing, Mahapatra said.
The U.S. and Europe have significantly reduced emissions from their electric power sectors in recent decades through gas recycling, leak prevention and the adoption of alternative gases and technologies. The European Union took another step in that direction in January, when it began phasing out SF6 in new electrical equipment.
“It’s something that can be done,” Lempp said of global SF6 emissions reductions. “And with the right push, it will be done.”

22efdfe10015.text: Vice President Vance has spent the past two weeks personally involved in indirect talks with Iran aimed at reaching a new ceasefire and resuming nuclear negotiations, according to two sources with knowledge of the matter. Why it matters: Vance's heavy involvement shows he's taking it upon himself to extract the U.S. from a conflict he blamed for the GOP's staggering losses in this week's election. It also elevates the latest round of indirect talks to the highest levels of the administration. The big picture: U.S. officials and regional sources say that for now Trump is willing to let diplomatic efforts play out and wants to see if any kind of deal is possible. "We're talking to them," Trump told reporters on Friday, when asked what his message to Iran was. But if he changes his mind and orders renewed strikes, the U.S. military is ready to launch strikes on a relatively short timetable. Behind the scenes: Vance has been speaking almost daily to Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, Pakistani Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and other mediators about the negotiations with Iran, sources with direct knowledge said. White House envoy Steve Witkoff and President Trump's adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner are also involved. Vance and Qatari and Pakistani mediators have been discussing the possibility of a working-level technical meeting between the U.S. and Iran in the coming days, but it hasn't materialized yet, the sources said. The vice president's office declined to comment. Catch up quick: Vance was the most skeptical voice in Trump's inner circle about the war before it began at the end of February, advocating instead for a diplomatic solution. He led the U.S. negotiating team to an April summit on Iran in Islamabad, and he was personally involved in talks that led to the U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding (MOU) in June. Vance then led the U.S. delegation to a round of direct talks with Iran in Switzerland, which ended with an Iranian commitment to invite UN inspectors to visit its nuclear facilities. But shortly after, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps resumed attacks on ships, leading to the collapse of the MOU. Driving the news: Two weeks ago, Vance sent a letter to the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council in Iran, Mohsen Rezaei, proposing to resume direct negotiations. Rezaei is one of the closest confidants of Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Iranian officials said Vance's letter created positive momentum toward restarting negotiations. On Wednesday, Vance said the war was the main reason Republicans were repudiated in the election. State of play: Sources involved in the mediation efforts say there has been progress, but it's been very slow. On Friday morning, Trump spoke to Emir of Qatar Sheikh Tamim al-Thani about Qatar's efforts to bridge the gaps between the U.S. and Iran on a deal. Sheikh Tamim stressed the need to "continue dialogue and pursuing diplomatic means to resolve differences, spare the region further escalation, and ensure freedom of maritime navigation and the security of energy supplies," per a statement from his office.

Cornell University's academic staff have passed a vote of no confidence over its leadership's handling of what staff call a "crisis of sexual assault" after a former student alleged she was gang raped while attending.
The woman, known anonymously as Jane Doe, is suing her former school and the fraternity over an alleged incident involving several men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024.
All seven of the accused have denied wrongdoing when contacted by the BBC's US partner CBS. None has been charged with a crime.
Friday's no confidence vote passed by 75 votes to 50. It is largely symbolic because the faculty senate does not have the power to remove leaders.
The resolution states that the faculty senate, which represents academic staff, "has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University".
It did not make any specific recommendations or suggest what administrators did wrong in response to the accusation.
It is a rebuke of university leaders including President Michael Kotlikoff, whom Doe has accused of asking why she waited several weeks to report the incident.
The Ivy League institution in upstate New York has said her account of Kotlikoff's reaction is "incorrect".
Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, responded to the vote's outcome in a statement, saying: "We recently learned that Cornell's Faculty Senate made a finding of no confidence in the Central Administration's ability to address the longstanding crisis of sexual assault at Cornell.
"We believe that the Faculty Senate did not reach this decision lightly and considered all available information."
Giuffra added: "We are hopeful that this will be yet another step forward to educate and support the Cornell community by addressing the longstanding scourge of sexual assault on campus."
Backlash against Cornell has been intense since Doe filed her lawsuit in September. She reported the alleged assault to campus police after it happened but the local prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time.
Cornell, after initially defending its disciplinary measures, has acknowledged it fell short in its handling of her case and has hired a former attorney general to conduct an independent review of the case. It also recently announced a series of measures due assault, including cancelling fraternity parties.
New York state prosecutors, led by Attorney General Letitia James, are carrying out their own investigation to decide if criminal charges are warranted.
Earlier this week, New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced that state police would investigate any future sexual offence complaints at the university.

The Democrats hold a narrow lead over the Republicans in the US Senate race in Mississippi, with both sides in a dispute over the counting of the remaining votes which could decide the outcome.
Lawyers for each campaign are preparing for a possible legal battle over the final results and weighing in on the examination of ballots.
The result could mark the end of almost 40 years of Republican control over Mississippi's senate seats and will determine the size of the Democrats' majority in the upper house.
Mississippi is the only US state which does not have a set procedure in place to trigger a recount - and the pressure is on to declare a winner with the state's 13 November deadline for certification approaching.
What ballots are left to count?
With 97% of the votes counted as of Friday, Democratic candidate Scott Colom is about 2,500 votes ahead of the incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Mississippi's Secretary of State Michael Watson said on Wednesday that 3,600 "absentee-by-mail ballots" were still to be counted. The state can accept these votes so long as they were postmarked by election day and are received by 10 November.
Watson said there are also an "unknown" number of provisional ballots, also known as affidavit ballots, to be counted. These are typically cast when a voter lacked the required identification to cast their vote. The deadline for voters to resolve any ID issues with provisional ballots, usually by providing acceptable photo identification, is also 10 November.
Mississippi Republican Party Chair Michael Hurst said on Thursday that they estimated there could be "approximately 20,000 outstanding ballots left to be counted".
Hyde-Smith's campaign said the same day that "thousands of votes remain to be counted from dozens of Republican counties" and it is "confident" this will secure her re-election. She has held the seat since 2018.
Colom said the election saw "historic voter turnout" and he is "confident that when votes are counted, we will flip this seat". If he wins, he would be the first black US senator elected in the state since 1875.
What have the campaign lawyers requested?
Colom said his campaign has an "an army of lawyers" ready to act - while the state Republican party said it has sent more than 50 volunteers, attorneys and observers across the state.
Lawyers from both campaigns have sent letters to Mississippi election officials about the counting of outstanding provisional ballots.
The Hyde-Smith campaign lawyers have requested that all 82 counties in the state keep all provisional ballots separate from regular or absentee ballots.
Their letter also requested that election officials preserve various records - including information on how the votes were processed - associated with the provisional ballots as "potential evidence" in a possible legal dispute.
The Colom campaign lawyers responded saying the move has "no legal authority whatsoever".
"Mississippi law does give any candidate a right to examine ballot boxes and their contents within 12 days after the relevant canvass and examination," says Ronald Rychlak, a law professor at the University of Mississippi. "Mississippi's affidavit-ballot statute also requires eligibility review and records concerning whether affidavit ballots were counted."
"Neither law, however, establishes a blanket requirement to segregate all affidavit ballots after they have been accepted," he adds.
The Colom campaign has said the request from Hyde-Smith's team could allow "a particular ballot to be traced to a particular voter", in violation of ballot secrecy laws.
"That's where he does have a more reasonable argument," says Rychlak, "as ballots in the US are private by law and when there's no clear procedure in place there could be a possibility a voter's privacy might be breached."
Could there be a recount?
Recounts rarely succeed - just three out of 37 completed state-wide recounts across the US since 2000 have reversed a result., external
However, in many states automatic recounts are triggered if a vote is very close, and in others there is an official process for campaigns to request one in a tight race.
Two states, Illinois and Tennessee, allow recounts if a candidate mounts a formal legal challenge.
Mississippi doesn't have a set procedure in place which allows for a result to be automatically recounted even if it's tight or contested.
It is effectively left up to judges in the state to decide how specific disputes should be resolved.
"Mississippi's lack of a formal recount procedure does not leave either campaign without a possible avenue to challenge the result," says Rychlak, "Ballot-box examination is an available post-election mechanism, and that can lead to discoveries that may result in a recount."
There could also be a legal challenge raised at a federal level - with the US Senate potentially having authority to determine who is entitled to the seat.
This would fall under Article I of the US Constitution as there is a provision which gives each chamber of Congress the power to be the "judge of the elections, returns and qualifications of its own members".
Additional reporting by Krystal Campos.

185a68ef5964.text: By — Jamey Keaten, Associated Press Jamey Keaten, Associated Press By — Philipp Jenne, Associated Press Philipp Jenne, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/seeds-and-preserved-hair-in-tomb-point-to-oldest-signs-of-cannabis-high-2800-years-ago-study-suggests Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Seeds and preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests Science Nov 6, 2026 5:19 PM EST GENEVA (AP) — People may have been getting high off cannabis earlier than previously thought — at least 2,800 years ago, a new study suggests. Archaeologists who led a dig at a monumental tomb in Siberia said they turned up evidence of the earliest known use of cannabis for psychoactive purposes. The findings point to cannabis consumption at least 300 years earlier than previously known use in neighboring China. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Ancient drug use has long intrigued scholars. The Greek historian Herodotus wrote about inhabitants of Central Asia smoking cannabis around 440 B.C., and recent archaeologists have found the seeds in tombs across its highlands. The team from Germany, Russia, Sweden and Switzerland said analysis of hair in the royal tomb where cannabis seeds turned up sheds new light on the plant's role in ancient societies. "It's extremely rare that we have both preserved plant parts and human soft tissue with the active compounds in it in the same context," said co-author Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the University of Bern. It's not clear whether the cannabis was consumed through inhalation or ingestion, he said. The dig took place starting in 2017 at a large burial mound at the Tunnug 1 site in the Uyuk Valley of southern Siberia, home to one of the earliest monumental tombs showing material culture of the Scythians — ancient nomads who migrated from Central Asia to southern Russia and Ukraine. READ MORE: A $28 billion hemp THC industry is fighting to save itself from a looming federal ban The team, deployed "essentially out in the middle of nowhere," lived in tents for months and faced a spring-to-autumn season that variously featured swamps, snowstorms, frosts and swarms of mosquitoes. Herds of horses ran freely across the grassy steppe. Larger artifacts on the site include weapons in the burials, horse gear and animal-style motifs. But the team "struck gold" as it also found tiny black spots that turned out to be cannabis seeds along with preserved human hair, Caspari said. "It's only so often as an archaeologist that you do get to drug test a person that's been dead for almost 3,000 years," he said. Radiocarbon dating on some of the more than 1,000 seeds helped establish the time of origin, and "they are not there by accident" but deposited within the tomb, suggesting that the plant material had significance in the community, he said. Results were published Thursday in the journal Science. Not all independent experts were convinced. A preserved human hair braid dating to about 2,800 years ago at the site of an ancient Scythian burial mound, in the Valley of the Tsars, the Republic of Tyva, south of Siberia, Russia, in this handout image released on Nov. 5, 2026. Photo by Frozen Corpses Golden Treasures, T.Wallace & G. Caspari/Handout via Reuters The hair analysis "is scientifically weak" and there's not enough evidence to tell whether cannabis was used, wrote Volker Auwaerter, head of the forensic toxicology section at the University Medical Center in Freiburg, Germany, in an email. "For a central part of the study, the article falls far short of what would have been possible," Auwaerter said. "This matters because the hair data carry the abstract's main claims (cannabis consumption and use for its psychoactive properties)." Today, scholars don't consider ancient accounts trustworthy without corroborating evidence. Because the cannabis plant has other uses — seeds are pressed for oil and fibers used for cloth — their presence alone doesn't confirm drug use. Auwaerter, who was not part of the study, said the data didn't distinguish consumption from external exposure — in other words, the hair could have picked up traces of weed simply by being buried together with it. He said a lab test involving forensic toxicology expertise would have been advisable and easy to arrange. But Elisa Guerra Doce of the University of Valladolid in Spain, who has written about use of consciousness-altering substances in European prehistory, said toxicological hair analysis was not new in archaeology and has been used to identify consumption of psychoactive substances. She was not involved in the study. In an email, she credited the authors for showing, through their methodology, that "cannabis was not merely deposited as a funerary offering but was actually consumed by individuals associated with the burial rite." Jenne reported from Vienna, Austria. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 51efe7201652.text: Angered over his midterm losses, President Trump announced Friday he was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff with longtime adviser Stephen Miller. Why it matters: Trump is trading one of his few moderating forces with one of the most maximalist champions of his agenda, a striking signal that the president may double down on the hardline policies that helped Republicans lose control of Congress on Tuesday. Driving the news: Wiles submitted her resignation on Thursday night. Sources told Axios her departure was a mutual decision, but driven by Tuesday's election results, for which Trump blamed her. Sources said Trump began expressing discomfort with the scale of the midterm losses and the money his political team spent on Wednesday. Wiles offered to quit for two days before she resigned. Trump accepted her decision on Friday. Trump did not ask for her resignation, said one informed source who spoke with Wiles, "but he couldn't get it out of his head that she was to blame, not him." "Susie could've stuck around, but what's the point?" that person said. "Whether it's right or wrong, Susie knows that serving the president means it's at his pleasure. And if she couldn't change the way he felt, there was no reason to stay." What they're saying: "I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026," Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that Wiles will move to the Trump Political Operation. Wiles said in a statement posted to X that "[s]erving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I'm so proud to have been a part of what we've accomplished together." Zoom in: Miller, who served in Trump's first administration, was already a co-equal of Wiles' in some respects. No one in Trump's government knows the levers of power, the operation of the White House and the bold use of the executive branch better than him. An architect of Trump's explosive first hundred days exerting executive authority, Miller has been working on plans to keep operating a muscular White House even in the face of big Democratic majorities. "Trump needs to prepare for war with the Democrats in Congress with all their investigations they're going to launch, and Stephen is a wartime adviser," a Trump adviser explained. Zoom out: Wiles is widely viewed as the most powerful person in the White House outside the president himself, and she achieved something few in his orbit could: earning his trust, influencing his decisions and bringing discipline to an administration defined by historic infighting and upheaval. She was Trump's longest-serving chief of staff, and commanded an extraordinary level of trust from Trump, often serving as the last person he consulted before making major decisions. Her exit also ends the tenure of the first woman ever to hold the powerful position. Her influence stemmed from a relationship with Trump that stretched back to his 2016 campaign when she led his efforts in Florida, and again when she agreed to manage his political comeback following the Jan. 6 riot. Between the lines: Wiles' strength was understanding how to navigate Trump rather than trying to control him. She avoided public confrontations, offered disagreements privately and sought to carry out Trump's priorities rather than restrain them. But her influence had limits. She was a critical voice against the war in Iran and repeatedly questioned the hardline immigration tactics championed by Miller. Friction point: In a grand irony, the very Trump decisions she opposed —the Iran war and the brutality of immigration enforcement — drove Tuesday night's midterm shellacking that led the president to lose confidence in her. Catch up quick: As recently as Oct. 16, Trump emphatically denied reports he was considering replacing Wiles. Trump noted at the time that Wiles would stay as long as she wanted, and he praised her toughness in surviving cancer while serving as his staff chief. Context: Wiles spent decades mastering the art of influencing powerful men while staying out of the spotlight. The daughter of famed NFL broadcaster Pat Summerall, Wiles has credited growing up with an alcoholic father with teaching her how to handle larger-than-life personalities. In Florida, she became a powerful behind-the-scenes operator for two moderate Republican mayors in Jacksonville, helped elect Rick Scott as governor in 2010, and rescued Ron DeSantis' struggling gubernatorial campaign in 2018. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

ba229bd58fc2.text: By — Josh Funk, Associated Press Josh Funk, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/dad-of-20-year-old-co-pilot-in-florida-jet-crash-says-her-final-radio-calls-showed-shes-tough Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Dad of 20-year-old co-pilot in Florida jet crash says her final radio calls showed 'she's tough' Nation Nov 6, 2026 4:52 PM EST The father of the 20-year-old co-pilot who died along with eight others when their Learjet crashed in Florida said Friday he has listened to his daughter's heartbreaking final radio transmissions "many times" since the crash. Allan Filgueiras, a pilot who helped teach his daughter to fly, was searching for answers as to why the plane plunged from the sky on Sunday. Instead, he found immense pride in how his daughter, Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, handled the crisis. "I did listen to that many times trying to find a clue. In my head. How'd that happen? And wow, she's tough," Allan Filgueiras said at a news conference Friday. "I wanted to be by her side," he said, at times holding back tears. "Inside the plane. To help." READ MORE: Parts of jet's tail found more than a mile from plane crash site in South Florida, official says In her conversation with air traffic control, Nathalia Filgueiras can first be heard calmly reporting ice buildup on the plane as it flew into a thunderstorm and turbulence tossed it up and down by 700 feet (200 meters). The situation quickly escalated as the aircraft fell at breathtaking speed. "Declare an emergency 722-Bravo-Delta. We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute!" she said. Her father and aviation safety experts are impressed that Filgueiras continued to call out updates on what was happening even as she realized the plane's fate was sealed. "For the family — it's like having the heart torn from my chest," her father said in Spanish. "I have to find a way to go on living." The family wants to push back against online criticism over whether she had enough experience to be in the cockpit of a high-performance business jet. She had more than 1,300 hours of experience and completed extensive training to earn her commercial pilot's license and get certified for a Learjet. The plane's captain, 55-year-old Jeff Gregory, is believed to have been at the controls in the aircraft's final minutes. So, on Friday, her father held a news conference that his lawyer said was intended to "preserve not just her memory, but her reputation." "She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years," attorney Stuart Grossman said, noting there were no immediate plans to file a lawsuit over the crash. It's far too early in the National Transportation Safety Board's investigation to know what caused the crash. As it fell, the Learjet accelerated beyond its design limits and pieces of the plane's tail were found miles away from the crash site. READ MORE: All 9 people aboard a jet that crashed in Florida have died, transportation secretary says Allan Filgueiras said he first took his daughter flying at age 12 and later started teaching her to fly. After she got a job as a pilot, she told her dad she couldn't believe she was getting paid to do something she loved. "It was her happiest moment, to fly," he said. Retired airline pilot John Cox, who is now the CEO of Safety Operating Systems, said earlier this week that his career began similarly to Filgueiras, as he started flying professionally at age 19. He said she was doing quite well to earn that co-pilot's seat. "To be in the right seat of a Lear 60, she had to impress somebody, because that's a good ride. I mean, that's great. I know she loved it," Cox said. Her father believes she handled the crisis better than most. "She showed me what it is to be a hero because once you see that coming, a lot of the big boys — military or whatever — they can't handle. And she was the one over there to the last minute fighting," Allan Filgueiras said. The crash victims included technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson; his wife, Helen Sharp; and their two young children, relatives said. The family's nanny, Ana María Ramírez Cetina, was also killed. 4237ed0b752b.text: Congressional Democrats see a target-rich environment next year. But they're also worried that if they investigate everything , they may appear to investigate nothing. Why it matters: Democrats want to move beyond the one-off hearings, fist-pounding document demands and subpoena threats that defined much of their oversight during President Trump's first term. The goal, according to senior Democrats, is to build a sustained narrative around the administration's "cost, chaos and corruption" — while showing voters they have legislative solutions to the problems they uncover. "We're trying to get to the answers that point to solutions," a senior Democratic aide said. Zoom in: Senate Democrats are actively coordinating investigations across committees and with their House counterparts, looking to turn Day One oversight of the Trump administration into a sustained case for their own legislative agenda. Think more Jan. 6 committee investigation, with slick videos and compelling witness testimony, than impeachment 1.0. The coordination, underway for months, is increasingly happening at the senator level, with lawmakers working to divide investigative responsibilities and avoid overlapping efforts. "We want to deconflict these with some of the other committees, right? We don't want to be duplicative with other committees," Sen. Chris Van Hollen told Axios. The other side: Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely chair of the House Oversight Committee, has a four-pronged plan to investigate the Trump administration. But he has a two-word taunt: "LAWYER UP." Between the lines: Nearly every House committee has the power to subpoena without getting sign-off from the minority party. In the Senate, only the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and its Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations (PSI) can issue subpoenas unilaterally. Trump's war in Iran will likely be the Senate's first focus, with the Senate Armed Services Committee preparing for hearings — and planning to call Hegseth to testify — in January. There will also be an immediate vote on a war powers resolution. "I've been very clear that we need to use every tool at our disposal to end the illegal [incentives] war in Iran, and that's beginning day one," Van Hollen said. What's next: As the scope of their victory comes into focus, Democrats across committees are eager to get to work. "I'm looking at you — Big Tech CEOs, Wall Street executives, and giant corporations. If you break the law, there will be consequences," Sen. Elizabeth Warren thundered on X .

d1bc5c81963a.text: By — Leah Willingham, Associated Press Leah Willingham, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/cornell-faculty-vote-no-confidence-in-university-leadership-after-alleged-fraternity-gang-rape Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Cornell faculty vote 'no confidence' in university leadership after alleged fraternity gang rape Nation Updated on Nov 6, 2026 4:59 PM EST — Published on Nov 6, 2026 4:28 PM EST Cornell University's Faculty Senate approved a resolution Friday declaring "no confidence" in the school's top leaders, a symbolic gesture reflecting deep discontent on campus in the wake of a former student's lawsuit saying she was gang raped at a fraternity party in 2024. The resolution passed 75-50, with five faculty senators abstaining and five others not voting, according to an email sent to Faculty Senate members on Friday afternoon. The vote followed weeks of debate among professors over whether Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators handled the woman's allegations properly and have done enough to curtail sexual misconduct at the prestigious university. READ MORE: Woman who accused Cornell students of rape says university president's response made her feel 'unsupported' While the faculty body has no power over the university's top leaders, backers of the resolution had said they hoped it would pressure Cornell's trustees to address longstanding institutional failures they identified. Board of Trustees Chair Anne Smalling said in a statement the faculty vote "reflects the deep anger across our campus" and sent a clear signal that what happened to the woman was unacceptable, but added that Kotlikoff and his administration were the right leaders to "thoughtfully and comprehensively" address the issue. Thomas Giuffra, an attorney for the woman who filed the lawsuit, said in a statement Friday that "we are hopeful that this will be yet another step forward to educate and support the Cornell community by addressing the longstanding scourge of sexual assault on campus." Lawsuit sparked outrage on campus The Cornell community has been distressed since mid-September, when a former student, identified only by the pseudonym Jane Doe in court documents, filed a lawsuit against the university and seven former members of the Chi Phi fraternity, saying she was given ketamine and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024. All of the men have denied her allegations, saying the sex was consensual or that they weren't involved. The local district attorney initially decided the woman had consented to the encounter and that no crime had been committed, but the investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York's attorney general. WATCH: Fraternity culture under scrutiny in wake of Cornell allegations Cornell disciplined several of the accused students following a monthslong Title IX investigation. Two were expelled, two received suspensions and probation, and two were required to write "reflection" papers and complete bystander training. A seventh man had already graduated and was barred from campus, according to records obtained by The New York Times. Kotlikoff also convened a task force to study the problem of sexual misconduct on campus, which released certain recommendations. Some faculty members have criticized Kotlikoff for not acting more forcefully to strengthen the school's disciplinary process, push for criminal investigations and change campus party culture. Paul Ortiz, a labor history professor who co-sponsored the no-confidence resolution, said last week that hundreds of students, staff, alumni and faculty approached the resolution's sponsors to emphasize that "the Jane Doe case is but a tip of the iceberg" and that "a veritable fortress of silence has been breached" around sexual violence since the resolution's introduction. Cornell's president defended his leadership Speaking to Faculty Senate members on the first day that they debated the no-confidence resolution, Kotlikoff pledged to make the university a leader in addressing sexual assault and asked for more time to make changes. Kotlikoff defended his leadership, arguing that replacing him would do little to solve complex problems and could damage Cornell's reputation. He acknowledged he had not read the campus police report, explaining that university policy barred top administrators from interfering in criminal investigations. He also rejected suggestions he had been indifferent to the woman's case, though he acknowledged only recently learning she had left Cornell. READ MORE: A gang rape allegation at Cornell highlights how Title IX guides campus sex assault cases Kotlikoff said the university needed to determine whether fraternities could operate safely and left open the possibility of sweeping restrictions on Greek life. He argued that decisions should be based on research and evidence rather than emotion. Some professors had said faculty should wait to vote until the release of an independent investigation by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, whom the university hired to examine both how Cornell responded to the woman's initial rape report in 2024 and its overall procedures for handling similar reports from other students. The no-confidence resolution did not call for Kotlikoff's resignation. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has appeared in court after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.
Markle was arrested on a federal complaint alleging he held images that show child sex abuse, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said.
The 82-year-old was arrested in Florida after the FBI searched two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for almost 20 years.
He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said. Markle has previously denied allegations of possessing images of child sex abuse, calling them "sick lies".
Markle's court hearing lasted for 30 minutes, and the charges were laid out against him by federal prosecutor Courtenay Derry, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
He was brought into court a wheelchair, escorted by two US Marshals. Markle was wearing black trousers and a black t-shirt.
The court ordered Markle to submit to home detention at his assisted living facility in Florida and electronic monitoring.
No plea was taken during the hearing, and an arraignment date in California will be determined in due course, a joint statement from the DoJ and the US Attorney's Office Central California said.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have not commented on Markle's arrest.
FBI director Kash Patel said authorities "moved quickly" when arresting Markle.
"Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," Patel said.
He added that the FBI would "use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids â any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide".
Markle was arrested after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in LA registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year.
Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.
Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.
In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.
Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.
Markle Sr moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was then reportedly living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.
In October, London's Metropolitan Police confirmed that it had received a letter in 2019 making a "number of claims" relating to Markle Sr.
The Met said information contained in the letter, which related to allegations against Meghan's father outside the UK, was passed on to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, but it did not share it with other law enforcement agencies.
The force has since voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IPOC) over its handling of the letter.
In a statement released in October after the allegations against Markle Sr emerged, the Duchess of Sussex said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year.

Blue wave presages a defense-spending showdown
A reconciliation bill is likely off the table, and the presumed HASC chair is talking about a $1-trillion cap.
The Democrats' impending takeover of the House and the Senate will have sweeping effects on the Pentagon, from budgets to leadership to defense policy. The biggest near-term issue is the fate of the proposed reconciliation bill, which the Trump administration is counting on for $350 billion of its plans to spend $1.5 trillion on defense spending in fiscal 2027.
Even before the election, some Republican lawmakers doubted their ability to pass a bill through the reconciliation process, which is rarely used for defense funding. A lame-duck effort is unlikely to succeed, and January's seating of the new Democrat-controlled Congress is expected to kill the bill for good.
Defense spending
The administration pushed many top priorities into the unusual reconciliation bill, including:
• Munitions funding. The bill is a major conduit for money that would nearly double munitions spending to $76.3 billion to help rebuild stockpiles following several years of equipment transfers to Ukraine and a depletion of inventories during the war with Iran. It was meant to underwrite a production surge for air and missile defense munitions such as Patriot, THAAD, SM-3, and SM-6; plus strike weapons such as hypersonic missiles. Munitions funding is also included in a proposed Iran supplemental that faces resistance from Democrats who oppose the war.
• Golden Dome homeland missile defense system. The proposal includes $17 billion for a new Golden Dome for America Fund plus investment for related programs such as a Space-Based Air Moving Target Indicator capability and a revamped Space Data Network that would serve as the communications layer of the defense system.
• Unmanned systems. The bill includes nearly $54 billion for the Defense Autonomous Warfare Group.
• Aircraft: several F-35s and KC-130Js for the Air Force.
• Warships: The Medium Landing Ship and some investment in the Virginia-class submarine.
If the reconciliation bill is dead, lawmakers will have to decide whether to move any of those items into the defense appropriations bill.
The Pentagon’s $1.1 trillion base budget request—that's $242.4 billion, or 28 percent, over the FY26 defense appropriations bill enacted by Congress—will face more resistance. Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., who is expected to once again lead the House Armed Services Committee after two years as its ranking member, said this week that he wants to keep total defense spending to $1 trillion in fiscal 2027.
The administration proposed to offset the Pentagon increase with reductions in domestic non-defense discretionary spending. The guns-versus-butter debate will be reignited, and it is unclear whether base budgets will stay above $1 trillion.
Political headwinds
Several programs are likely to face increased scrutiny in the new Congress.
Golden Dome’s space-based interceptors are a likely target for Democratic opposition. The Pentagon initially selected a dozen companies to work on SBIs, including Anduril, General Dynamics, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, and SpaceX. SpaceX, which has received $6.5 billion for the Space-Based Air Moving Target Indicator and Space Data Network programs, could face new roadblocks.
Also at risk: the Navy’s Trump-class battleship, the signature component of the proposed Golden Fleet. This author has already raised concerns about the practicality and affordability of the battleship, and Democrats are likely to push back on the program’s rapid development and construction plans. The Navy has chose General Dynamics Bath Iron Works and Huntington Ingalls Industries to build the ships, which would use a distributed construction approach. Leidos’ Gibbs & Cox was tasked with supporting ship design and engineering. If this program falls through, the Navy may revisit plans for the DDG(X) destroyer, which had been shelved in favor of the battleship.
The next Congress will also push the administration to end the war with Iran, which continues to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Democrats have been unwilling to act on the Iran-war supplemental request without establishing guardrails or an exit strategy. At the same time, Democratic majorities in the House and Senate are more likely to push for greater support for Ukraine, which could include more money, faster arms transfers, and pressure on the White House to avoid actions that could harm Kyiv.
Areas of alignment
The new Democratic minority is expected to continue to fund replenishing munitions stockpiles depleted during operations against Iran, despite Democratic opposition to the war itself. Counter-unmanned aircraft systems investment will remain a priority, from low-cost munitions to directed energy. Congress, which has long supported Navy shipbuilding, can be expected to add money for it, even if lawmakers disagree about specific platforms. There will also be continued support for developing autonomous gear and the networks that support them.
More budget delays expected
Congress failed to pass most budget legislation before the 2027 fiscal year began on Oct. 1, and the government is currently operating under a continuing resolution through December 11. That's not enough time to finalize a full spending plan, so the lame-duck Congress will likely pass another CR that extends into the next calendar year. Under the new Congress, passage of a final spending bill could be hindered by negotiations over the status of the Iran war, topline spending levels, the debt ceiling, or other policy issues.
Lawmakers might also pass a long-term CR, covering several months or even the rest of fiscal year. These stopgap spending bills typically restrict new start programs and production rate increases. Although lawmakers can provide workarounds for these limitations, as they did in fiscal 2025, a long-term CR could put a hold on dozens of new program

0b937070ad8e.text: Between the GOP's thrashing at the polls, another one of President Trump 's planned D.C. construction makeovers being halted and an uphill battle to overturn his conviction on 34 felony counts, this week has netted a string of setbacks for the president. Why it matters: Trump's administration is entering its lame-duck era, facing criticism and potential investigations as its power to reshape the federal government dwindles . But Trump is showing little inclination to change course. Driving the news: Trump has remained defiant about the midterms, blaming the Iran war and the GOP's candidates for the losses while spending a lot of time discussing planned D.C. construction projects . On Friday, Trump announced he would replace White House chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller , a champion of his most hard-line policies. The move could signal that the president plans to push even harder on some of his unpopular policies, Axios' Marc Caputo and Andrew Pantazi write. Zoom in: Voters told Trump loud and clear they're dissatisfied with his policies, particularly on the Iran war, cost of living and economy. Roughly two-thirds of voters said Trump's agenda had fueled inflation, per the AP's Voter Poll. Trump admitted the unpopular war helped Republicans lose their majorities. With Democrats poised to control Congress and potentially restrict war funding, he has few good options for a decisive win. As one of his former advisers told Axios' Barak Ravid: "It's one thing to lose the midterms. But Trump doesn't want to look like a loser twice." What they're saying: "I don't think conciliatory is in [Trump's] vocabulary or ethos," Republican strategist Barrett Marson told Axios, calling Miller's appointment evidence that Trump won't "go away quietly." "He's taken the architect of many of the worst policies and elevating him. I'm not really sure how that is sort of acknowledging voters' discontent," Marson said. Marson said Trump's inability to run for president again could make him even less concerned about political consequences. He also noted that Trump has a massive war chest that he could wield to control GOP politicians as the 2028 election cycle begins. Republican strategist John Feehery , who spoke to Axios before Friday's chief of staff shake-up, said Trump could still cut deals with Democrats to cement his legacy, but acknowledged his influence over congressional Republicans could wane. "I don't think he's going to control the Republicans to the extent that he did, I think Republicans are going to try to figure out their own brand," Feehery said. Zoom out: The president's headaches also extend to his legal battles and ambitious construction projects. A New York appeals court heard arguments Thursday in Trump's bid to overturn his conviction on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records. His lawyers argued the conviction was tainted by legal errors and inadmissible evidence, but the court has yet to rule. In the wee hours of Friday, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a temporary restraining order barring construction on Trump's planned 250-foot Triumphal Arch for 14 days, just hours after the National Capital Planning Commission approved the project. The order was in response to a lawsuit brought by D.C. and Virginia and blocked construction, excavation, and road closures related to the arch. The project would tower over a road leading to Arlington National Cemetery and has drawn opposition from preservation groups, military veterans and families of people buried at the cemetery. The other side: "As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Axios in an emailed statement. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people." On the arch, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle blasted the judge's ruling, saying the administration was confident it would be "fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds." The bottom line: Trump is the political comeback king — and no one should expect him to roll over during his lame-duck season. Go deeper: Trump, under pressure, embraces Builder-in-Chief role

Please check your inbox to confirm. In her first term, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs had vetoed more than 540 measures passed by the Republican-led Legislature on policies including taxes, immigration and voting laws. Hobbs has said she's looking to address water issues and affordability, and take on fraud and abuse in the state's school voucher program. The Associated Press called enough legislative races to confirm that both chambers flipped on Friday. The news organization calls races individually and it can take several days after voting, depending on when election officials tally the votes and how close the elections are. Besides Arizona, those wins were in the battleground states of Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Wisconsin. READ MORE: Democrats win full control of more state governments and the Texas House The flips weren't just in states that are normally competitive. Democrats won control of the Texas House, which Republicans have held since 2003, and elected Gina Hinojosa as the state's first Democratic governor since George W. Bush ousted Ann Richards in 1994. Republicans held onto the state Senate. Democrats also flipped the lower chambers of the legislatures in Maine and North Carolina and both chambers in New Hampshire, where Republican Kelly Ayotte was reelected. The count could grow as results are tallied in additional states. The National Council of State Legislatures says it's likely to end up as the election with the most legislative seats and chambers changing parties since the 2010 election, when Republicans took over governments across the country amid the Great Recession. Democrats will also hold the governor's office in at least 28 states. Results are still pending in Alaska and Kansas. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy.
