There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests, on 5.
The electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Kipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests.
The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens â who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops â saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices â for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

65e9cbe23818.text: Stephen Miller is no Susie Wiles: He believes in almost limitless presidential power, considers the Democratic Party an extremist organization, and dreams of ruthless crackdowns on immigration and foreign adversaries. Why it matters: Miller, the new White House chief of staff, isn't just unlike anyone who's had the job under Trump — he's unlike any to occupy the powerful position in the modern era. He puts the hard in hard-liner and understands how to pull the levers of power to get his way and make the U.S. government a MAGA machine. Miller's appointment sets the stage for two years of partisan warfare with the new Democratic-led Congress, which is likely to launch investigations of Trump's administration, political committees and allies. "Stephen is Trump's wartime consigliere," Roger Stone, one of the president's oldest friends and advisers, told Axios. The big picture: Despite his post-midterm comments about finding ways to work with Democrats, Trump's choice of Miller signals that he's not looking for truces. He's prepping for war, and sees Miller as a brass-knuckle general and tactical expert impervious to criticism or traditional restraints. Trump's MAGA brain for a decade, the 41-year-old has detailed his Miller Doctrine in speeches, policies and press conferences: Presidential power is "very substantial and will not be questioned." Miller said those words about Trump's Muslim travel ban in 2017 on CBS's "Face the Nation," but to him they broadly apply to other areas of the executive's authority. Court authority is limited. In May 2025, when courts blocked aspects of Trump's deportation policies, Miller said the rulings were the work of "radical rogue judges" who were "at war" with the executive and legislative branches. The political opposition is a threat to America. "The Democrat Party is not a political party. It is a domestic extremist organization," Miller told Sean Hannity in August 2025. He also warned that if Democrats won Congress, "it's game over." They just won it. Homeland security is the nation's spine. A key architect of the administration's hard-line immigration policies, Miller said in a March speech: "Our national security, our homeland security, the safety and well-being of our people begins at home, begins in our neighborhood, begins in our home region." America should use "hard power" in the Western Hemisphere. "The cartels that operate in this hemisphere are the ISIS and the al-Qaeda of the Western Hemisphere, and should be treated just as brutally and just as ruthlessly as we treat those organizations," Miller said in the same speech, to foreign leaders at the Shield of the Americas conference. Behind the scenes: Miller's Shield of the Americas speech indicated the depth of his involvement in Trump's Latin America policy. He has a keen interest in Mexico and was a driving force in the military action leading up to and including the deposing of Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro. Miller has a close working relationship with Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio, and he has friendly relations with El Salvador leader Nayib Bukele, a crucial Trump ally in extending U.S. power. "Stephen makes Marco more aggressive on policy, in a good way. When Stephen isn't around, Marco defaults back to being more of the politician," said one White House official who worked with the two. "If people thought regime change in Cuba was going to fall by the wayside, Stephen Miller should make them think twice," the source said. "Today is a bad day for the Cuban regime." Go deeper: Trump advisers see Miller's elevation as a way to reenergize the president's populist base, which failed to turn out in sufficient numbers for the midterms — and in some cases voted for Democrats. Advisers point to Trump's handling of the Epstein files and his decision to attack Iran — which in turn escalated fuel prices — as reasons he lost support among those voters. Without winning them back, Republicans say, they'll have no chance in the 2028 elections. Critics also fault the harsh immigration enforcement championed by Miller, as well as voters' perceptions of corruption in Trump's administration, as additional drags on Republicans. Miller's allies dismiss questions about his management experience, noting that he has overseen the Department of Homeland Security and regularly runs morning meetings with the White House staff focused on immigration policy. They also point to the size of his White House policy team, one of the administration's largest. With Trump's legislative agenda effectively stalled, Miller's allies argue he is particularly well suited to a White House that will increasingly rely on executive orders and legal battles — areas in which Miller has extensive experience. Yes, but: Some critics worry that Miller's elevation could mean Trump turns Miller's hard-line immigration agenda into a centerpiece of his final two years in office — something that could continue to alienate independent and moderate voters, as it appeared to do in the midterms. Trump's administration and supporters expect the criticism and are unfazed. "It's Miller Time," said another Trump adviser. "Buckle up."

Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies.
Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest.
Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.
The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.
Zelensky wrote on Telegram, external that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".
Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow.
"The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said.
"In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."
In his latest update, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply system is back to operating normally. He also said around 60% of the city's apartment buildings were connected to the heating system.
The energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, said there were power cuts in five regions but did not say how many homes were affected.
Zelensky added that beyond Kyiv, substations were damaged in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions.
The latest attacks come after US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday.
She called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine following a truce last week in the southern region of Kherson.
She thanked both Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.
Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.
"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.
Earlier this week, a number of people were killed when glide bombs hit an aid centre near Zaporizhzhia, with the death toll rising to 55 as teams search deeper into the ruins.
Zelensky added in his Telegram post on Saturday following the latest attacks that Ukraine was counting on increased bilateral support from the United States.
He wrote: "We are counting on unity between both parties on issues of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin.
"The resolve and consistency of the United States in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer."
Meanwhile, Zelenksy's spokesperson would not be drawn on reports that the Ukrainian president is to be invited to the UK for a state visit next year.
Additional reporting by Daniel Wittenberg

The warming of Nepal’s mountains is dramatically transforming some of the grandest landscapes on Earth, leading melting glaciers to collapse, thawing permafrost that can slide from steep peaks and crumbling ice dams to release vast lakes. But other impacts are barely the length of a fingernail.
As the alpine cold recedes, disease-bearing mosquitoes are taking its place. Over the past decade, researchers have documented Aedes aegypti—the primary mosquito species responsible for transmitting the dengue virus—at elevations up to 2,500 meters (8,200 feet). Its expansion into Nepal’s mid-hill and high-altitude regions is driving a major shift in the geographic footprint of insect-borne diseases in the Himalayas.
“In Nepal, Dengue used to be the problem of lower altitude regions, mainly the disease of Terai (the lowlands of Nepal and India),” says Sunita Baral, a research associate at Nepal Health Research Council. “When we were younger we used to hear and even experience the mosquito bite in Terai and we used to ignore going there during the monsoon and post-monsoon. But after a few years, a dengue outbreak occurred in hilly regions like Kathmandu and mosquitoes began to appear here.”
According to a literature review published in January in the journal Clinical Infection in Practice, dengue transmission in Nepal has escalated over the past two decades from localized outbreaks to major nationwide epidemics.
First reported in the country in 2004, the virus caused major public health crises in 2019, 2022 and 2023. Transmission is no longer restricted to the lowland Terai region along the border with India; sustained outbreaks now occur routinely in densely-populated areas at higher elevations. Recent health data reported by local Nepalese media shows the virus has reached 76 out of the country’s 77 districts, with roughly 9,000 recorded infections and at least six deaths in 2025 alone.
“Climate change has a huge impact on geographical distribution and establishment of these vectors in a new area,” explained Ishan Gautam, an associate professor at Tribhuvan University in Kathmandu. “Years ago they were only found in the tropical regions, but they have migrated thousands of meters up to Kathmandu Valley.”
The expansion is driven by a combination of changing climatic patterns, population mobility and unplanned urbanization. Higher average minimum temperatures allow Aedes mosquitoes to survive and reproduce at altitudes that previously acted as natural thermal barriers.
At the same time, rapid urban growth in cities like Kathmandu has created severe water infrastructure challenges. Chronic shortages lead residents to store water in open drums, buckets and construction cisterns, providing optimal breeding conditions for both Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. Flash floods from unusually strong monsoons have overwhelmed municipal drainage systems and washed out water pipelines in cities like Kathmandu, leaving more standing water for breeding mosquitoes.
“They lay eggs in different types of building habitats, so as they disperse and continue to lay eggs in varying places, the population continues to increase,” Gautam continued. “Dengue vectors are rapidly increasing.”
Beyond climate conditions and urban density, specific biological characteristics of a given vector can accelerate the speed of disease transmission. According to Gautam, infected mosquitoes frequently bite seven to eight individuals before reaching repletion–the state of being fully engorged with a blood meal.
This high feeding frequency means a single infected vector can transmit the virus to multiple hosts within a short time frame, creating a transmission chain driven by a mix of biological compulsion and favorable climate conditions.
Despite these growing risks, public health response efforts are constrained by a widespread lack of community preparedness.
“Many of the communities who are at risk are not aware of dengue vectors and their likelihood of contracting dengue disease,” Gautam noted. “They don’t know about all of the potential breeding sites, so they aren’t able to eliminate them.”
The presence of multiple distinct strains of the virus circulating in Nepal further heightens the risk to public health. A secondary infection with a different strain significantly increases the likelihood of severe dengue, which can cause plasma leakage, severe bleeding and organ impairment.
Additionally, both Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus serve as vectors for other insect-borne diseases. Chikungunya is already documented in Nepal, and health officials warn that established vector populations create a serious risk for local Zika virus transmission.
“Due to the news of dengue outbreaks, communities are becoming more aware of dengue, but still they do not recognize mosquito breeding sites around their houses,” said Baral. “In newly affected mountain communities, dengue is still relatively unfamiliar, which can delay recognition and response.”
Because dengue-carrying mosquitoes bite during early morning and late afternoon hours, when most residents in the affected communities are awake and active, relying on bed nets while sleeping provides a false sense of security.
The implications extend beyond the emergence of individual diseases. Together, the presence of two competent vector species and multiple dengue serotypes suggests that Nepal’s mountain regions are becoming increasingly suitable for forms of transmission once associated primarily with warmer lowlands.
The warming trends unfolding in the Himalayas mirror shifts happening across tropical highlands globally, from the Colombian Andes to communities in Costa Rica’s central valley. Historically, these high-altitude regions were shielded from vector-borne illness because lower temperatures slowed mosquito development and virus transmission.

452e690ba866.text: Israeli President Isaac Herzog announced Saturday that he will task Gadi Eisenkot , leader of the opposition Yashar party, with forming a new government, dealing a major setback to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu . Why it matters: Eisenkot will have 28 days to establish a new government. This is the closest Netanyahu has been to losing power since 2021, but deep divisions could still prevent them from forming a government. Driving the news: Netanyahu's Likud party won the most seats in the Oct. 27 election, but his coalition lost its majority, winning just 53 of the 120 seats in parliament. Eisenkot's bloc won 48 seats, but the two Arab parties, which won 19 seats, backed his bid to form a government. During consultations held earlier this week, 67 members of the Knesset recommended Eisenkot to form the new government, while only 46 recommended Netanyahu. United Torah Judaism, an ultra-Orthodox ally of Netanyahu, declined to endorse him and signaled it could join an Eisenkot-led coalition. This is a breaking news story. Check back for updates

e7877f48abd2.text: By — Giovanna Dell'Orto, Associated Press Giovanna Dell'Orto, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/israels-president-taps-opposition-candidate-eisenkot-to-form-a-government-in-setback-for-netanyahu Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Israel's president taps opposition candidate Eisenkot to form a government, in setback for Netanyahu World Updated on Nov 7, 2026 3:45 PM EST — Published on Nov 7, 2026 3:39 PM EST JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli President Isaac Herzog said Saturday night that he was giving opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot the first opportunity to form a governing coalition following elections on Oct. 27. Eisenkot, a former military chief who ran as the main challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is now a step closer to ousting Israel's longest-serving premier. He has up to six weeks to form a coalition, a challenging task in a deeply divided country reeling from the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks and the three years of wars that have followed in Gaza and beyond. READ MORE: Israel's president takes first steps on building new government after accepting election results In discussions with the president this week, representatives from most of Israel's main parties recommended Eisenkot be tasked with assembling a new government, but putting together the parliamentary majority needed remains fraught. Netanyahu and his allies lost their majority in parliament in last month's elections. But the bloc led by Eisenkot also didn't win a majority. That left Arab-led parties, which made historic gains, as potential but politically fraught kingmakers. An Arab party has been part of a governing coalition just once in Israel's history. Forming such an alliance could be especially divisive for Eisenkot after more than three years of war in Gaza. Netanyahu has been on a campaign to head off any alliance between Eisenkot and the Arab-led parties, including unsubstantiated claims that Arab parties "stole" the elections. Shortly before Herzog's announcement, he called for a "national unity government" in a video statement and warned against "hastily swearing in a government with terrorist supporters" — language he uses to refer to the Arab-led parties. Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly portrayed the Arab-led parties as a threat to national security, while Eisenkot has indicated a willingness to partner with them under certain conditions, including calling Hamas a terrorist group that needs to be destroyed. Eisenkot and Netanyahu, whose Likud is the single largest party in parliament, could seek to create a broad unity government with major Jewish parties. However, the men have deep differences over many issues that will be difficult to bridge. That includes Netanyahu's reliance on religious parties that demand draft exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men, as well as Netanyahu's opposition to a formal investigation into the failures surrounding the Oct. 7 attacks. Eisenkot could also seek to create a "minority" government — shored up by external support from Arab parties that are not formal members of his coalition. However, other members of his bloc have said they would reject such an alliance. Eisenkot's party, Yashar, slammed the prime minister's video with a statement posted on X and urged members of his party, Likud, to disavow their alliance with "radical parties," in an apparent reference to the far-right parties in his religious-nationalist base. The statement argued that Eisenkot would only include parties and parliament members who support its principles. Associated Press writer Julia Frankel contributed from Jerusalem. At least six people have been killed and several others injured after a gunman suspected to have ties to the far-right opened fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland. Here's everything we know so far.
How did the attack unfold?
The attack began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's Main Market Square, the bustling central point of the city.
Police said a man drove into the square before beginning to fire "at random people from his car".
Footage from the scene shows scenes of panic as people fled, with the sound of gunfire clearly heard.
A passing tram was shot at during the apparently random attack, shattering windows but no passengers were injured.
Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the attacker, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.
The gunman was shot but is alive and has been arrested.
Distressing footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows the moment a police officer confronts the suspect on the ground before firing his weapon several times.
The officer then falls to the ground, apparently having been injured himself.
Shop windows in the square have signs of damage, seemingly from bullets, with glass shards scattered along the floor.
City officials have urged people who live in the city and tourists to stay away from the area while an investigation continues.
The suspect's car, found at the intersection of Dietla and Stradomska streets, is being checked for possible explosive devices, police say. Residents of nearby buildings are being evacuated while the operation is under way.
How many people have died and been injured?
Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed, including a foreign national.
Sixteen people, including five foreigners and the attacker, were taken to hospital. Among those being treated are two police officers who were shot while detaining the attacker.
One of the police officers was described as being in a "very critical condition" by a Polish government minister after being shot three times while arresting the attacker. The officer is undergoing surgery, he added.
Polish authorities have not confirmed the names and ages of the other victims.
What do we know about the suspect and motive?
Police have identified the attacker as a 25-year-old Polish man but have not confirmed his name.
The suspect was wearing "military-style attire" and had a military-grade weapon, according to a police spokesperson. However, authorities have confirmed the attacker was not a soldier.
"Many pieces of weapons and ammunition were found in his vehicle", the spokesperson added.
Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home.
A minister has said early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.
His home is being searched with support from counter-terrorism police.
How did witnesses describe the attack?
The shooting happened in one of the largest medieval squares in Europe, a busy location which is also a popular tourist destination.
Jonathan Balshaw from Ipswich was there with his Polish girlfriend Dominika. The couple were outside St Mary's Basilica, in the corner of the square, when the shooting started.
Jonathan said: "We ran down the side of the church and through the side door and hid with several other people until the gunfire died down.
"A lot of shots were fired, more than 20 with it sounding like multiple different firearms - there were two distinctly different noises."
Caitlin Shasby from Newcastle arrived in Krakow yesterday with her friend Jon for a long weekend.
She said they heard shots from their hotel room but were not sure what was happening until their hotel rang them and told them to "stay in our rooms until further notice".
What has the reaction been in Poland and internationally?
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk is on his way to Krakow and is expected to give an address later on Saturday.
Earlier, he said he was being kept informed by the interior minister and that police were investigating "the background and all the circumstances".
Krakow Mayor Åukasz GibaÅa has signed an order declaring a period of mourning in the city which will last until Wednesday, November 11.
President Karol Nawrocki said he was "deeply concerned" and was awaiting "a full explanation of the circumstances surrounding these tragic events".
US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose described it as a "savage and murderous attack".
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the shooting was "a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland".

US President Donald Trump has asked Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be White House press secretary, in a social media post.
"Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Dana, please take the job!"
It's unclear whether the president's public job offer is genuine. The BBC has asked the White House and TKO Holdings, the parent company of UFC, for comment.
The vacancy for White House press secretary has been open since mid-October, when Katie Zacharia exited after just a few days on the job.
Trump's post comes after his fellow Republicans were routed in the US midterm elections, losing their congressional majorities.
In Saturday afternoon's post, Trump called White "a violent Fighter and Warrior" and asked that he bring a number of high-profile UFC fighters with him on the job "even though some are not from our Country".
"We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," Trump wrote, alongside photos of the six fighters.
Following Trump's post, White posted an Instagram photo of himself behind the podium in the White House press briefing room.
"On to the next chapter," White's post said, though it was unclear if the post was tongue-in-cheek.
Famously combative, White has at times clashed with journalists covering the sport during news conferences.
In 2020, he released a video targeting reporters who had questioned the UFC's decision to hold fights early in the pandemic.
In 2009, he released an expletive-laden video tirade using an anti-gay slur while rebutting a journalist's story about changes to backstage credentialing rules at UFC events.
White is a longtime ally - and friend - of Trump.
When White and his business partners bought the then-struggling UFC organisation for $2m in 2001, the sport was facing intense bipartisan backlash.
Just five years earlier, Republican Senator John McCain had famously labelled mixed martial arts "human cockfighting", sparking bans in 36 US states.
"None of the venues wanted [the UFC]," White told CBS, the BBC's US partner, in 2025. "They didn't believe in it. They didn't like it, and they were worried about the type of crowd that would show up for this type of event."
With mainstream arenas shutting them out, White credits Trump with saving the organisation by hosting two UFC events at the Trump Taj Mahal casino in Atlantic City, New Jersey, in 2001.
This summer, the UFC held a cage match on the White House lawn.
White became a speaker for Trump's White House campaigns at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.

88070b1a304c.text: By — Darlene Superville, Associated Press Darlene Superville, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/melania-trump-and-lsu-announce-a-scholarship-program-for-students-who-were-in-foster-care Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Melania Trump and LSU announce a scholarship program for students who were in foster care Politics Updated on Nov 7, 2026 3:18 PM EST — Published on Nov 7, 2026 2:35 PM EST BATON ROUGE, La. (AP) — Melania Trump on Saturday announced a multimillion dollar partnership between Louisiana State University and her "Fostering the Future" program to provide scholarships for LSU students who came through the foster care system. "This achievement will give young people from foster care an anchor of stability, a strong educational foundation and a chance to build a wonderful life," she said at an event with LSU President Wade Rousse. There are 14 scholars under the program at LSU and nine at Alabama, she said, part of a group of 100 students supported across 26 schools this semester. The broader "Fostering the Future" initiative is an offshoot of the "Be Best" campaign that was her signature issue during President Donald Trump's first term. "At LSU, we believe talent is everywhere but we understand that opportunity is not," Rousse said. "That is why access is one of our highest priorities. Students who have experienced foster care have already demonstrated resilience, determination and potential. Our responsibility, our responsibility is to make sure circumstances beyond their control do not stand between them and a life-changing higher educational experience." The first lady started working on foster care issues after the Republican president's first term ended in 2021, and created "Fostering the Future" to provide resources and support, including scholarships. LSU is among more than 20 colleges and universities nationwide that participate in the program. Earlier this year, Melania Trump was on Capitol Hill to push Congress to pass a legislative package that would broaden access to services for young people in foster care by updating a decades-old program. The measures cleared the House and are pending in the Senate. WATCH: First lady Melania Trump announces new investment accounts for foster youth During the appearance, she told members of the House Ways and Means Committee that young people in foster care face barriers to housing, transportation and other challenges outside of the classroom that affect their performance in school along with their future financial independence. "We can close this gap," she said in April. "New legislation for the foster care community is a moral imperative." Last November, the first lady spearheaded an executive order signed by the president linking the federal government, colleges and universities, the private sector and charitable groups to create educational and employment opportunities for those in foster care. She also created "Fostering the Future Together," a global version of the program with more than 45 participating countries. Alabama and LSU, meanwhile, are historical regional rivals and both teams entered the week in contention for a College Football Playoff berth. Thousands of people, many of them tailgating before the game, filmed the first lady's motorcade as it drove through campus. Donald Trump has attended two prior LSU games as president: one at Alabama in 2019 and one in New Orleans in January 2020, when LSU defeated Clemson for the national championship. Melania Trump accompanied him to the second game. The president was not scheduled to attend Saturday's game. AP Sports Writer Brett Martel in Baton Rouge, La., contributed to this report. d7987518bc58.text: By — Gary Fields, Associated Press Gary Fields, Associated Press By — Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-wants-former-u-s-attorney-to-investigate-whether-the-government-misled-her-in-trump-golf-case Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge wants former U.S. attorney to investigate whether the government misled her in Trump golf case Politics Nov 7, 2026 1:34 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge said Saturday she intends to appoint an ex-top federal prosecutor in the nation's capital during President Donald Trump's first term to investigate whether she was purposefully misled by lawyers and administration officials in a lawsuit challenging one of his prized Washington construction projects, the renovation of a historic public golf course along the Potomac River. Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, would examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Department of Justice violated ethics or misled U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes during the course of the case that was initiated in February by the DC Preservation League and two golfers. The Republican administration plans to close the East Potomac Golf Course and park on Nov. 15 with the intention of constructing a "World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events." An injunction issued by Reyes last month temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the course and the administration must give 10 days' notice in writing before making any "irreparable modification" to any "forms or features" of the course while the lawsuit is active. Reyes is giving each side a chance to be heard on her plan to name Liu as special master in the case. They must do so in writing by Friday, when the next court hearing in the dispute is scheduled. READ MORE: Trump's Washington projects are a likely casualty as Democrats claim Congress Reyes, who was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden, wants to know whether federal officials lied about the extent of renovation plans during months of hearings. She also wants to know if they were truthful about various steps they took, including cutting hundreds of trees early last month. She announced during a hearing Oct. 30 that she was starting a formal investigation of the government's conduct. Earlier in the case, she had rejected numerous motions from the plaintiffs to step in, saying she trusted the government attorneys. As the city's chief federal prosecutor, Liu oversaw some of the matters referred to her office by then-special counsel Robert Mueller during his investigation into possible ties between Trump's 2016 campaign and Russia. Trump later nominated her to be associate attorney general, the third-highest ranking Justice Department job. Liu withdrew from consideration after running into opposition on the Republican-led Senate Judiciary Committee because of her past membership in a lawyers' group that has supported abortion rights. She eventually resigned from the group because, she said previously, it took left-leaning positions, and she is now part of her own law firm, Liu Shur Kravis LLP. Super said it also is a reflection "of the difficulty she had in determining who initiated the tree-cutting in defiance of the assurances DOJ provided. She doesn't have the time to keep holding long, complex hearings and so wants a special master to narrow the issues." Reyes ordered the Oct. 30 hearing after multiple Truth Social posts by Trump indicated there were plans for the golf course and construction was expected to begin Nov. 15. Trump said the park would be closed for 15 months while work goes on. The presidential posts, which began Oct. 18, created a tense dynamic in multiple court hearings afterward when administration officials could not confirm the existence of the plans under questioning from Reyes. She eventually asked whom she should trust. The Justice Department filed notice Oct. 28 that the plans were real. Bedayn reported from Austin, Texas. The US has announced a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear programme.
The State Department's Rewards for Justice is also offering to potentially relocate the person who provides such details.
President Donald Trump claimed last year that Iran's nuclear facilities had been "completely and totally obliterated" following a bombing campaign by the US and Israel.
Iran insists its nuclear programme is peaceful and that it has no intention of developing a nuclear weapon.
Meanwhile, the US military says it is setting up a task force to enhance Washington's efforts to restrict Iran's movement of weapons and sanctioned material across its borders.
The US military's Central Command (Centcom) said Task Force Iron Gate would operate from Tampa, Florida, and would work with other US government agencies.
As well as the movement of weapons, it will also focus on dual-use and illegal revenue streams.
Centcom estimates that its naval blockade of Iran's ports has prevented the country from exporting more than $25bn in crude oil.
A US State Department statement about its multi-million dollar reward said it was offering the money for information about the Iranian programme, including "facilities, equipment and associated personnel".
It said Iran's "lack of compliance with the IAEA [the International Atomic Energy Agency] on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like [nuclear] centrifuges".
Centrifuges are needed to produce enriched uranium, which can be used to make reactor fuel for civilian use but also for nuclear weapons if enriched to around 90% purity or higher.
There had been mounting speculation that the US might resume significant strikes in Iran after the midterm elections, though Trump told reporters, prior to the polls, that he was in "no rush" to do so.
In an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms, the president also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme.
This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump said.
The president has repeatedly threatened to bomb the suspected underground site on previous occasions.
However, both Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have said public opposition to the war on Iran fuelled heavy losses for their Republican Party in this week's midterm elections, which has led to speculation the White House may no longer seek an escalation in the conflict.
On Friday, Trump insisted that Iran was keen to end the eight-month conflict with the US, stressing the damage to Tehran's economy and military.
"We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," he said.
Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said on Tuesday that both sides were "reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented" and that it remained hopeful of a deal being agreed.
Iranian negotiators had discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

e087d4bd9030.text: By — Isabel DeBre, Associated Press Isabel DeBre, Associated Press By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/with-an-ode-to-mate-pope-leo-urges-faithful-in-uruguay-to-build-bridges-of-fraternity-and-faith Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter With an ode to mate, Pope Leo urges faithful in Uruguay to build bridges of fraternity and faith World Nov 7, 2026 1:14 PM EST PAYSANDÚ, Uruguay (AP) — Pope Leo XIV urged an estimated 40,000 people in Uruguay on Saturday to build bridges of fraternity and faith, using his first Mass in South America to deliver an ode to the region's beloved mate tea and raise the profile of the Catholic Church in its most secular country. The crowd erupted in the stadium chant of "Olé, olé, olé, olé, pope, pope!" when Leo's plane landed in Paysandú, in western Uruguay on the border with Argentina. They cheered again, blew horns and waved yellow handkerchiefs when he arrived in his open-sided popemobile at the Mass site in Parque París Londres, a sprawling green space on the southern edge of the city. In his homily, Leo reminded them that the Catholic faith had been "part of the life of the Uruguayan people since their earliest days, and it must be passed on to future generations with creative courage!" READ MORE: What to know about Pope Leo XIV's trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru More than 30,000 people — many from Uruguay but also from neighboring Argentina and Brazil — had registered in advance to attend the service, around 375 kilometers (230 miles) from the capital, Montevideo. The Vatican said Saturday that another 10,000 had attended, despite the morning rain and blustery, gray skies. Because of its accessible location on the Uruguay River, the city was chosen to host Leo's first Mass at the start of his three-nation South American tour that was in doubt after he underwent lung cancer surgery on Oct. 13. "He's the representative of Christ but he's human. And we weren't sure if he could make it, but he pushed through for us," said Soledad Sánchez, 73, who had driven to Paysandú from northern Uruguay, her eyes filling with tears. "He made it here to give us a message of peace because he knows our world needs it right now." A visit to try to propose the Catholic faith Leo, who arrived in Uruguay on Friday, is urging the people in South America's most secular country of 3.5 million to turn to the Catholic faith for strength in confronting today's problems and challenges. In his homily, Leo asked the faithful to build bridges of fraternity, recalling the nearby bridge over the Uruguay River that connects Uruguay and Argentina and over which many pilgrims crossed to attend the Mass. He also pointed to the ritual of drinking mate, the bitter herbal tea that Uruguayans and their neighbors carry everywhere, as a poignant symbol of unity and encounter that he suggested should be applied to spreading the faith. Mate, a cherished national symbol in Paraguay, Argentina and Uruguay, is above all a sharing ritual. The leaves are steeped in a hollowed gourd and the drink is sipped through a metal straw called a bombilla, and the gourd passes from hand to hand among friends, family and sometimes strangers, refilled for hours. READ MORE: Pope Leo XIV welcomes Bob Dylan to the Vatican in a brief visit Everyone drinks from the same straw, and Uruguayans drink more mate per person than people anyone else, roughly 9 kilograms (about 20 pounds) of the dried leaf a year, according to industry estimates. "We must reflect on these symbols that we share, which give us identity and a sense of belonging, which speak to us of our origins and point us toward the future," Leo said. The message landed. "I'm not religious. I'd never go to Mass if it weren't the pope, but he surprised me. He made it appealing, the way he talked about things we all have in common, like mate," said Jorge Monzón, 64, from Paysandú. "I personally felt a sense of communion." Leo was to press the message of the church's commitment to helping Uruguayans later Saturday by touring a Montevideo neighborhood beset by drug trafficking and gang violence. The church is working in the area with municipal authorities to build housing and provide rehab programs for addicts. His final event Saturday was likely to drive home the call to reject religious indifference and embrace the faith: a prayer vigil in Montevideo's Centenary Stadium. Argentines flock to see Leo across the border Located in western Uruguay and just across a bridge from the eastern Argentine city of Colón, Paysandú was easier to reach for many Argentines than any of the stops on Leo's tour in Argentina, his next stop after Uruguay. In Argentina, Leo will visit Buenos Aires, Luján and Córdoba before heading to Peru, his second homeland and the final destination of his tour. "Argentina is a much more religious country than Uruguay, and there's this desire to be here to witness something historic," said Luciana Lobato, 20, an Argentine tour agent who organized buses for 180 pilgrims from across the border. Some young Catholics involved in local church groups hoped the sight of a pope drawing crowds would challenge Uruguay's image as a country indifferent to religion. "The reality I see in my town is that there are tons of young people who are really interested in religion, who are trying to find meaning and community in difficult moments," said Teresa Sabellini, 18, from Paysandú. "And now look around here. This place is full of people," she added. READ MORE: Leo XIV has become the first pope in history to vote in a U.S. general election Leo's mention of bridges in his homily resonated with Laiana Córdoba, who drove 20 hours and crossed the border from Cascavel, in southern Brazil, to hear it. "It's something we understand, being neighbors means more than just sharing a border. It means finding ways to connect, opening paths to each othe

Gaza wedding festival sees 250 couples married at the same time
Amid the ruins of destroyed buildings and displaced people's tents, Gazans gathered to celebrate a mass wedding for Palestinian brides and grooms.
The ceremony, organised by the UAE's humanitarian mission Operation Gallant Knight 3, brought together brides and grooms from across Gaza for a celebration of what organisers described as love and new beginnings in the besieged enclave.
A ceasefire came into force in Gaza in October last year, but Israeli air strikes have continued almost every day.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Israel responded by launching a military campaign against Hamas in Gaza, during which more than 74,640 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry.

(AP) — Democrat Scott Colom hasn't won Mississippi's U.S. Senate race, but the local prosecutor was welcomed as a historic figure Friday as he strolled through the Farish Street business district where civil rights leaders once organized. "It's so wonderful! It's so wonderful to have Scott Colom as our representative," said Maati Jone Primm, who owns Marshall's Music & Bookstore in Jackson. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The state is still tallying ballots that could make Colom the first Black senator from this Deep South state since post-Civil War Reconstruction. The possibility of Colom defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith puts many Black voters somewhere between cautious optimism and outright celebration in a state where nearly 40% of the population is Black but the top representation for generations has been white. "I'm so glad we are at the point where we are," said Sorie Tarawally, a 76-year-old attorney who has long known Colom's father. He called the 43-year-old candidate "the man, our messiah, our savior." The contest remains too early for The Associated Press to call, and Colom's historic bid will hinge on a tedious process playing out in elections offices across Mississippi's 82 counties. Local officials are receiving and examining absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots, before deadlines next week. Volunteers and lawyers representing each campaign look on in anticipation of potential litigation. Live Results: Mississippi Senate midterm election "We're going to make sure everything is followed according to the law, and I have confidence in those local officials," Colom said. "They're doing their jobs. Got to be patient with them." Colom said ballots tallied since Tuesday's election lean in his favor, and he chided Hyde-Smith for not explaining her strategy going forward. "She's still our senator. Where is she? Why is she not doing any interviews?" Colom asked. "Why can't she explain what her pathway to success is?" Hyde-Smith has not appeared publicly since election night, when she essentially declared victory despite a razor-thin margin with ballots still uncounted. "We are not backing down," she posted Friday on social media. "This election is not over. Our team is working across Mississippi to monitor the remaining ballots and protect the integrity of the process. We will see this through to the very end!" The precise number of outstanding ballots is not known The pool of outstanding ballots includes absentee ballots, which can be counted in Mississippi as long as they are received by Tuesday, five business days after the election. The rest are affidavit ballots, which are cast at the polls when there's a glitch: Perhaps the person's name was not on the rolls or the person did not have proper identification, or a poll worker determined the person's identification did not precisely match the name on the list. Citizens who had identification issues have until Tuesday to address those matters in person at their local elections office. For people who were not on a precinct's rolls, local officials can verify a person's status using previous records and information on the affidavit that person filed when filling out a ballot. That person typically has no responsibility to come to a local elections office; ballot status can be found on the Mississippi secretary of state's office website. Counties have until Friday to certify complete results to the secretary of state. Mississippi law has no provision for a statewide recount. Campaigns could seek court orders, usually county by county, seeking to examine ballots. The seismic effect would be in Mississippi, not Washington Democrats already have won control of the Senate, so the result in Mississippi would not change the balance of power in Washington. But it would mark a seismic shift in the state, where white conservatives have dominated the Statehouse and congressional delegation for nearly 150 years. Through Jim Crow segregation and the Civil Rights era, those leaders were nearly all Democrats. After the Civil Rights Movement, they overwhelmingly shifted to Republicans. For Black Mississippians, the result was the same: a lack of proportional representation at the top levels of state government and in Washington. Colom was initially viewed as a long shot, and it wasn't until late October that Senate Democrats' top campaign group started spending on advertising to support him. But the midterms revealed a broad backlash against redistricting efforts in the South that were aimed at boosting Republicans and, by extension, reducing Black representation. Primm's bookstore, where Colom visited on Friday, opened in the 1930s and is recognized as the oldest Black-owned bookstore in the U.S. She said the Farish Street neighborhood still represents Black Mississippians' "first migration, from the plantation to the city." Having Colom there as a potential senator "makes us so proud, and it gives us someone to aspire to. Our youth need to see the possibilities for their lives, and we do when we see our next senator from Mississippi." READ MORE: The election brought a wave of historic firsts. Here are some groundbreaking winners As he campaigned, Colom emphasized that he can represent all Mississippians, and he said President Donald Trump's policies — the war with Iran and tariffs, especially — cut across all demographic lines. "We have millions of people coming in from different cultures and different ways of living and different belief systems." Miller also warned that "a generation from now," people "will not know the country that they are living in. These consequences are permanent. Unless there's massive large-scale deportations by the millions, it will be irrevocable." He called a Minneapolis man killed by ICE a 'domestic terrorist' After federal agents shot and killed Alex Pretti during protests against the Trump administration's hardline immigration policies in January, Miller posted on social media that the 37-year-old Minneapolis resident was a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin" who had "tried to murder federal agents." Later, Miller said in a statement that the federal officers in Minneapolis "may not have been following" protocol. America 'created' Venezuela's oil industry and Greenland 'obviously' should be part of the US In January, after a daring U.S. military operation captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, Miller used a lengthy post on X to decry "reverse colonization" in which he suggested that Western nations were sacrificing too much for the developing world and that such a practice "has been a long self-punishment of the places and peoples that built the modern world." Its tyrannical expropriation was the largest recorded theft of American wealth and property. These pillaged assets were then used to fund terrorism and flood our streets with killers, mercenaries and drugs." He defended Trump's assertion that the U.S. was now running Venezuela, by telling CNN's Jake Tapper: "You can talk all you want about international niceties and everything else. But we live in a world, in the real world, Jake, that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power. These are the iron laws of the world." In the same interview, Miller also argued that the U.S. could seize Greenland by military force from NATO ally Denmark. "Obviously, Greenland should be part of the United States," he said. "Nobody's going to fight the United States militarily over the future of Greenland," Miller said. Speeding up deportations by suspending habeas corpus In May of 2025, Miller suggested that the Trump administration was looking for ways to expand its power to deport migrants who are in the United States illegally. "So, I would say that's an option we're actively looking at," Miller said. "Look, a lot of it depends on whether the courts do the right thing or not." Family separation: 'No one is exempt from immigration law' During Trump's first term, Miller championed a strict immigration deterrence policy that previous administrations had been hesitant to adopt: family separation. It called for routinely having federal agents separate children from their parents if families were apprehended illegally crossing the border. Miller defended the policy to The New York Times in 2018, saying it "was a simple decision by the administration to have a zero tolerance policy for illegal entry, period." ed27f6d8a335.text: By — Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press By — Stefanie Dazio, Associated Press Stefanie Dazio, Associated Press By — Beata Zawrzel, Associated Press Beata Zawrzel, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/gunman-opens-fire-in-polish-city-of-krakow-killing-6-people-and-injuring-15 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Gunman opens fire in Polish city of Krakow, killing 6 people and wounding 16 World Updated on Nov 7, 2026 3:22 PM EST — Published on Nov 7, 2026 12:21 PM EST KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — Six people were killed and 16 wounded after a gunman opened fire Saturday afternoon in a busy market square in Krakow, authorities said, in what Poland 's defense minister called an "act of terror" on the people of the city. The suspect, a 25-year-old Polish citizen, opened fire with an automatic weapon in the city's Main Square, a major tourist destination. He was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held "very radical" and "ultra-nationalistic" views, Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said at a news conference. WATCH: Ukrainian refugees face growing hostility in Poland Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called Saturday's fatal shooting an "act of terror" on the people of Krakow, Poland's second-largest city, which receives 15 million visitors a year, most of them passing through the Main Square. Four women and two men were killed. Two police officers were wounded, one seriously, Kierwiński said. Thirteen of the 16 people injured were brought to the hospital with serious injuries, and one of them was a foreign citizen. It was not immediately clear how many of the victims had suffered gunshot wounds, though two people had already been released from medical treatment within hours of the attack. People were wounded at several locations The perpetrator was shot and wounded during a gunfight with officers a short distance away from the initial violence, police said. He was taken to the hospital for surgery. Katarzyna Cisło, a spokesperson for the Krakow police, said the perpetrator was wearing military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest and used a military-type long gun in the attack. Police found many other weapons, as well as ammunition, in his car. He kept firing at the police even after being shot himself, she said. The attacker engaged in a "wild ride" around the Main Square, Cisło said, which is why people were wounded at several locations. Police vehicles block a street at the site of a shooting near the main market square of Krakow, Poland, on Nov. 7, 2026. Photo by Jakub Porzycki/Reuters Cisło added that the gunman acted alone and that the public is safe. Krakow mayor Łukasz Gibała said the city will be in official mourning until Wednesday. He vowed that Krakow will remain open to visitors despite the tragedy. "The square will belong to us again," Gibała said in a video posted to X. Mass shootings are rare in Poland Videos posted on social media by witnesses show people running away from the square to take cover on small streets nearby, as well as first responders trying to resuscitate victims. In one of the videos, a policeman is seen repeatedly shooting the attacker, who is lying on the street, only to later slowly collapse himself to the ground. Photos showed a Polish Medical Air Rescue helicopter after it landed in the square. It was not immediately clear whether the firearm used in Saturday's attack, or the guns found in the perpetrator's car, were legal. Around 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million, and interest in gun ownership has been rising. Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, in a post on X, praised the police officers who responded to Saturday's tragedy. Polish President Karol Nawrocki said his thoughts were with the victims, the wounded and their families. READ MORE: Poland says it thwarted Russian plot to kill an American citizen in a NATO country A tram driver reported around 3 p.m. that his vehicle was shot at from a man in a moving car while passing nearby the main square, the Krakow municipal transport company said. The window to the tram driver's cabin was shattered. Animal rights group OTOZ Animals said the attacker also shot two horses. Both animals are alive, but one was grazed by a bullet and the other hit in the leg. White carriages drawn by horses are a main tourist attraction in the square. Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski announced increased security measures, including road barriers, along main streets in the old town in the Polish capital in the aftermath of the Krakow attack. The number of people wounded rose from 15 to 16, officials said late on Saturday. Authorities earlier said the gunman was 24 years old, but later corrected his age to 25. Ciobanu reported from Warsaw, Poland and Dazio reported from Berlin. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 7072e2d52289.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/paraguays-ousted-president-faces-prosecutors-after-his-removal-over-bank-collapse Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Paraguay's ousted president faces prosecutors after his removal over bank collapse World Updated on Nov 7, 2026 1:44 PM EST — Published on Nov 7, 2026 12:10 PM EST Paraguay's former president was taken to the attorney general's office for questioning Saturday, just hours after being ousted by Congress over the collapse of a major bank. The Central Bank said it was working to compensate hundreds of thousands of people who were locked out of their accounts this week. READ MORE: Paraguay prosecutor will seek charges against embattled president after bank collapse Drone footage taken by Paraguay's Telefuturo showed ousted President Santiago Peña arriving at the attorney general's compound in a black SUV, escorted by police officers. He wore navy blue pants and a white shirt and was not handcuffed. Paraguayan prosecutors on Friday ordered the arrest of Peña and former Central Bank chief Carlos Carvallo as part of a criminal investigation into alleged breach of trust and other offenses tied to the collapse of Ueno Bank. Peña was transferred to a military base late Friday as hundreds of protesters gathered outside his home. The arrest order was issued soon after the Senate removed Peña from office in a unanimous vote. The vote came just three days after regulators seized Ueno Bank, freezing nearly 3 million customers' access to their savings and triggering a political crisis. Peña was replaced by Vice President Pedro Alliana, who began naming a new Cabinet Saturday. The Central Bank said Saturday that 1.2 million Ueno customers had received partial or full reimbursement of their insured deposits under Paraguayan law. Lawmakers accused Peña of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending. Peña has denied wrongdoing. People protest on the street near Congress, following former President Santiago Peña's removal from office in an impeachment trial that found him guilty of poor performance over his links to the collapse of digital lender Ueno, in Asuncion, Paraguay, on Nov. 6, 2026. Photo by Cesar Olmedo/Reuters The removal of U.S. President Donald Trump's ally marks the biggest political crisis in Paraguay in over a decade. The landlocked country of 6 million people returned to democratic rule in 1989. Since then, it has mostly been governed by the conservative Colorado Party. Peña submitted his resignation Thursday, but Congress did not accept it and pressed ahead with an impeachment trial. Opposition lawmakers insisted on his removal to prevent him from leaving office with immunity. "He must go, but not home. He must go to a maximum-security prison," opposition Sen. Yolanda Paredes told reporters. "The public is fed up with impunity." In a farewell message released shortly before he was ousted Friday, Peña expressed hope his departure would spare Paraguay further harm. "I do not want my presence to be a cause of greater division or instability," he wrote. "My responsibility is to put the country above my personal fate." Public outrage has intensified by the day. Thousands of protesters demanding access to their frozen savings and accountability for Ueno's failure have clashed with police firing rubber bullets and pepper spray this week. Paraguay's largest teachers' union, which has more than 40,000 members, plans to begin an indefinite national strike Monday to press for protection of public pension funds. Media linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen say that at least 25 people, including women and children, have been killed in airstrikes by Saudi Arabia.
There has been no comment from the Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government in Yemen.
Live video footage on Al Masirah - a television station run by the Houthis - has shown rescuers pulling bodies out of the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.
The bodies of young children can be seen among those dug out from the ruins.
The television station has also shown a number of injured people being carried on stretchers to hospital.
Saba news agency, which is also run by the Houthis, said the attack was carried out by Saudi Arabia.
The Saudis have led a coalition that has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.
The war in Yemen had been dormant for several years but reignited as a result of the Iran war.
A truce began to fall apart when Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Sanaa - which is controlled by the Houthis - to prevent an Iranian plan landing there.
The Tehran-backed Houthis subsequently targeted Abha airport in Saudi Arabia, then began hitting Saudi ships that have been using the Red Sea off the coast of Yemen as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz.
Major fighting has since resumed in Yemen between the Houthis and forces fighting for the Saudi-backed government of Yemen.
On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province, which has been the focus of much of the recent fighting, is reported to have killed 30 people.
The Houthis accused the Saudis of carrying out the strike, while government forces accused the Houthis of having fired a missile at the site.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.
The Saudis have regularly bombed Houthi positions, while the group has fired multiple missiles at targets inside Saudi Arabia, including airports and oil facilities.
Hours before the strike that hit al-Shariyah, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a missile heading towards Riyadh.
A Houthi leader, Mahdi al-Mashat, has vowed that the group will take revenge for the latest attacks in Yemen.

5acd7f3196f4.text: By — Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/justice-department-drops-bid-to-force-california-to-set-aside-disputed-ballots Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Justice Department drops bid to force California to set aside disputed ballots Politics Nov 7, 2026 11:50 AM EST LOS ANGELES (AP) — The U.S. Department of Justice on Friday requested to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots it alleged went to noncitizens until their immigration statuses could be verified. The move comes days after Republicans' significant losses in the midterm elections and about a week before a scheduled hearing where a special master was slated to evaluate the accuracy of the list of alleged noncitizens. California officials have previously said the list is out of date and includes legitimate voters — a sentiment that the federal judge presiding over the case echoed in his blistering order denying the federal government's request. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The case was at the forefront of President Donald Trump's administration's effort to assert control over state-run elections across the country, which Trump has said are rife with noncitizen votin g without providing evidence. Available data indicates occurrences are exceedingly rare. The Justice Department remains enmeshed in litigation with multiple immigrant and voting rights groups seeking to limit its use of the list of what it says are suspected noncitizens. It said in a statement Friday evening that it would continue to prosecute and litigate suspected violations of election law through other legal cases. READ MORE: Trump administration appeals to Supreme Court to sideline 20,000 disputed California mail ballots The department also filed a motion in support of a separate lawsuit filed in May that alleges that California violates national voting laws by failing to sufficiently remove ineligible voters from its rolls. The intervention is part of a broader effort to continue to "pursue every available civil and criminal remedy to ensure that only eligible American citizens vote in American elections," top Los Angeles prosecutor Bill Essayli said. California had processed roughly 9 million ballots as of early Friday, with nearly 5 million still left to be counted, according to state election officials. The motion to dismiss the lawsuit said that, by the time of the upcoming hearing, the state will have already irreparably "commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones." "The relief the United States sought and needed is no longer available—rendering voluntary dismissal necessary," the motion said. The lawsuit was filed in mid-October, when ballots had been sent to all of the state's 23 million registered voters, and after hundreds of thousands of ballots were already processed. Once a ballot is processed, it is completely anonymized. READ MORE: Analysis: More than 40% of names on DOJ list of alleged noncitizens not on California's voter rolls Justice Department spokesperson Kiersten Pels on Friday doubled down on earlier accusations that "California chose to protect illegal voters and thus refused to cooperate" with the federal request to set aside ballots, and said that "thousands of likely noncitizens remain on California's voter rolls and voted in the 2026 elections." California prosecutors in recent weeks have arrested over 30 noncitizens who are accused of illegally registering to vote. Some who were arrested were also accused of voting in previous elections. U.S. District Judge David O. Carter appointed the special master in late October, shortly after allowing California to proceed with elections as planned. Carter, who was appointed by former President Bill Clinton, argued in his order that separating ballots at such a late stage would risk disenfranchising citizens and warned it would "wreak havoc" on the midterm elections. The special master would have also considered whether or not California election officials did in fact have a mechanism for separating the ballots. Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani says he has been targeted by "cyber-criminals" who published his personal data online because of his country's support for Ukraine.
"For days now, cyber-criminals have been publishing my personal data on the dark web and seeking further information, effectively exposing me to new threats and intimidation," Tajani wrote on X.
He did not specify the nature of the threats, but said the hackers were also targeting his family.
The dark web is a hidden part of the internet that is not indexed by common search engines and can only be accessed with specialist software.
"Our position on Ukraine is the political reason I have been targeted," Tajani said.
"Defending the freedom of a sovereign state, taking a clear stand in support of a nation's democracy and independence, is dangerous in the eyes of these criminal entities."
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni blamed the incident on pro-Russian hackers and offered Tajani her "full solidarity".
"The sale of confidential information about institutional representatives is a cause of serious concern and must be tackled with the utmost determination," she said in a statement.
Moscow has not publicly responded to the allegations.
Meloni also expressed concern about "circulation of false images" which she said were shared by members of Italy's opposition. She did not give details about the content of the images.
The Italian government has provided humanitarian and military support to Ukraine in its war against Russia.
Tajani, who is also the deputy prime minister, said the government was taking the threats seriously.
