The lawmaker in pole position to lead the US House of Representatives after Democrats take control of Congress in January has said he is "a hard yes" for impeaching Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.
New York congressman Hakeem Jeffries told ABC programme This Week that Hegseth had "abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran".
Outgoing Republican congressman Thomas Massie, a foe of President Donald Trump, has said he plans to introduce a resolution to impeach Hegseth as early as Monday. The BBC asked the Pentagon for comment.
Congress returns to session this week after the Democrats' midterm elections landslide.
Massie's resolution contains eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, including accusing him of violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973 for America's role in the war with Iran.
"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," Jeffries told ABC on Sunday.
"Pete Hegseth has got to go," he continued.
Jeffries, who is favourite to be next House Speaker, the most powerful member in the lower chamber of Congress, has vowed that the newly empowered Democrats will serve as a check and balance on the Trump administration.
But he said after the midterms results that House Democrats were not currently focused on impeaching President Trump.

08428c515246.text: By — Amanda Becker, The 19th Amanda Becker, The 19th Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/the-midterms-energized-a-powerful-political-constituency-abuse-survivors Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter The midterms energized a powerful political constituency: abuse survivors Politics Nov 8, 2026 1:41 PM EST This story was originally published by The 19th. When Leanna Rocheleau saw the ad that Ohio gubernatorial hopeful Vivek Ramaswamy created, weaponizing his opponent Dr. Amy Acton's childhood sexual abuse, the Columbus-area mother and small business owner felt "triggered." Rocheleau, like nearly half of all U.S. women, is a survivor of sexual violence, and the ad hit at a gut level. In it, Acton's long-estranged mother suggested her daughter had lied about the well-documented abuse and neglect that Acton had discussed during her campaign. Court records confirmed Acton's account. Ramaswamy spent $4 million airing the ad anyway. Then Acton, a Democrat, won by 8 points in a state where her party hasn't been elected to the governor's mansion in nearly 20 years. WATCH: Democratic and GOP strategists on the deeply personal attack ad in Ohio "I was disturbed by the ad — but also fueled to jump back into the fight," said Rocheleau, who has become an activist at the Ohio Statehouse pushing for legislation to protect survivors. "Being able to have a woman survivor as governor of Ohio? I have high hopes that we're going to be able to move some of this legislation into law," she added. Rocheleau has been in the fight for about five years now, since her own sexual assault by a massage therapist and the series of obstacles she confronted as she sought justice. She reported the alleged assault to the owners of the facility where it occurred — nothing happened. She went to the local police department — it took them a year to take her official report. A prosecutor told her they would not bring charges due to lack of evidence. She went to the state medical board. Attorneys advised her to wait for the medical board's findings to bring a civil lawsuit. By the time the board's investigation concluded, the statute of limitations had run out. The massage therapist received a six-month suspension after the board's investigation. "I needed somewhere to put that energy and anger, so I started talking to [state] legislators about changing all of the barriers that I faced," she said. Rocheleau started talking about her assault during Statehouse hearings and in meetings with lawmakers, urging them to pass legislation protecting survivors. Along the way, she met Chris Graham, a survivor of childhood sexual abuse who has become a well-known advocate in the halls of the Ohio Capitol, organizing fellow survivors and coaching them on how to engage in citizen advocacy. READ MORE: After a flurry of ethics cases, sexual harassment rules for Congress are under review Graham and Rocheleau are part of a growing movement of survivors of sexual abuse and gender-based violence who are showing up at statehouses, lobbying the U.S. Congress and coming forward to share their experiences with political candidates — and they're getting results. Sheerine Alemzadeh, the founder of Healing to Action, a grassroots organization focused on ending gender-based violence through survivor leadership, said she thinks of the movement as "a political constituency." She has a book on the subject out next month. In Ohio, Ramaswamy's ad was seen largely as a desperate attempt to regain momentum in the waning days of a losing campaign. In northern Ohio, U.S. Rep. Max Miller lost a seat that Republicans have held since World War II amid allegations of spousal abuse during a contentious divorce. Nationally, Graham Platner, a Democratic U.S. Senate candidate in Maine, was pushed out of the race after an ex-girlfriend accused him of rape. U.S. Rep. Jimmy Gomez, a four-term Democrat in California, lost to a Democratic challenger amid a House investigation into potential sexual misconduct. In Arizona, Democrat Bernadette Greene-Placentia, who said she was raped during her House campaign, was trailing her opponent by less than 3 points on Thursday in a district Republicans won by 13 points in 2024. Survivors of the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein toured the country this year calling for the release of investigatory files related to the disgraced financier and urging voters to demand accountability. In a Wednesday morning note, Liz Roberts, the chief executive of Safe Horizon, the country's largest nonprofit services agency for survivors of abuse and violent crime, called the midterms results "a win for survivors, period." "We saw candidates accused of sexual assault and abuse withdraw from their campaigns, we saw candidates accused of violence lose their race. A survivor of child abuse, who speaks openly and without shame about her experiences, was called a liar by her opponent in a message backed by millions of dollars and still won. She was believed, not just by the survivor community, but by her constituents, voters, and the public across the nation," Roberts wrote. READ MORE: House Ethics Committee opens investigation into domestic abuse allegations against Ohio Rep. Max Miller Graham, who was raped by a priest when he was 14, said the Ramaswamy ad was particularly disturbing because it used Acton's mother against her. Many children who experience sexual abuse do not tell their parents due to fear or shame. "Amy Acton faced that monster in a way that a lot of people in Ohio, and across the world right now, are thinking to themselves: 'The plan was to never tell anybody about what happened to me but what if I did the opposite? What would that look like?' And they're inspired," Graham said. One of two surgeons who treated victims on the streets in the aftermath of a mass shooting in Krakow, Poland said his colleague"undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer.
The pair were eating near the city's Main Market Square on Saturday when a gunman began firing at random, killing six and injuring 15.
The doctors raced to treat both the attacker and two officers shot while subduing the perpetrator.
On Sunday, the officers - both hailed as "true heroes" by the prime minister for preventing further deaths - emerged from comas.
Prosecutors launched a terror investigation after ministers previously said the 24-year-old Polish attacker - who remains in a critical condition - was apparently inspired by "far-right ideologies".
A British national and Austrian woman were among those killed alongside four Poles.
Professor Michal PÄdziwiatr and Dr Mateusz Wierdak were having lunch in central Krakow with their families when they heard gunshots, local media reported.
"Suddenly my son ran up and said: 'Dad, they're shooting at people there, people are falling to the ground'," PÄdziwiatr told news outlet Fakt.
PÄdziwiatr said when they got to the scene, they treated both the apparent attacker and the police officers.
"When it comes to saving lives, it doesn't matter who is who," he added.
Once the shooting stopped, PÄdziwiatr said he took care of the other victims and the perpetrator, while Wierdak began working on the police officer who was shot in the chest during the gunfight.
"He, to put it colloquially, stuffed all the bandages into [the police officer's] chest and stuck his hands in," he told Fakt.
"If not for that, I don't know how things would have turned out, as there was a long wait for the ambulance."
Meanwhile, PÄdziwiatr said he called John Paul II Hospital where the Department of Thoracic and Cardiac Surgery is located.
"I insisted they take him there because, in my opinion, he had the best chance of survival there, where there were specialists for precisely this type of injury," he told Fakt.
According to local media, Wierdak is a renowned surgeon in Krakow. The University Hospital in Krakow states PÄdziwiatr is head of General, Oncological, Metabolic and Emergency Surgery.
The police officers have been identified as senior constables Jakub Kulik and Artur MoraÅski.
The attacker has not yet been named by authorities.
When his house was searched after the attack in central Krakow, the bodies of his parents and sister were found.
The National Public Prosecutor's Office in Poland launched an investigation into the attack with a unit specialising in "terrorist offences" taking the lead.
Separately, reports emerged that six Dublin Civil Defence volunteers also assisted in the aftermath of the shooting.
James McConnell, an officer, told RTE News the group were on a city break and were close to the main square, external when the shooting happened.
The volunteers who are trained to provide medical care immediately sought to help injured people, providing "CPR and haemorrhage control".
Witnesses who were close to the attack described panic and confusion around the square as it unfolded.
Ruby Catherine Warren, from London, heard gunfire and "yelled at my friends to run and we all sprinted for our lives".
Not knowing where the gunman was - or if there were multiple - they "just kept sprinting", eventually finding a hotel to hide inside.
Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, was inside a McDonald's near the square when he heard "multiple gunshots and saw people running for cover".
He continued: "I then walked into the square and saw paramedics working on someone outside [a shop] and there was a dead body covered in foil blankets 20 meters away."
The suspect wore full military tactical gear during the attack and was described as having a military-grade weapon - but the government said he was not a member of the Polish armed forces.
Poland's Interior Minister Marcin KierwiÅski said "everything suggests" the suspect was "fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held ultra-nationalist views.
The rampage began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) on Saturday in the historic centre of Krakow.
Footage showed the attacker's vehicle speeding through the centre of the city, and people fleeing as the sound of gunfire rang out.
The glass front of shops were shattered by bullets and a tram was shot at during the attack, which police say lasted for around three minutes.
The mayor of Krakow said he had submitted an urgent request for the two officers injured while stopping the attacker to be awarded titles of honorary citizens of the city.
Main Market Square reopened on Sunday evening after a security cordon was lifted.

6a8bccaaa4b4.text: By — Garance Burke, Associated Press Garance Burke, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/staff-at-u-s-center-for-ai-safety-are-reporting-to-the-white-house-raising-independence-concerns Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AP sources: Staff at U.S. center for AI safety are reporting to the White House, raising independence concerns Politics Nov 8, 2026 1:05 PM EST SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — With public anxiety growing over mounting reports about out-of-control artificial intelligence agents, the tiny U.S. government division charged with assessing the safety of new AI offerings lacks a permanent leader and has stopped publishing its research. Officials with the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence, or CAISSI, an independent division of the Commerce Department, recently were asked to informally report to an office of the White House. That's according to two former government officials with knowledge of the ongoing conversations who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to avoid repercussions for current staffers. The new arrangement concerns some critics, who worry that the executive branch might be politicizing decisions that could affect everything from cybersecurity to bioweapons and that the center's findings could be altered or muted in deference to the tech industry, which has been largely entrusted to police itself. Please check your inbox to confirm. "These are really powerful institutions that can drastically improve our lives, or the alternative. And the hope is that you can put in nonpartisan or bipartisan technocratic experts to enact policy in a way that best serves the American public," said Caroline Siegel Singh, an AI and emerging technology program manager for the Federation of American Scientists. Others argue that bringing AI safety officials closer to the orbit of President Donald Trump, who has taken an outwardly hands-off approach to the issue, could give the division more prominence — and perhaps more funding. The center, which has experienced departures and until recently was called the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation, is allocated $10 million per year. That's about one-eighth the annual budget of its counterpart in the United Kingdom, which is far less celebrated for its frontier technologies. READ MORE: Trump names national intelligence director Jay Clayton to lead a new federal AI task force In April, the division's director was hired and then fired within days. His replacement lasted a few months before he resigned, and the center has been without a permanent leader ever since, although the head of its parent institute doubles as its acting director. In August, Congress started asking why the center suddenly stopped making public its reports about how safely certain AI systems were performing. San Francisco giant OpenAI also had chimed in by then, asking policymakers to throw more money and support behind the division. The White House didn't respond to specific questions about CAISSI. But it said in a statement that Trump had formally established his new Super Intelligence Force — the president's preferred term for artificial intelligence. Trump has commissioned a report on risks from his Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, and will ensure "continued U.S. leadership on SI for the benefit of the American people," the White House said. An industry that polices itself The federal government often takes an active role in deciding what is safe for the public. Take the automobile industry, for example. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration sits crash test dummies in cars and then runs them into walls to measure how human bodies are affected by vehicle collisions. Government researchers then analyze the crash test data, share it with the public and prescribe national standards to improve vehicle safety, all with the mission of saving lives and lowering economic costs from crashes. With AI models, safety testing looks very different. Under then-President Joe Biden, leading AI companies voluntarily agreed to promote "safe, secure, and transparent development" of their models by sharing details with the newly created division of the Commerce Department and following the administration's guidelines for tests and transparency reports. WATCH: Trump announces accord signed by top AI companies to 'self-police' development In September, following alarming reports of AI systems eluding their makers' control, Trump asked leading AI companies to undertake "tremendous self-policing" as part of a voluntary safety pact, but his administration hasn't said how it will monitor the AI companies' implementation. The technology is advancing so rapidly that many models are now deployed instead as AI agents that work without human prompting and can plan out myriad steps in real-world environments, such as in a recent case in which an AI agent sent a false tip to Philadelphia police about an unsolved homicide case. As AI capabilities have grown, the government's capacity to independently check these systems hasn't kept pace. There still is no standard process for testing how safely AI agents are acting in the real world, even in simple cases such as when AI agents book a flight, said Sayash Kapoor, an incoming assistant professor at the University of California, Berkeley School of Information. "Our previous methods would just look at the final answer, the final check, whether the flight was correctly booked. And in this case, it might seem as if the task was solved correctly," said Kapoor, the co-author of a new paper examining agent evaluations. 452250771f5c.text: President Trump told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a phone call Thursday that he wants him to take steps to implement his Gaza peace plan , according to two sources with knowledge of the matter. Why it matters: The roadmap calls for disarming Hamas and demilitarizing Gaza, as well as transferring responsibility for governing the enclave to a new Palestinian technocratic government. But it has been on hold for months because of the Israeli elections held on Oct. 27. The Trump administration did not want implementation of the plan to become a politically explosive issue during the Israeli election campaign. Trump endorsed Netanyahu shortly before the election. Now that it's over, the president wants to forge ahead with his Gaza plan, regardless of whether Netanyahu or his opposition forms a new government. Catch up quick: A year ago, Israel and Hamas agreed to the first phase of Trump's 20-point plan, which led to a ceasefire in the Gaza war and the release of the last 20 living hostages taken during the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks. Trump's Board of Peace, which was established as part of the Gaza agreement, has been working for months on an implementation plan that includes the establishment of a Palestinian technocratic government and an International Stabilization Force. Last July, the Board of Peace reached an agreement with Hamas on a 15-point plan to disarm the armed groups in Gaza and transfer civilian and security control to the new Palestinian technocratic government. Since then, Netanyahu's government has largely refused to move forward with implementing it, mostly for domestic political reasons. In an August visit to Israel, Trump adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner told Netanyahu that Hamas for the first time had agreed to disarm. He urged the Israeli prime minister to take steps to test whether that commitment was real. Netanyahu was and still is extremely skeptical that Hamas will ever demilitarize. He says the group is reconstituting and rearming in Gaza. Zoom in: Over the past three months, Trump's Board of Peace has been working with the Israeli government and military to refine details of the plan and address Israeli concerns about demilitarization in Gaza. A U.S. official said the process would be gradual. Reconstruction would only begin after progress in disarming Hamas had been verified. Trump's Board of Peace unveiled a six-month, $2.45 billion initial recovery plan for Gaza during the U.N. General Assembly in September. The 66-project proposal offers one of the most comprehensive roadmaps yet for what the early months of post-war recovery and governance in Gaza would look like. But for the plan to move forward, the Board of Peace needs Israel and Hamas to cooperate. A source with knowledge of the details said the Trump administration, Board of Peace and Israel agree that the plan remains the best way forward and that there is no credible alternative. Behind the scenes: Secretary of State Marco Rubio as well as Kushner and Trump envoy Steve Witkoff also participated in the call between the president and Netanyahu. A source with knowledge of the details described the call, which Netanyahu initiated, as constructive. It also addressed the war in Iran. The White House and the Israeli prime minister's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment. State of play: A day after the call, former British Prime Minister Tony Blair, who is a member of the Board of Peace, visited Israel. He met with Netanyahu and his opponent Gadi Eisenkot, who's been tasked with trying to form a new government to replace Netanyahu's. A source with knowledge of the visit said Blair urged Netanyahu and other Israeli political leaders to give the plan a chance. What they're saying: "The implementation will be difficult but we believe it is a good plan for Israel. Nevertheless we can't do it with one hand tied behind our back," the U.S. official said. "We want to move forward collaboratively and we need full cooperation and partnership from the Israeli government," the person added.

45aac469a793.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/collision-between-2-trains-in-egypt-kills-7-and-injures-more-than-100 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Collision between 2 trains in Egypt kills 7 and injures more than 100 World Nov 8, 2026 12:40 PM EST CAIRO (AP) — Seven people were killed and over 100 others injured when two trains collided Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, the Chief Prosecutor's office said in a statement. It also said the train's conductor was among those killed. The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 52 kilometers (32 miles) south of Cairo, when a train traveling to the southwestern Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the Transportation Ministry. WATCH: Shock, anger and mourning in Spain after 2nd major train crash this year The Chief Prosecutor's office said late Sunday its investigators had arrived at the site. An inspection indicated that the crash took place when the Giza-Fayyoum train collided with the last carriage of the Cairo-Aswan train, that was stationary on the same track and traveling in the same direction, officials said. Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system which has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years, the government announced modernization initiatives to improve its railways. Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people living nearby rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances, Gamal said that he saw around 80 of the injured were taken by ambulances to nearby hospitals. Some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and were dead when they were pulled out, he said. President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi said in a social media post that he ordered a prompt investigation into the crash. Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian Railway Authority said. Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district. Egypt's deadliest train crash was in 2002, when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train journeying from Cairo to southern Egypt. fcafcaba90ec.text:
- Published
At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.
The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.
Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.
Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".
The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.
The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.
Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.
The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.
The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.
Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.
Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains.
The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.
The train continued for around nine kilometres (5.6 miles) before coming to a halt.
In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.
Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.
There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.

71f298312da2.text: By — Wufei Yu, Associated Press Wufei Yu, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/floods-bring-rare-relief-to-u-s-southwest-reservoirs-as-lake-powell-rises-20-feet Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Floods bring rare relief to U.S. Southwest reservoirs as Lake Powell rises 20 feet Nation Nov 8, 2026 12:31 PM EST PHOENIX (AP) — Recent flooding across the U.S. Southwest is providing rare relief to thirsty reservoirs that had fallen to record lows amid a yearslong megadrought. WATCH: How the West is preparing for a drier future as water supplies hit lows Storms in late October and early November sent torrents of water through normally small or dry creeks that overflowed their banks and flooded local communities. Hundreds of people were told to evacuate, and the flooding cut off access to some areas. Yet most of that water will end up feeding depleted lakes and underground aquifers, said Martin Hoerling, a climate scientist and hydrologist at the University of Colorado, Boulder. "That's somewhat of an unexpected boost from Mother Nature," Hoerling said. Last winter's lackluster snowfall did little to recharge water bodies when it melted in the spring and summer, when they typically get their biggest bump of the year. Then came the chaotic climate phenomenon, El Niño, that has intensified heavy rain and floods. Experts say its impacts will last several more months, potentially further boosting water supplies across the West where water primarily is stored in lakes, aquifers and snowpack. READ MORE: Colorado River plan to cut water amid drought brings uncertainty for cities and farmers Lake Powell, the second-largest reservoir in the U.S., rose more than 20 feet (6.1 meters) from its mid-September low — dwarfing its gains from this year's snowmelt, Hoerling said. Still, the lake remained just over a quarter full, and 15 of its 17 boat launches remained unusable as of Friday. The floodwaters and additional rain could raise the lake along the Arizona-Utah border further, for a total of over 1.2 million acre-feet — enough to support around 4 million average families for a year, Hoerling estimated. Rain brings temporary relief to regional and local water supplies Cities in the region reported some of their wettest weather in decades. Before storms began dumping about 7 inches (17.78 centimeters) of rain around Pagosa Springs, Colorado, in October, more than 10,000 people in the town and surrounding communities were under water restrictions. Restaurants were encouraged to serve water only on request, town manager David Harris said. Those restrictions are now lifted. "While the storm was destructive, I think there is a silver lining," Harris said. "You're getting a good start to the winter snowpack in the higher elevations." WATCH: Tipping Point — The Colorado River Reimagined | A PBS News Special Upper Lake Mary, which captures spring snowmelt in Northern Arizona and supplies Flagstaff, Arizona, with up to 40% of its water, received more than 3 billion gallons of water since early October, said Flagstaff water production manager Brian Huntzinger. Storms last weekend dumped the equivalent of more than two years of water into the town's surface water supply and provided a buffer for an operation that depends heavily on underground aquifers, Huntzinger said. "It's just a great, great thing to see," Huntzinger said. "We might be overflowing at this rate before we see any snow fly." In central Arizona, heavy floodwaters that trapped people in their homes gushed into streams that feed the Verde River. That prompted water officials to release water from two nearly full dams into the Verde's normally dry stretch in metro Phoenix, said Bo Svoma, the principal meteorologist at the Salt River Project that manages reservoirs on the Salt and Verde rivers. Wet weather is unlikely to change decisions on the Colorado River The region remains in drought despite the intense rains. And decisions already have been made to divvy up water in the Colorado River basin. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, which manages reservoirs in the West, is unlikely to change its water releases from Lake Powell or other areas until it knows when snowpack has peaked, typically around April, said Jack Schmidt, a Utah State University professor who studies the Colorado River. READ MORE: Lake Powell hits record low, threatening key water and electricity supply for millions Reclamation spokesperson Mary Carlson acknowledged conditions have improved but added "considerable uncertainty remains." Under the federal plan for managing the Colorado River's Lower Basin, California, Nevada and Arizona will collectively reduce water use by 1.25 million acre-feet (about 1.54 billion cubic meters) annually in the next two years. That is enough to fill over 600,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools, with the possibility of larger cuts depending on conditions. Nevada and Arizona are challenging the plan in court. Some Arizona cities have agreed to fund preliminary work to reduce reliance on the Colorado River by expanding an existing dam on the Verde River to capture runoff from storms, Svoma said. "We need to figure out how to be resilient in a drier future. And we're not quite there yet," Hoerling said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. ab20afc74f55.text: Attorney General Todd Blanche refused Sunday to rule out prosecuting Democratic lawmakers who say they'll investigate Trump officials, a day after President Trump ordered the Justice Department to probe lawmakers. Why it matters: The confrontation threatens a constitutional crisis over the separation of powers: Trump is ordering prosecutors to go after lawmakers in a potential effort to hamper Congress' power to hold the executive branch accountable. Driving the news: In a Truth Social post Saturday, Trump accused Democrats of threatening administration officials and Republican donors with investigations and impeachment. "This is extortion at the highest level, and they should be held accountable for this," Trump wrote. He singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), accusing her of threatening young people who hold Republican views. "The imprisonment should be against these EXTORTIONISTS," Trump wrote. "By copy of this statement, I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!" he added. The latest: On CNN's "State of the Union," Blanche acknowledged Congress' constitutional oversight authority but argued that Democrats' rhetoric had crossed a line. Asked whether DOJ would investigate Democratic lawmakers, Blanche did not identify a criminal statute or confirm that an investigation had begun. Asked whether lawmakers could face imprisonment, Blanche said it depended on what crimes they had committed. On Fox News, he said the possibility of criminal charges depended on what Democrats had said. The White House and Justice Department have not responded to requests for comment. What they're saying: Blanche singled out incoming House Oversight Committee Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who warned officials, including incoming White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, to "lawyer up." "I would be very worried if I was a member on that committee," Blanche told CNN. He also said the department would provide legal defense for administration officials facing congressional scrutiny, including incoming White House chief of staff Stephen Miller. The other side: Garcia accused Blanche of trying to intimidate Congress and said Democrats would not back down. "They can come after us however they want. We're not going to be intimidated," Garcia told CNN. Garcia said his committee would pursue alleged wrongdoing involving Trump's administration, family and corporate allies. Flashback: In February, a federal grand jury rejected DOJ's attempt to indict Slotkin and five other Democratic lawmakers over a video urging service members to refuse unlawful military orders. What's next: It remains unclear whether DOJ has opened an investigation in response to Trump's order, which lawmakers it might examine or what conduct it believes could constitute a crime.

f32bb7044351.text: By — Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Melanie Lidman, Associated Press By — Giovanna Dell'Orto, Associated Press Giovanna Dell'Orto, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/israels-president-formally-gives-eisenkot-the-first-chance-to-form-the-next-government Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Israel's president formally gives Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government World Updated on Nov 8, 2026 1:13 PM EST — Published on Nov 8, 2026 11:32 AM EST JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli President Isaac Herzog formally gave opposition politician Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government Sunday evening. Complex coalition negotiations still lie ahead, but it marked a significant step in the former military chief's effort to oust Israel's longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, after elections held in a deeply divided country. Israel remains scarred by the Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, and the multifront wars they triggered. READ MORE: Israel's president taps opposition candidate Eisenkot to form a government, in setback for Netanyahu "I hope with all my heart that whatever government is formed will lead to unity, connection and healing among all segments of our people — for our very existence depends on it, and we have only one country," Herzog said at the ceremony at the presidential residence in Jerusalem. The announcement doesn't guarantee that Eisenkot, a former army chief, will become the next prime minister. He has up to six weeks to form a coalition government by securing alliances, a daunting challenge because the Oct. 27 election gave neither his bloc nor Netanyahu's a clear majority in parliament. Herzog said that in consultations with the parties, a majority of members of parliament, known as the Knesset, supported giving Eisenkot this task. At Sunday's ceremony, Eisenkot promised to give the country leadership that people can trust, that will act in the interests of the public and that represents all parts of society. "An absolute majority of Knesset members representing the Israeli public support change," he said. "I intend to navigate the situation with patience, humility, composure and a deep commitment to a Jewish, equal, liberal, and secure Israel." Politically fraught coalition choices lie ahead Among the possible kingmakers — and most politically fraught potential allies — are the Arab-led parties. They made historic gains in the election thanks to high voter turnout among Israel's Arab citizens. Only one Arab party, Ra'am, has ever joined a governing coalition, in 2021. Ra'am has said it will support Eisenkot, but the party does not have enough seats on its own to give Eisenkot a parliamentary majority. Breaking with decades of precedent, the second Arab-led party, the Joint List, has offered to support Eisenkot from outside the coalition to end Netanyahu's grip on power. But that cooperation is fraught for both sides. For the Joint List, it would mean backing a government unlikely to end Israel's wars or curb settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. For Eisenkot and other opposition parties, it would mean aligning with parties that not only criticize Israel's policies but reject its identity as a Jewish state. READ MORE: Israel's president takes first steps on building new government after accepting election results One of Eisenkot's partners, the more conservative Yisrael Beytenu party, already has said it will not join a coalition with Arab-led parties. Eisenkot has laid out four conditions for parties that want to join him. They must recognize Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accept its declaration of independence, support military, national or civil service for all citizens, and declare the Hamas militant group a terrorist group. It remains unclear whether his would-be Arab partners are ready to accept these conditions. Furthermore, Netanyahu has repeatedly asserted unsubstantiated claims that the election was "stolen" by Arab parties. In a pressure tactic on Eisenkot, he says any alliance with these parties would be an act of betrayal. Israel's Shin Bet security agency has launched an investigation into possible foreign interference in the vote, but the country's Central Elections Committee — and Herzog — say the vote was valid and even if wrongdoing is found, it did not have a significant impact on the electoral results. Eisenkot faces significant challenges on the road to becoming prime minister Eisenkot has vowed to form a government as quickly as possible. But each likely scenario appears to entail compromises or broken promises. Aside from seeking the support of the Arab-led parties, Eisenkot has two options: a power-sharing agreement with Netanyahu or an agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which demand military exemptions for their community. Eisenkot and his partners made equal military service a central part of their campaign. Specifically, they are seeking an end to the long-standing draft exemptions. WATCH: What Israel's election deadlock means for Netanyahu and the region The religious parties, which were part of Netanyahu's outgoing coalition, want to preserve them, calling them essential to their devout lifestyle. But the exemptions have grown especially controversial among the broader public during the past three years of war. Anticipating its position as a swing vote, the ultra-Orthodox party United Torah Judaism has left the door open to cooperating with Eisenkot. Eisenkot has 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible two-week extension from the president. If he is unable to form a government, Netanyahu could then be given a chance to put together a coalition. If Netanyahu is also unable to do so, the country would return to elections early next spring. Israel's new members of Knesset will be sworn in on Tuesday evening. Netanyahu and his cabinet will remain in office in a caretaker capacity, with limited powers, until

Footage shows derailed carriages after fatal train crash in Egypt
A train collision has killed at least seven people and injured dozens in northern Egypt.
Footage showed multiple overturned carriages and dozens of people surrounding them.
One train was travelling from Giza to the Fayoum oasis, south west of Cairo, while the other was heading from Cairo to Aswan in the south.
It is yet unclear what caused the accident but Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said an investigation was underway and would "hold accountable anyone who proves their negligence".

a5b6c69c23f2.text:
- Published
Millions across India are celebrating Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and colourful lights to symbolise the triumph of light over darkness.
The festival falls on the darkest night of the Hindu lunar month of Kartik, when the moon is not visible in the sky.
Although Diwali traditions vary across India's regions and communities, the festival is widely marked by prayers, family gatherings, the exchange of sweets and the lighting of firecrackers.
But the celebrations come amid growing concerns over air pollution, particularly in northern India.
Seasonal weather conditions and the burning of crop residue contribute to deteriorating air quality, while firecrackers set off during Diwali can make the situation worse.
Air pollution in the Indian capital Delhi has reached such hazardous levels that it is the most polluted Diwali festival in a decade. New measures to improve air quality do not seem to have been successful.
India's financial capital, Mumbai, has also experienced high pollution levels in recent weeks.
In an effort to limit pollution, India's Supreme Court on Monday permitted the manufacture, sale and use of certified "green" firecrackers in Delhi and surrounding areas for a limited period.
These firecrackers are designed to produce 20-30% fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. But critics have questioned how effective they are at reducing pollution and raised concerns that conventional firecrackers could still make their way into the capital from neighbouring states.
Despite the debate over fireworks, Diwali is about much more than firecrackers.
The festival celebrates the return of Lord Ram to Ayodhya after his victory over Ravan, the main antagonist in the Hindu epic Ramayana, and symbolises the triumph of good over evil, light over darkness, and knowledge over ignorance.
In the days leading up to the festival, families clean and decorate their homes with flowers, colourful lights and traditional oil lamps known as diyas.
The celebrations also bring families and friends together for prayers, elaborate feasts and the exchange of gifts, and lots of traditional Indian sweets.
Colourful patterns known as rangoli are created at entrances to homes, while markets bustle with shoppers buying festive essentials beneath brightly lit decorations.
The celebrations began on 6 November with Dhanteras, when buying gold, silver or new utensils is considered auspicious and believed to bring good fortune.
The second day, known as Chhoti Diwali, or small Diwali, is marked by the lighting of oil lamps and, in some households, setting off firecrackers.
The third day is the main celebration, when families offer evening prayers to Lakshmi, the Hindu goddess of wealth and prosperity, before gathering for festive meals and fireworks.
The fourth day is celebrated differently across India, with family gatherings and New Year festivities in some communities. The fifth and final day, known as Bhai Dooj, celebrates the bond between brothers and sisters.
The festival is also celebrated by Sikhs and Jains along with other important religious observances.
Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas, or Prisoner Release Day, commemorating the release of their sixth guru, Guru Hargobind, from imprisonment at Gwalior Fort in the early 17th Century.
For Jains, Diwali marks the attainment of moksha, or liberation from the cycle of rebirth, by Lord Mahavira, the 24th and last Tirthankara, or spiritual teacher, of the current era.
With Indian communities spread across the world, Diwali is also celebrated internationally, with families and friends coming together for festive gatherings and exchanging gifts.
The festival is considered an auspicious time to make new purchases, which many believe bring prosperity and good fortune. India's stock exchanges even hold a special one-hour trading session for investors who consider buying and selling shares on Diwali favourable. Known as Muhurat trading, it will take place on 8 November this year.
Although rooted in Hindu traditions, Diwali is celebrated by people across different faiths and communities.

- Published
Iran has executed three men accused of carrying out armed unrest during January's anti-government protests, according to state media.
Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were accused of throwing Molotov cocktails and grenades, using bladed weapons and firearms, and setting fire to public facilities in the city of Karaj, west of Tehran, Iran's state news agency Tasnim, external reported.
The executions are the latest in a series linked to the protests, including those of people accused of having ties to Israel and the United States.
The number of executions in Iran has increased since US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic began in late February.
The protest movement initially sparked in December last year by the high cost of living rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on 8 and 9 of January.
Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, and blamed the violence on "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the US and Israel.
However foreign-based NGOs gave higher figures and the BBC received multiple accounts from Iranians of security forces opening fire on unarmed protesters.
Tasnim reported that the three men were executed after the Supreme Court upheld their convictions and found them guilty of "participating in operational activities on behalf of the Israeli Zionist regime, the United States and hostile groups".
The damage allegedly included an electricity substation in Karaj which caused power outages in some areas.
Dioband was arrested on 11 January after investigations identified him as a suspect in attacks on public property and incitement to violence.
Ten others accused of taking part in the unrest under his supervision were later arrested.
Reuters news agency reports that they received prison terms of 5 to 10 years.
The latest executions in Iran come after the UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk said he was alarmed by the rise in death penalties.
In August, TÃ¼rk said at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests.
Iran is thought to be the world's second-most prolific executioner after China. Last year, it put to death at least 2,159 people, according to Amnesty International.
The human rights group said that was the highest figure on record since 1981 and included 45 executions of suspected dissidents on national security-related charges.

362b11a3bad3.text: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani can't be president, so he's trying to be the next best thing: a progressive kingmaker for 2028. Mamdani has been meeting privately with union leaders, urgently talking up the need for a labor-aligned or leftist candidate to run for the White House, four people familiar with the talks told Axios. He's arguing that progressives can't afford to squander their midterm momentum. Why it matters: Behind closed doors, Mamdani has made a striking admission that helps explain why he's so eager to huddle with allies about 2028: He's uncertain whether New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, his close political partner, will launch a White House run, the sources said. If Ocasio-Cortez stays out of the 2028 race, it would upend the Democratic primary — and potentially leave the party's insurgent left without a candidate. Zoom in: Mamdani — who's ineligible to be president because he was born in Uganda — wants to coordinate with progressive leaders partly to prepare to unite against any leading centrist presidential contender they aren't happy with, according to one of the sources who has spoken with the mayor. Mamdani "wants the progressive ecosystem to mobilize quickly, strategically and efficiently if a moderate candidate is clearly on the rise," the person said, pointing to how former President Barack Obama appeared to help Joe Biden consolidate support against Bernie Sanders in 2020. Last month, Mamdani summoned the president of the International Union of Painters and Allied Trades, Jimmy Williams Jr., to Gracie Mansion to talk about 2028. Mamdani asked Williams which potential presidential candidates he liked and how his union's endorsement process would unfold. He also asked Williams whether he'd ever considered running for office, the sources said. The source who has spoken with Mamdani noted that the mayor recruited — and helped elect — several left-wing congressional candidates in New York this year. Sara Nelson, president of the Association of Flight Attendants-C.W.A, also met with Mamdani recently to discuss 2028 and other issues. The mayor plans to get together soon with yet another labor leader — Shawn Fain, president of the United Automobile Workers. Zoom out: Mamdani's efforts to influence the 2028 contest come as many progressives are growing anxious about the prospect of a presidential race without a left-wing contender. Many think Ocasio-Cortez is leaning toward a Senate bid in 2028 instead of a White House run. She's said she's considering both options. Some allies hope that progressives' success in battleground states in the midterms will encourage her to go for the White House. But Democrats of all political stripes won races in last week's nationwide rebuke of the Trump administration, so the postelection case for left-wingers in 2028 isn't necessarily stronger than it is for centrist Democrats. What they're saying: Williams, the IUPAT president, told Axios he's "absolutely supportive" of people from the labor movement running for office up and down the ballot. "We put a freaking ironworker in Congress. We put a IUPAT member in the Senate," he said, referring to Democrats who won in the midterms. But Williams said he's not interested in running for elected office. Spokespeople for Mamdani, Fain and Nelson did not comment. Asked by WNYC last month if he wants to see Ocasio-Cortez run for president, Mamdani said, "I want to see AOC do whatever it is that AOC wants to do" and called her "an inspiration." Between the lines: With Ocasio-Cortez's future a question mark, some progressives are beginning to look elsewhere for a presidential candidate. Some on the left hope Abdul El-Sayed, the incoming senator in Michigan, will take a look at 2028. Others are lining up behind California Rep. Ro Khanna, who's widely expected to run. Bhaskar Sunkara, a 2020 Sanders surrogate and president of the liberal publication The Nation, wrote an op-ed last summer calling for Ocasio-Cortez to run for president. More recently , he's been talking up the idea of a labor candidate. "Progressive ideas only win when working-class voters see themselves in the fight," he told Axios. "There's no better way to do that than to run an actual worker for president, not a professional politician." Williams, Nelson and Fain are widely seen as some of the most progressive labor leaders in the country. Fain is known for railing against billionaires, and Nelson joined Sanders' "Fighting Oligarchy" tour. Williams wrote in 2025 that he "was proud that my union was among the first to call for a ceasefire in Gaza." Some left-wing activists have encouraged Fain, whose union helped elect El-Sayed, to consider a presidential bid. But he told the Detroit News last month he has "no plans" to run.

A youth-friendly banking app, Ueno collapsed amid allegations of insider lending and proximity to the countryâs longtime ruling party, which is closely aligned with Washington.

f9b91d609f86.text: By — Isabel DeBre, Associated Press Isabel DeBre, Associated Press By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/pope-arrives-in-argentina-and-tells-milei-that-people-not-the-economy-should-come-first Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope Leo arrives in Argentina and tells Milei that people, not the economy, should come first World Nov 8, 2026 5:42 PM EST BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Pope Leo XIV delivered a diplomatic but subtly strong critique of Argentine President Javier Milei's austerity measures and libertarian agenda as he arrived Sunday in Argentina, insisting that political leaders must put people, not the economy, first. Leo used his first public speech in Argentina to lay out a vision of governance, democracy and society sharply at odds with Milei's, exposing differences over spending cuts, social justice and artificial intelligence that the government had sought to play down ahead of the visit. "The economy must serve the person, not the person the economy," Leo told officials, diplomats and civic leaders upon his arrival in Buenos Aires from Uruguay. READ MORE: With an ode to mate, Pope Leo urges faithful in Uruguay to build bridges of fraternity and faith Leo's visit to Argentina is by far the most politically delicate of his three-nation South American tour, and a place where Leo will also confront the complicated legacy of Argentine Pope Francis, who never returned home during his 12-year pontificate. Milei, a self-described anarcho-capitalist, has staked his presidency on slashing public spending to tame inflation, while describing the notion of social justice as "a horror," a "moral aberration" and "theft" in recent speeches. Much like its allies in the Trump administration, Milei's government has portrayed the cuts as part of a necessary reform process to remake Argentina's troubled economy and eliminate fraud and waste in the federal bureaucracy. Ahead of Leo's arrival in Argentina, the first by a pope in nearly 40 years, Milei's officials had dismissed the prospect of a political clash. "There's no way the pope is coming here to comment on local politics," Human Capital Minister Sandra Pettovello said in an interview with a Buenos Aires radio station last week. In a message welcoming Leo, Milei said he hoped the trip would "strengthen the faith, renew hope and bring a message of peace to all Argentines." A call for civility in politics People hold a banner depicting Pope Leo as they await his visit to the Monument to General San Martin at Plaza San Martin during his 12-day trip to South America, on the first papal visit to Argentina since 1987, in Buenos Aires on Nov. 8, 2026. Photo by Matias Baglietto/Reuters Leo took up that message of peace, opening with a call for gentler politics in deeply polarized Argentina. Democracy depends on "careful use of words" and "the ability to see those who think differently as fellow citizens with whom we share a common future," he said. Milei's style is far more combative, costing him allies in Congress and public support. He posts dozens of times a day on social media, branding critics "traitors" and "human trash" and tagging posts #NOLSALP, a Spanish acronym for "We don't hate journalists enough." Milei, who once called Francis the "representative of evil on Earth," paid homage to the late pope in welcoming Leo on Sunday. Interrupted by applause, he called Francis an "exceptional figure" and "undoubtedly the most important Argentine in history" whose teachings continue to resonate. He also struck a rare conciliatory tone in welcoming politicians, diplomats and civil society representatives from across Argentina's ideological spectrum to Leo's ceremony. "There are causes and occasions that transcend our differences," he said. On the economy, Leo nodded to Milei's free-market instincts, urging Argentina to encourage "whatever creates opportunities" and "stimulates private initiative." But growth must also benefit "those who are disadvantaged," he said, including the unemployed, retirees and "all those who, despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household's needs." READ MORE: What to know about Pope Leo XIV's trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru Milei's austerity drive has produced a rare budget surplus and slashed annual inflation from 200% to about 32%. But real wages remain below where they were when he took office in late 2023, and roughly 300,000 formal jobs have vanished. Retirees who say they can't afford medicine on an average monthly pension of $510 have protested outside Congress every Wednesday for more than two years. Milei has mocked the widespread complaint that families can't make it to the end of the month as "huge stupidity." A missionary priest in Peru for two decades, Leo has embraced a pastoral style reminiscent of Francis, who as archbishop of Buenos Aires expanded the ranks of priests serving in the city's crime-ridden informal settlements. Leo laid out a Christian vision of democracy, authority and economic progress that ran counter to Milei's. But he couched the implicit rebuke by referencing the church's social doctrine and papal pronouncements spanning more than six decades, invoking St. John Paul II, the last pope to visit Argentina, in 1987, among others. That tradition also ran through Francis' papacy. His 2020 encyclical "Fratelli Tutti" criticized laissez-faire economics and defended social justice and workers' rights. Argentina's bishops, many of them appointed by Francis, have become some of Milei's most persistent critics. Of the 44 documents on public policy published by the country's bishops' conference between January 2024 and September 2026, 42 criticized Milei's administration, on issues from poverty to migration, according to an analysis by sociologist Sol Prieto from Argentina's national research council. - Published
US tech giant Nvidia has opened an independent investigation following reports its CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
The company, one of the most valuable in the world, said its board had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, adding that the CEO was committed to continuing to lead the company.
Separately, Jensen Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.
US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.
Jensen Huang said he took "full responsibility" for what he did, adding that he had fallen short of his responsibilities to Nvidia's employees, board and shareholders.
Nvidia is one of the world's largest companies and seen as central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, and Jensen Huang has been in charge of it for more than 30 years.
He said: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."
His statement continued: "Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, Nvidia's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully.
"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American."
A separate statement issued by Nvidia's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
It continued: "The Board prioritises US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders.
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information."
Jensen Huang rescued Nvidia from almost going broke on more than one occasion, and he took a punt on AI a long time before the rest of the world did.
His decision to make Nvidia chips, originally designed for gaming, become the best in the business for AI development, has now paid off in spades and the company is worth trillions.
This is a big blow for a man who is renowned for being a workaholic, a perfectionist and someone who expects incredibly high standards from his staff.
Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, is linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed.
The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation.
Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, providing chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta.
The microchip manufacturer is worth some $4.5 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies ever.
China has previously rejected allegations of an espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief, describing the claims as "groundless speculation".
US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by The New York Times.
Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".
It remains unclear what information Alice Huang â who is also known as Huang Le â allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.
Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.
Last week, members of Congress wrote to Jensen Huang, asking him to appear before them in the light of the reported relationship.
Three House Republican committee leaders asked the CEO to appear later in the month, to talk about Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage" given his reported relationship with Alice Huang.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information.
"The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the letter said.
Nvidia's AI chips have been a major focus of the rivalry between the US and China, and Washington has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

5aae36239c40.text: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is positioning himself for a presidential run. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is running away from the idea of his own campaign for the White House. Why it matters: The political posturing of the two Florida Republicans — or the efforts to draft either for 2028 — underscores the sudden volatility of the way-too-early GOP preprimary campaign to succeed President Trump . Before Tuesday's midterm Republican wipeout, the party's 2028 primary looked like a relatively easy coronation for Vice President Vance (if he runs, as expected). Now there's a nascent movement to kneecap Vance and promote other possible opponents. Zoom in: As Trump's home base, Florida was bound to take center stage in the conversation. But two things distinguish Florida from other states: DeSantis and Rubio have national profiles rooted in their own prior presidential campaigns, in 2024 and 20216, respectively. Florida was the lone red-wall state that the national blue wave couldn't top, which DeSantis has been happy to emphasize repeatedly since Tuesday. "The alligator people are stirring," said one national Republican consultant with extensive Florida experience, referring to the Sunshine State's official reptile. Zoom out: The differences between DeSantis and Rubio are vast when it comes to their political futures and styles. DeSantis is hungry. Rubio isn't. DeSantis terms-out of the governor's office in January and is looking for work. He hasn't made an official decision on whether to run for president — but he has stoked speculation with a media blitz that began with an Election Day appearance on Stephen A. Smith's podcast. Rubio repeatedly has said he plans to stay put in the Trump administration and serve out the rest of his term, until January 2029. He also said in May that he wouldn't run against Vance, and hasn't changed his position publicly. The intrigue: During the somber election watch party at the White House on Tuesday night, Rubio's phone "blew up" with supporters urging him to reconsider running for president, according to a source familiar with the scene. "There was this sense of 'We lost the Latino vote , you can get it back, etc.,'" said the source. "To some people, Rubio seemed to entertain the idea for the first time. Or he didn't shut it down fast enough." Two days later, two publications reported that Rubio was actively considering resigning to lay the groundwork to run for president. Rubio denied it to the New York Times, and longtime associates of Rubio's told Axios that the reporting was bogus. "Now if Vance doesn't run or if POTUS tells him to step aside so Marco can run, does he? Maybe. I don't see that. But maybe," said one insider. That same night, Vance got feedback from one supporter who said he shouldn't run. And some GOP donors said they would back DeSantis, according to The Wall Street Journal. What's next: There's no debate about whether DeSantis is considering a bid. He is. DeSantis's postelection appearance on CNN with Jake Tapper was a sign he learned a lesson from his 2024 presidential campaign : Earning free media by sitting for more podcast and TV interviews is crucial. Asked whether he plans to run again, DeSantis wouldn't say. But he emphasized that "I haven't planned anything because I just think this is a very uncertain time. But last night should be a wakeup call for our party." "We really got blasted into oblivion," DeSantis added. "And Florida is kind of the last one standing."

13129d88ae3a.text: An unusual coalition wants to recruit outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie as the Libertarian Party's 2028 presidential nominee, betting that MAGA fractures can turn a third-party candidacy into a spoiler for the Republican nominee. Why it matters: Organizers see a fighter in Massie, a frequent critic of President Trump who pushed hard on releasing the Epstein files and lost a bitter primary rather than quietly walking away. Massie raised almost $10 million in the process and has a large online donor list and base. For his parting act in Congress, Massie is pushing an impeachment vote against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth . Driving the news: For months, Libertarian Party operatives and MAGA defectors have been privately and publicly encouraging Massie to run under a rebranded party. "Libertarian Jesus is Ron Paul, and one of our saints is Thomas Massie," Larry Sharpe, a perennial Libertarian candidate and longtime third-party operative, told Axios. Sharpe has spoken with Massie several times about a potential presidential run. Aside from playing GOP spoiler, organizers believe the Libertarian Party's existing ballot access and infrastructure could help them win 5% of the national vote — which would qualify its next presidential nominee for federal funding. Massie didn't respond to several requests for comment. The big picture: The plan is for libertarians to claim dibs on the "America First" agenda, mainly focusing on anti-war sentiment. Organizers believe they can build consensus among supporters of the MAGA wing that's closer to Tucker Carlson, former Trump official Joe Kent and former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.), as well as disillusioned "Make America Healthy Again" activists and populist-inclined voters on the right and left. "A party that would speak clearly about the disaster of the war in Iran, that would speak clearly about the mistake to continue to give military aid, taxpayer-funded military aid, to Israel — that would perk up a lot of ears among young people," said James Fishback, a former GOP gubernatorial candidate in Florida who met with the organizers in October. "The idea is if one can take 5, 10, 15% of the vote from one of these parties, then that party has to listen and cave to interest of the people," Bret Weinstein, a lead organizer of this effort, said on his podcast last week. Zoom in: LP operative Michael Heise, a leader and founder of the Mises Caucus, is a main organizer for this rebranded party. Heise's caucus took over the LP in 2022. The LP picks its presidential nominee at conventions by delegates voting on the floor. Those who bring the most delegates can take over a convention. Heise is also a skilled fundraiser — by third party standards. The Mises PAC, which is bankrolling this "draft Massie" operation, according to the website, raised $394,000 in 2024's election cycle. The PAC has previously received donations from Kimbal and Christina Musk, Elon's brother and sister-in-law; Abigail Rockefeller, a former Robert F. Kennedy Jr. campaign and Democratic-leaning donor; and Patricia Duggan, a MAGA Inc mega-donor and longtime LP contributor, according to FEC records. Heise declined to comment.
