92ce6f25a384.text: By — Josh Boak, Associated Press Josh Boak, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/voters-demanded-economic-relief-trump-and-democrats-face-tough-choices-on-how-to-deliver Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Voters demanded economic relief. Trump and Democrats face tough choices on how to deliver Economy Nov 8, 2026 4:59 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Voters have sent a strong election-year message to the new Democratic congressional majority and President Donald Trump: Repair the damage inflation has done to the economy. Trump, who campaigned on the idea that a Democratic victory in the midterms would trigger a 1929-style economic depression, has maintained that the economy is booming. Since his party lost in Tuesday's voting, he has claimed he is willing to work with Democrats in the House and Senate, though that's not something he has done much of in the past. "I'll get along, probably, with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive," Trump told reporters last week. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. After Friday's strong jobs report showed employers adding 165,000 jobs and the unemployment rate dipping to 4.1%, Trump was defiant. "Democrats may control Congress, but I will NEVER stop fighting for you, and I will VETO anything that hurts America," he said in a text message to his supporters. Democrats are seeking to check Trump's power and are preparing for early fights on government spending. Other challenges include chronic budget deficits, tariffs, artificial intelligence and difficult choices about a Social Security system that could run short of money in as little as six years. But as long as rising prices keep making middle-class lives less affordable, Democrats and Republicans alike face the risk of angering and alienating voters in the next election cycle. "Until inflation and interest rates are under control, the likelihood of change elections is going to be high on an ongoing basis," said Marc Goldwein, senior vice president at the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. Americans want lower prices Trump's tariffs and the war against Iran that he launched in February contributed to the consumer price index climbing to 3.7% annually. The president also tried to bully the Federal Reserve, an independent body tasked with keeping inflation low, to slash its benchmark interest rate in ways that could have worsened inflation. The gridlock of a Republican White House and Democratic Congress gives the Fed more room to maneuver, possibly smoothing the central bank's ability to return inflation to the 2% target it has failed to reach for nearly six years. "I think that one of the surprise winners Tuesday was the Fed," said Douglas Holtz-Eakin, an economist and president of the center-right American Action Forum. READ MORE: AP Voter Poll: The economy and the state of democracy are voters' top issues The Democratic Senate could block Trump's ability to fill potentially open spots on the Fed board, Holtz-Eakin said, removing "Trump's incentives to meddle with the Fed" and clearing a path for Fed Chair Kevin Warsh "to follow his instincts and aggressively reduce inflation." Trump has maintained that the costs of oil, gasoline and diesel will all plummet once the Iran war ends. The problem is he refuses to say when or how the war will come to a conclusion. John Cochrane, an economist at Stanford University's Hoover Institution, stressed that the Fed's efforts to combat inflation would be helped if the federal government reduced budget deficits. "It takes monetary and fiscal restraint," he said. The federal government keeps borrowing about $2 trillion annually The U.S. government keeps amassing debt as tax revenues fall short of burgeoning spending on Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security and other programs. Paying the interest on the national debt now tops $1 trillion annually and exceeds spending on the military. The problem could spiral because investors have pushed up the interest rates charged on government debt over the past year. Neither the White House nor Democrats ran on spending cuts. The president wants an additional $500 billion a year for the military, while some Democratic candidates have pushed for restoring Affordable Care Act subsidies that lapsed under Trump. WATCH: What to know about a better-than-expected jobs report amid AI bubble concerns Since August, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has repeatedly said the administration would put forward a plan to trim the roughly $2 trillion annual budget deficit. Bessent is working with White House budget director Russell Vought on cuts they're branding as a "fiscal consolidation plan," to be released after the election. Deficit reduction would likely require some combination of tax increases and spending cuts, Goldwein said. But he said that the lowest hanging fruit would be to trim Medicare expenditures in ways that save money for both the government and patients. "It's not rocket science," he said. "The most important thing you can do is reduce healthcare costs and find policies that lower the costs of Medicare, which will reduce deficits and interest rates." AI could power stronger growth, but voters have concerns about the technology When Harvard University economist Jason Furman thinks about the most important economic issues facing the United States, AI is at the top of his list. "It's the most screamingly obvious investment boom this country has ever had, or, possibly, second to railroads" in the late 19th century, Furman said. Using AI, Furman has built an economic analysis tool called Econvitals that replicates some of the work done when he was chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers in Democratic President Barack Obama's administrat

1c2c792f9e67.text: By — Savannah Peters, Associated Press Savannah Peters, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/native-american-women-made-history-in-tribal-state-and-federal-elections Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Native American women made history in tribal, state and federal elections Politics Nov 8, 2026 4:15 PM EST ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (AP) — A third-grade field trip to the Navajo Nation Council sparked Crystalyne Curley's political ambition when she witnessed a fiery debate erupt between two tribal lawmakers. "I thought to myself at a very young age, that's where I want to be," Curley said. On Election Day, Curley surpassed that childhood dream and broke a barrier she says she never imagined as a nine-year-old: She was elected the first woman president of the Navajo Nation. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. This week's elections brought a wave of milestone victories, from the nation's first Black female governor to the first openly gay man and first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. It also marked a turning point for Native American women, whose leadership in their families and communities has rarely translated to formal political power. Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman elected to the Senate, Deb Haaland the first to win a state governorship, and Curley the first to lead one of the largest tribes. "This is a win for all Navajo women," Curley told The Associated Press. Jordan James Harvill, a Cherokee Nation citizen and strategist with the advocacy group Advance Native Political Leadership, said decades of political organizing are bearing fruit as more Native women run for and win office. "This is a seismic shift that is happening in our communities," he said. The Navajo Nation elects its first woman president Lene Bitsui supported Curley in the Navajo Nation election because she felt she was best positioned to restore order to the tribal government after what she sees as a period of dysfunction. But when Bitsui cast her ballot, she felt pessimistic. "I thought our people weren't ready for a female president," Bitsui said. "I was wrong, and I feel so happy to have been wrong." The modern, centralized Navajo government has been led by men since its establishment under federal pressure over a century ago. Navajo has the largest land base of any federally recognized tribe, spanning 27,000 square miles (70,000 square kilometers) in Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, and is second in population to the Cherokee Nation in Oklahoma. Some Navajo people believe traditional teachings prohibit women from holding top government positions. Others say women's absence from the presidency stands in contrast to the matrilineal structure of Diné society. READ MORE: The election brought a wave of historic firsts. Here are some groundbreaking winners "You see the language of tradition used to both deride the possibility of a woman being president and to say that women's leadership is needed now," said Jennifer Nez Denetdale, a professor of Diné studies at the University of New Mexico. Curley, who narrowly defeated attorney Justin Jones, according to unofficial results, told the AP she faced sexist rhetoric while campaigning and expects to be held to a higher standard as the first woman president. "As women, we have to work twice or triple as hard, especially within Navajo politics," said Curley, who also was the first female to lead the tribe's legislative branch as speaker of the tribal council. After Curley and her running mate Chris Deschene take office in January, they plan to transition the Navajo Nation away from coal development, historically a major economic engine for the tribe, and reassert its leading role in national discussions around federal Indian policy. The Seneca Nation of Indians in western New York also elected its first woman president, longtime council member Tina Abrams, on Tuesday. Native women make gains in U.S. Congress At her Senate victory celebration in St. Paul, Minnesota, Democrat Flanagan, a citizen of the White Earth Nation and the state's outgoing lieutenant governor, credited supporters from her community. "I could not run for the U. S. Senate without Native women. I could not exist in the way that I do without Native women," Flanagan said. More than 230 years after the U.S. Senate was established, only four Native people have served in the chamber, all men. "This is a win that shows we can break every single glass ceiling," Harvill said. Live Results: Peggy Flanagan wins Senate election in Minnesota Flanagan will join Oklahoma Republican Sen. Tom Cole, a citizen of the Chickasaw Nation. A victory for Democrat Mary Peltola, a Yup'ik woman, in Alaska's still unsettled Senate race, would mark the first time three Native people have served in the chamber simultaneously. In the House, Kansas Democrat Sharice Davids, Ho-Chunk, and Oklahoma Republican Josh Brecheen, Choctaw, won reelection. New York Democrat Claire Valdez, a citizen of Ysleta del Sur Pueblo, and Michigan Democrat Sean McCann, a citizen of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation, became the first Native Americans elected to represent their states in Congress. Deb Haaland notches another first in New Mexico Haaland's political career has been defined by historic milestones. She was one of the first two Native women elected to Congress in 2018 before becoming the first Native American to lead a U.S. Cabinet agency, the Interior Department. Now, in her home state of New Mexico, the Laguna Pueblo citizen, will break ground as the first female Native governor of a U.S. state. "I think it's a long time coming," said Haaland, who traces her ancestry in what is now New Mexico back 800 years. WATCH: New Mexico's Deb Haaland on making history as first Native

008e2f0c0e07.text: Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday dismissed former Trump health adviser Calley Means' corruption allegations against senior White House officials, even as a former FDA commissioner described pressure from tobacco lobbyists and a Republican congressman called for scrutiny. Why it matters: The feud inside President Trump's coalition raises a central question about Trump's health agenda: Were his advisers undermining it, as Means alleges, or were they carrying out the president's wishes? The latest: Asked on CNN's "State of the Union" whether the DOJ would investigate Means' allegations, Blanche responded: "Something that someone says on a podcast? No, I do not listen to that. Absolutely not." Blanche called Means a "disgruntled former administration official" and praised former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles , who Trump announced Friday would be replaced by Stephen Miller . On "Fox News Sunday," Blanche said allegations about Wiles' financial dealings did not concern him. But Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) told CNN that "any allegation of any impropriety like this should be looked at." Driving the news: Means, who alleged widespread corruption in a Friday interview with Joe Rogan, told CBS' "Face the Nation" that he had wanted Wiles removed. Means accused Wiles of blocking an initiative to examine children's sugar consumption because she wanted sugar-industry donations for the midterms. He also alleged that Wiles' deputies pushed policies favorable to the flavored-vaping and kratom industries over the objections of officials working on the Make America Healthy Again agenda. Means accused Trump pollster Tony Fabrizio of advising against defining ultra-processed foods while receiving money from PepsiCo. The White House and the Justice Department did not respond to Axios' request for comment. What they're saying: Former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary backed up part of Means' account in a statement to CBS. "Big tobacco exploited their connections to administration and HHS officials," Makary said, alleging repeated pressure to approve fruit-flavored vapes. Makary said kratom lobbyists similarly tried to undermine his attempts to restrict the substances. He did not identify which officials pressured him. The other side: Former White House adviser James Blair, one of Wiles' allies that Means has accused of wrongdoing, disputed Means' allegations in messages to Axios. "I didn't promote flavored vaping specifically at all," Blair said, adding that he never weighed in on individual applications or which flavors should be approved. Blair said he was following Trump's instructions to ensure the FDA made timely decisions on applications, whether approving or denying them. "The voters elected President Trump. Not me, and not Calley Means," Blair told Axios. He said he never dealt with kratom policy and is reviewing his legal options. When speaking to Axios, Fabrizio called Means' allegation that he was "in the pocket of Big Pharma" "ridiculous" and "demonstrably false," citing his firm's polling showing support for lower prescription drug prices and policies that would cut into pharmaceutical profits. Fabrizio also said he encouraged Republican lawmakers to campaign on Trump's "most favored nation" drug-pricing proposal. In a statement on X, the lobbying firm Ballard Partners took exception to Means' "false" accusations about its interactions with Wiles, who had worked at the company seven years ago. Ballard Partners said it did not lobby Wiles or anyone in the White House on fruit-flavored vapes or another issue Means mentioned, glyphosate, the active ingredient in the weedkiller Roundup, owned by Bayer. In February, Trump outraged MAHA activists by signing an executive order to grant "immunity" to glyphosate producers as Bayer struggled under the weight of lawsuits over roundup. In June, the Supreme Court ruled 7–2 that federal law preempts state lawsuits concerning pesticide sales, thereby making it tougher for people to sue for cancer claims regarding Roundup use. Between the lines: Means has portrayed Trump as unaware of decisions his advisers made. But the Wall Street Journal reported in May that Trump personally pressured Makary to approve flavored vaping products. Pressed by CBS' Margaret Brennan, Means said he did not know whether Trump had called Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. after meeting with tobacco-industry representatives. Means argued advisers manipulated what reached the president and invoked Trump's authority to advance their own priorities. Blair rejected that characterization, telling Axios: "In the White House, I implemented the President's agenda always." Editor's note: This story has been updated with a statement from Ballard Partners.

US President Donald Trump's administration has vowed not to change course on its mass deportation plans after last week's midterm elections defeat.
"This administration will not slow down its efforts to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens who terrorise our communities," the White House said in a statement to the BBC.
Trump's promotion on Friday of immigration hawk Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff had signalled no climbdown from the administration on border security.
Exit polls indicate immigration was the third most important issue for midterm voters, after the economy and the state of democracy.
In historically conservative states like Texas, a swing of Latino voters towards Democrats helped seal the party's landslide congressional majorities.
But multiple US officials sources told the BBC's US partner CBS that the administration had put the midterm losses down to concerns about the economy, affordability and the war with Iran, rather than its immigration crackdown.
The White House maintained on Sunday there would be no change of direction.
"There has never been a President stronger on immigration enforcement than President Trump," said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) also said it would forge ahead.
"ICE is NOT backing away or slowing down," a DHS spokesperson told CBS.
"Under the leadership of President Trump and Secretary Mullin, DHS will continue to enforce our nation's laws and remove criminal illegal aliens from our streets."
Following Tuesday's results, Vice-President JD Vance had appeared receptive to adjusting their immigration strategy.
"I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement - by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labour, for instance," Vance wrote in a lengthy online post reflecting on the results.
But the White House's posture appears to have hardened after Trump promoted Stephen Miller on Friday to become his new chief of staff.
Miller is widely seen as the architect of the administration's hardline immigration policy during the first and second Trump presidencies.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) sources told CBS that in recent weeks officials have been instructed to aim for about 2,700 arrests of illegal immigrants per day, an increase from an earlier 2,000 daily arrest target.
Enforcement sweeps this year spurred anti-ICE demonstrations in cities including Chicago, Minneapolis and Los Angeles.
In Minneapolis, two US protesters, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were fatally shot by immigration agents.

The big picture: The company's board launched an independent investigation into reports that he was targeted by Chinese intelligence. Driving the news: "I owe my family and all of you an apology," Huang wrote in a draft email to Nvidia employees obtained by Axios. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did." Huang said he took "full responsibility" for his actions, adding that he had fallen short of his responsibilities to Nvidia's employees, board and shareholders. "Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life," Huang wrote. "I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence." Meanwhile: Nvidia's board said an independent committee, assisted by outside counsel, will investigate the matter. The board said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised and expressed confidence in Huang's leadership. Flashback: Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned top Trump officials about Huang's relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believed was a Chinese spy, The New York Times reported Friday. The woman, Alice Huang, was recruited to seek information and potentially push for Nvidia's advanced chips to be made available in China, countering existing restrictions, the Times reported. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," John Rizzo, head of public policy communications at Nvidia said in a statement.

ff03caaaf5f2.text: By — Rafal Niedzielski, Associated Press Rafal Niedzielski, Associated Press By — Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press By — Beata Zawrzel, Associated Press Beata Zawrzel, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/poles-mourn-rare-mass-killing-as-authorities-say-attacker-had-far-right-views Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Poles mourn rare mass killing as authorities say attacker had far-right views World Updated on Nov 8, 2026 5:14 PM EST — Published on Nov 8, 2026 3:02 PM EST KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — Mourners on Sunday laid candles and flowers alongside bullet holes in Krakow, Poland, after the city's central square turned into a site of bloodshed and grief. A 24-year-old man with far-right views opened fire a day earlier, killing six people and wounding 15 before police shot and wounded him. Poland on Sunday began two days of national mourning following the attack the day before, which Poland's defense minister described as an "act of terror." The violence began Saturday at around 3 p.m. when the assailant drove through the Main Square, in the heart of Krakow's Old Town. The square is a major tourist hub in the country's second-largest city. READ MORE: Gunman opens fire in Polish city of Krakow, killing 6 people and wounding 16 St. Mary's Trumpet Call, a traditional five-note melody played every hour from the highest tower of St. Mary's Basilica on the Main Square, was paused overnight, the first time the call had been missed since World War II. On Sunday afternoon, St. Anne's Church in Krakow filled with mourners attending a memorial service. The square reopened soon after and locals and visitors alike showed up to reclaim it after the tragedy. "I come here so as not to get caught up in a spiral of fear and anxiety," Krakow local Maciej Sikorski told The Associated Press from the square. "In a situation like this, it's all too easy to stop living — to start being afraid instead, and just vegetate. That is something I really want to avoid." Authorities also found the bodies of the assailant's sister, mother and father at the man's family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow. They likely died from gunshot wounds. Woman injured by shrapnel while saving another Witness Andy Hill told the BBC that he'd felt as though he was in a movie scene. "It doesn't feel real," the British tourist said. "And the trouble is, you have such an instantaneous moment to make a decision: Run. Stand still. There's an element of shock. But I just thought the easiest thing to do is dive through a doorway and just take refuge behind the windows." Warsaw native Magdalena Frączak, meanwhile, was visiting Krakow with her friend when shots rang out and the gunman drew closer. "I threw an elderly woman behind the flower planter because she had become tangled in the blanket she had on her lap. I covered her with my body," Frączak told the AP. "I also saw him out of the corner of my eye — he passed just one meter behind my back. That's why I have shrapnel wounds in six places on my back. Only after he had passed did I pull the woman up, and we ran into a café." People gather by a makeshift memorial in the Main Market Square as authorities reopen the area to the public following the Saturday mass shooting in Krakow, Poland, on Nov. 8, 2026. Photo by Jakub Porzycki/Reuters On Sunday, she forced herself to return to the Main Square to grieve among other mourners. "I can't put it into words. Because I knew that I would never come back to Krakow if I didn't come in here," she said. "When I found out that they had reopened the Main Market Square, I told my friend that I had to come here." American tourist Marylin Green mourned the losses in the "beautiful city" during her first trip to Poland that also included the capital. "I'm Polish, my parents were from here," she said. "I loved Warsaw. So I was really looking forward to coming here, too." Police officers described as heroes Prosecutors said Sunday they opened an investigation into the murder and attempted murder of numerous people, including police officers, with the act "constituting a terrorist offense." Four women and two men were killed in the shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, Krzysztof Jan Klęczar, the Malopolska regional governor, said on Sunday. A man from the U.K. and a woman from Austria were also among the dead. A video posted on social media showed a police officer repeatedly shooting the attacker, who was lying on the street. The officer later slowly collapsed to the ground. The two police officers who stopped the gunman, in actions authorities hailed as heroic, remain in the hospital. They were both conscious by Sunday afternoon. "If it weren't for the efficient and selfless intervention of these two young men, the number of victims could have been significantly higher," Klęczar said. Michał Pędziwiatr and Mateusz Wierdak, two local surgeons who were having a bite to eat nearby, also stepped in. WATCH: Ukrainian refugees face growing hostility in Poland Wierdak "took care of the officer who subdued the attacker because he truly needed urgent help," Pędziwiatr told the Polish news website onet. "Without protection, without gloves, he simply focused on the officer, stopping the bleeding in his chest. This probably saved his life." Five foreigners are among the wounded. They come from the U.K., Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria. The suspect is also in critical condition after undergoing multiple surgeries. There was confusion on Saturday about his age, with authorities first saying 24 and later 25. On Sunday they confirmed that he is 24. The suspect's dead sibling was a young artist studying at the Krakow Academy of Fine Arts. "Nothing will ever be like before. A print by a Yorkshire artist commissioned by Nasa in the early days of space travel will go on show as part of a pop art exhibition.
Komtek I by Michael Fossick, who studied at Bradford School of Art, was created in 1962 to celebrate a Hong Kong company that produced microcomputers in the early days of space travel.
The print was part of a Nasa project to document the effort of sending the first humans to the moon and is on display as part of the Pop Art at Cartwright Hall exhibition.
The display tells the story of the British International Print Biennale, which took place at the Bradford gallery on 11 occasions between 1968 and 1990, and runs until March 2027.
While the exhibition also includes work by Andy Warhol and David Hockney, there is "definitely stuff that people won't have seen before", said curator Jill Iredale.
"It's a completely bizarre sort of connection somehow that an artist born in Sheffield that went to Bradford School of Art was somehow commissioned by Nasa," said Iredale.
"It was actually a screen print, but it was made from a very early computerised image," she said.
In March 1962, Nasa administrator James Webb awarded commissions to 38 artists, including Fossick, to document the space agency's achievements.
John H. Glenn became the first American to orbit the earth on 20 February 1962 and in the following decade Nasa's Mercury programme led to the Apollo missions, and eventually to Neil Armstrong setting foot on the moon in 1969.
Fossick chose to honour Komtek I, a microcomputer produced by Komtek Technologies Ltd in Hong Kong that was significant in the early years of the space programme.
He submitted the print to the First British International Print Biennale held at Cartwright Hall in 1968 where it won a prize.
Created by a group of local print makers and artists, at its height the British International Print Biennale included more than 500 works selected from more than 3,000 entries.
It received work by artists such as Andy Warhol, Roy Licthenstein and David Hockney, which remain in the gallery today.
Hockney was invited to be a judge on the first biennial in 1968 and created the poster for the show, which is on display in the exhibition.
Iredale said the pop art explosion in Bradford was a reaction to the seriousness of the World War Two and the boost in commercial print culture.
"Bradford had quite a strong, experimental kind of light, pretty kind of DIY aesthetic with artists and with the college as well," she explained.
"There was simply loads more young people around, post-baby boom, and an increase in opportunities for working-class youth."

How many clothes, items of bedding and other fabric have you thrown away this year?
While resale sites are growing in popularity, in the UK we still bin about 711,000 tonnes of textiles annually, external â roughly the weight of seven US aircraft carriers, external.
The global fashion and textiles industry is one of the most wasteful, but recycling firms in Peterborough and Northamptonshire are using technology to change that.
They are gaining the attention of major brands but say they need laws, as well as consumers, to support them.
In a warehouse next to the A14 in Kettering, a mountain of crumpled fabric is slowly fed into a machine.
There are dressing gowns, duvets, branded banners and lanyards from events including the Commonwealth Games.
All are made from polyester â the world's most commonly used textile fibre â and all have been thrown away.
Traditionally they would be burned or buried in landfill but Project Re:Claim is trying to change that.
The partnership between The Salvation Army's trading arm (SATCoL) and Plan B Circular operates what they say is the first commercial-scale polyester textile-to-textile recycling facility in Europe â technology adapted from a bottle recycling plant.
The Salvation Army collects the items and those that cannot be reused in their current form are shredded and melted.
Impurities such as dead skin cells and hair are removed and polyester pellets (rPET) are produced which can be used to make new clothes.
"It's the future: using the clothing we have today to make the clothing that we need tomorrow," says Plan B Circular founder Tim Cross.
"We process 500kg of fabric an hour but we could easily scale up if there was demand.
"The problem is encouraging clothing manufacturers to change from using virgin polyester to recycled polyester from old textiles. And to design their new clothes to be easily recycled at their end of life."
"A polyester blazer doesn't need nylon buttons and labels. A sports top doesn't need metal zips. It can all be polyester."
That is important because the plant can only recycle items that are 100% polyester.
Most clothing "is a fibre mix like polyester-cotton, or often three or four different materials," says Majonne Frost, head of sustainability at SATCoL.
Researchers are trialling ways to separate these fibres, external, but doing it at scale remains difficult and costly, so most of those items are eventually destroyed.
Project Re:Claim says its rPET requires 89% less carbon to make than virgin polyester.
"We send the pellets back to China in what would otherwise be empty shipping containers, and it's spun back into yarn," Cross adds.
"We have the technology but we're way behind with legislation. It absolutely should be driving the way we design and make clothing."
EU rules are already changing, external and are forcing manufacturers to reduce the waste they produce, their environmental impact, and to make the industry circular.
It must ensure products are not only made from recycled content but are themselves recyclable at the end of their lives.
The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, external (Defra) says it is "funding the UK Textiles Pact, external, which is driving ambitious targets to cut waste and increase the life cycle of materials".
However, that scheme is voluntary.
In addition, Defra says "a taskforce of experts and businesses is looking at options to reduce waste in homes and businesses and will report back on next steps later this year".
Peterborough-based Gen Phoenix feels global consumer attitudes and legislation are beginning to drive change.
Every year it recycles thousands of tonnes of waste leather into new fabric which has been used by major brands, including Dr Martens, Nike and Coach.
It also specialises in train, bus and aviation seating.
"Jet2 was our first commercial customer, and now we're on one in every five commercial aircraft flying today," says chief executive John Kennedy.
"Our material has similar properties to traditional leather but with an 80% lower carbon footprint and it's lighter. Weight is important for airlines.
"We've saved more than 18,000 tonnes of material from landfill."
Leather is itself a waste product from the food industry, but still much is wasted that Gen Phoenix feels could be salvaged.
"If you think of an animal hide, it's the bits like the neck, the shoulders, the armpits, the belly â bits that don't make good finished leather," says Richard Peace, the company's senior director of research and technology.
The company ships in the waste as "wet blue" â the name given to hides partway through the leather process â from tanneries around the world.
It breaks the leather down into a fibre fluff, which is sprayed on to thin sheets of tissue paper.
The sheets are then sandwiched around a fabric â usually recycled polyester â before high-powered water jets bind all the fibres back together.
Called hydro-entanglement, it forms the new fabric without the need for resin binders, making the new product more easily recyclable.
"The importance of sustainability is seeing a groundswell, both in terms of legislation and consumer attitude - especially with Gen Z coming through," says Kennedy.
"Brands are definitely more invested and are being fairly quiet about the great work they're doing.
"We're continuing to innovate and expand, looking at recycling end process leather too.
"Peterborough is where we do all of our manufacturing and R&D (research and development), and while we may establish other sites, this is where the magic happens."

Jensen Huang is one of the technology industry's most high-profile figures.
He rose to prominence as the business he leads - artificial intelligence (AI) chip giant Nvidia - became one of the world's most valuable companies.
As the face of the AI boom, Huang also became close to Donald Trump as the president pushed for the US to keep its dominance of the technology over China.
The 63-year-old who was once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" and referred to as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan is now mired in scandal after an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Who is Jensen Huang?
Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US.
He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia.
He has an estimated fortune of $155bn, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.
"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine - a biography on Huang, tells the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang.
Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged.
"I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country".
Huang has long found himself at the centre of US-China tensions. Trump has repeatedly said the two nations are in a race for dominance.
Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities.
The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips.
Since 2022 the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security.
But it means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Jensen Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. In recent years Huang has engaged in a flurry of shuttle diplomacy, dashing between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way.
Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China.
Quarter after quarter of late, Nvidia has been locked out of that lucrative market. Despite his ostensible closeness to Trump, Huang has not managed to wrest this concession from the administration.
What is Nvidia?
Huang founded Nvidia with fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993.
The company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games.
Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates.
"In 2012 these machine learning neural net researchers started to use it for that purpose and Jensen immediately recongnised that this was going to be a massive industry and the future of computing. He began to pour enormous amounts of resources into building what was essentially the AI hardware market," says Witt.
"Today when we think of that, we think of these giant data centres - none of that existed. There were no customers for the stuff he was building. In fact his first customer was Open AI at the time they had 30 people - he actually gave it to them, he donated it to them."
Nvidia is now worth some $4.5 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies ever.
"The first real neural net of modern times on an Nvidia network was Alex Krizhevsky's Alexnet and they trained that on two Nvidia cards in Alex's bedroom. Now we do the same thing but we do it with 200,000 - 300,000 cards and instead of doing it in a bedroom we do it in a giant barn full of computers called a data centre," adds Witt.
"So when you think about a data centre buildout, when you hear the AI infrastructure buildout, Jensen runs a tollbooth. All of that goes through him. And it made his company at least temporarily, the most valuable company in the world."
Nvidia's board has announced a probe following reports by the New York Times that Huang had engaged in a romantic relationship with a woman believed by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy.
For now, though, Nvidia's board appears to have little appetite for removing Huang, saying in a statement on Sunday that they have "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team".
Sources tell the BBC his removal is unlikely because there is so much money at stake. There is also no clear successor to the 63-year old tech boss.
Who is Huang's wife?
Huang met his wife Lori at Oregon State University, where she was also studying electrical engineering and was his lab partner.
They married in 1985, about eight years before he co-founded Nvidia, and have two children, Madison and Spencer.
He has credited Lori and Madison for making black leather jackets his signature style.
In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation.
The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn.
Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University.

A charity wants to raise Â£70,000 for a project aimed at boosting wildlife populations on farmland in the Thames Valley.
The Berkshire, Buckinghamshire and Oxfordshire Wildlife Trust (BBOWT) said the money would form part of its Nature Recovery Fund and would be used to tackle falling numbers of birds, bees and butterflies.
The trust said farmland bird populations had fallen by 63% since 1970, while half of the UK's 27 bumblebee species were in decline.
It said measures to help wildlife could include using fewer chemicals in farming to create healthier soil and less polluted waterways, as well as setting aside corners of grassland for animals.
BBOWT's chief executive Estelle Bailey said: "Farmland makes up 68% of our three counties, so to truly have an impact on nature's recovery, our work must expand far beyond our precious nature reserves."
In 2023, a report produced by government agencies, environmental groups and universities found one in six species in the UK were at risk of extinction.
Bailey added: "I want future generations to experience the joy of countryside filled with life - swallows darting above fields, butterflies and bumblebees feeding on abundant wildflowers, hedgerows alive with the sound of birdsong, and to eat locally grown food that supports a healthy, resilient landscape."

Warning: Strong language and descriptions of sexual violence
Although she had just bought hashish from a drug dealer, the woman decided to call the police.
It was because, along with the illegal drugs, she had been handed a note by the young seller during their brief meeting on a Marseille housing estate in 2022.
"We're being held captive and need help. We are 15-years-old," it read.
The teenage dealer, a French court heard earlier this year, was one of two boys being held by a gang which they had both initially approached looking for paid work - albeit illegal.
One boy had been tasked with handling money, the other worked streets around the Frais-Vallon estate. Soon though, bosses had accused them of being responsible for "shortfalls" in takings.
What followed were regular beatings, the court was told, and being forced to dance naked in front of a camera as a form of blackmail. One of the boys was also raped.
Hours after the woman was passed the note, the two teenagers had tried to escape from a second-storey window, injuring themselves in the process. One managed to get away, while the other was caught, beaten and stabbed, but survived.
Arrests were made. Photos on the phone of one of the boys' alleged torturers showed several other young men in a similarly distressed condition. Six men have since been handed hefty sentences for what happened to the two teenagers.
The boys' story highlights the grip that drug gangs hold over parts of France's second city.
While the blend of Mediterranean culture, street art and hip-hop scene has made Marseille a popular tourist destination - beyond the city centre, it is another story.
After months of trying, a BBC team managed to enter this dangerous world - centred on deprived streets and high-rise housing estates in the port city, which police do not enter lightly.
We found an environment where ruthless gangs lure vulnerable young people with promises of easy money, but end up trapping them in a world of drug dealing, brutality and exploitation.
We saw how gangs use social media to recruit hitmen and spoke to several young men caught up in the violence. From prison, one gang member accused of involvement in several murders explained how his "cold-bloodedness" had helped him rise through the ranks.
The city's most powerful gang, DZ Mafia, emerged victorious from a bloody turf war and is now one of the most feared criminal organisations in France.
DZ is the official internet country code for Algeria, where one of the gang's founders, a French-Algerian called Mehdi Laribi, was detained earlier this year under a French arrest warrant.
The criminal outfit rose to prominence in 2023, when it became the first French gang to capitalise on its notoriety by releasing video statements - using social media to market itself as a brand - says the head of the country's anti-drug trafficking unit, Dimitri Zoulas.
Its most recent statement came in July, when the mayor of a nearby town had to be placed in police protection, after intelligence suggested he was in danger of being targeted by the group.
In an online video, six masked men dressed in black stood behind a table - as one of them read a statement denying DZ Mafia's involvement.
France's expanding illegal drugs market - which has seen a surge in cocaine imports alongside high volumes of cannabis and synthetic drugs - has also helped the gang grow rapidly.
The number of cocaine users in France is expected soon to reach two million, says Zoulas, up from 600,000 in 2017. Drug smuggling across France generates â¬7bn (Â£5.9bn) a year, involving 200,000 people, he adds.
Many of those distributing the drugs are children and the authorities say the number of minors caught up in trafficking is increasing. During 2025, more than 10,000 children were involved in some way, according to official figures.
DZ Mafia is a prime example. To reach more customers, it needs more gang members - more children.
We have found it is now recruiting young people from across France - not just to sell drugs, but to carry out kidnap, torture and murder.
They are a generation seen as easy to corrupt, but also expendable, by the kingpins who typically control them from prison or overseas.
And, as police and judges warn, once these children enter Marseille's underworld, it is very hard to get them out.
Few know the human cost of Marseille's gangs like mother Karine Brouillard - who lives at the other end of France, almost as far from the Mediterranean coast as you can get.
Her son, Hugo, first ran away aged 15 - from his home in a village in the Nord department - after an argument with his family. He was picked up by police three days later, almost 1,000km (600 miles) away in Marseille, with money and cannabis on him. He was taken home.
But several years later, in 2023, Hugo planned to return south, telling his parents he had secured a holiday job at a restaurant near Marseille.
"He gave regular updates," Karine remembers. "He called me, everything was going well."
Three weeks later, a doctor called. Karine says she will never forget his words: "Your son arrived last night. He took a bullet to the head."
Police believe Hugo was brought for medical help from a gang-controlled area and suspect he was involved with one.
That area was Quartier Nord.
Our best way into Quartier Nord, where DZ Mafia wields power, is with the help of resident Fadella Ouidef, a 41-year-old mother-of-four who gives us a tour.
Thirty-seven seconds after entering one housing estate, we find ourselves cornered.
Car horns sound the moment Fadella's Peugeot passes a gang checkpoint - the teenagers manning the post immediately spot our camera. "Wait, stop filming," Fadella warns, as a grey 4x4 forces us to the side of the road.
"I'm making a report for my housing association," she tells the inquisitive driver. He eventually agrees to let us leave if we stop filming.
It is unnerving to see a non-police vehicle move so assertively and a relief to watch it leave.

Pope Leo XIV has said Argentina's economy must benefit everyone including the poor, in a diplomatic but pointed critique of President Javier Milei's austerity measures.
The Pope was speaking as he arrived in Buenos Aires, the second stop on a 12-day tour of Latin America, only three weeks after having had surgery for lung cancer.
In response, right-wing leader Milei said his government was working to avoid "punishing the Argentines of tomorrow in order to benefit the Argentines of today".
This leg of the Pope's journey was expected be the most politically sensitive, with the president's agenda of slashing public spending having been denounced by the Catholic Church for hitting the poorest hardest.
"The economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy," Pope Leo said.
He stressed the plight of those who, "despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household's needs", and urged that "particular concern be shown for those affected by illness, dependency and disability" - a veiled reference to the government's controversial cuts to disability assistance.
In what appeared to be a rebuke of Milei's combative style and language, the Pope said strengthening democracy required a "willingness to listen" and the "careful use of words".
Milei had been particularly outspoken about Leo's predecessor Pope Francis, whom he called "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor.
On Sunday, however, Milei struck a conciliatory tone, calling Francis an "exceptional figure" and "undoubtedly the most important Argentine in history".
He was also keen to welcome the current Pope earlier, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy".
Pope Leo urged Argentina to safeguard its democracy. "Those who exercise authority have a duty to act with prudence, to acknowledge the limits of the power entrusted to them, and to direct their decisions toward the good of the entire community," he said.
In his own address welcoming Leo to Argentina, Milei defended his libertarian policies, saying the rights to life, liberty and property are the backbone of Argentina's constitution and of Western democracies.
The Argentine leader, who has said he will seek re-election next year, is a strong supporter of US President Donald Trump, who has criticised Pope Leo for his opposition to the Iran war.
Pope Leo's trip to Argentina has been described as a homage to Francis, who did not return to his homeland during his own papacy.
The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.

Thereâs little precedent in US corporate history for the crisis facing Nvidia after reports that Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese âhoneytrapâ operation. The national security implications of the allegation, the chipmakerâs founder-CEOâs centrality to his companyâs growth story, and Nvidiaâs pivotal place in the AI ecosystem all mean the fallout is likely to stretch further than other cases of executive infidelity.
Nvidiaâs board on Sunday announced an independent investigation, but expressed confidence in Huang. In his own statement admitting that he had been unfaithful to his wife, Huang said he remained âfully committedâ to the company.
Nvidia is, at the time of writing, the worldâs second-most valuable company after Apple, with a market capitalization of $4.5 trillion â almost 12% of the Nasdaq 100 index. And no public company has been more important to the AI revolution or its impact on stock markets: The ravenous appetite from hyperscalers such as Amazon and Google for Nvidiaâs chips propelled its annual revenue from under $11 billion to more than $130 billion between 2020 and 2025. The most bullish analysts think its sales will hit $1 trillion in 2029.
Huangâs personal indiscretions do not change Nvidiaâs order book. But he has been inseparable from its commercial success story, helming its new product presentations, negotiating the loans to customers that have made Nvidia âthe central bank of AI,â and dealing directly with President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a moment when access to the worldâs most advanced AI chips has been called âthe defining strategic questionâ facing the two superpowers. On Sunday, Sequoiaâs Shaun Maguire, a Huang supporter, called him âirreplaceable for Americaâs AI leadership.â
The nod to earlier US intelligence warnings that China is targeting US tech leaders will serve as a cautionary tale for many of Huangâs peers in Silicon Valley. Meanwhile, any challenge to investorsâ confidence in Huangâs leadership, or any allegation that his personal relationship influenced Nvidiaâs lobbying in Washington, could have serious implications for his position and his companyâs valuation. Nvidiaâs stock already took a beating from a wider reversal in chip stocks as US votersâ protests against data centers shook confidence in the marketâs AI trade.
Extramarital affairs and relationships that were not disclosed to board members have felled CEOs at companies as prominent as Boeing and McDonaldâs in the past. In many cases, boards and investors focused on ethical breaches, such as executives using company funds inappropriately or advancing the careers of romantic partners who reported to them.
The allegations about Huang are more serious, but the reaction to those past peccadilloes offers some clues to what Nvidia can now expect. Directors will now face questions about when it knew of the allegations, and whether the earlier investigation it reportedly conducted was thorough enough. That could test a board that is short on corporate heavy-hitters â thereâs not one sitting CEO on the board other than Huang â or people with deep experience of national security or political crisis management.
The company can also expect litigation from shareholders, and possible regulatory action, if Huang or the board held back material information from investors (Nvidia previously denied the allegations of an affair to media outlets). And Huang is unlikely to avoid high-profile investigations from Congress, whose incoming Democratic-led majority is suspicious of Big Tech CEOs and is already preparing a rash of subpoenas for Trump allies.
Huang, unlike many other Silicon Valley founders, is not in control of his own fate: He has run Nvidia as if he fully controls it, but he lacks the dual-class stock that shields tech founders like Metaâs Mark Zuckerberg and Alphabet cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin. While his near-4% stake gave him a net worth of $155 billion at Fridayâs close, it does not protect him should the board or investors try to oust him.
For now, that outcome looks unlikely. There is no obvious successor waiting in the wings, lawmakers are fully aware of Nvidiaâs strategic significance to the US, and Wall Street knows Huang as a brilliant founder who has made fortunes for his shareholders. Bill Ackman, the hedge fund manager, was among the investors urging support for Huang on Sunday.
Huang has promised to cooperate with the investigation his board has launched. He has no choice. Investors who struggle to imagine Nvidia without him have $4.5 trillion reasons to hope and expect that he rides out this crisis. But his serious lapse in judgment will dent confidence in one of the worldâs most consequential companies, at the very moment when investors have shown that their faith in the marketâs AI growth story has limits.

A cruise ship pianist was found treading water around 20 miles (32km) off the Californian coast after falling overboard, according to US media reports.
Two fishermen discovered the Royal Caribbean employee near Catalina Island on Friday and officials believe he may have been in the Pacific Ocean for nine hours, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.
"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat; let's get all of our lines in," Grant Garrett was quoted as saying, recalling the moment he and Sean Norton spotted him.
The man, who has not yet been identified, was taken to hospital in a stable condition, the US Coast Guard told the BBC, adding it was investigating the incident.
The fishermen say the man identified himself as a pianist on a 14-deck cruise ship called the Ovation of the Seas.
"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.
The Coast Guard said in a statement it had received a report from "a Good Samaritan who recovered a conscious individual from the water".
The person was handed over to Newport Beach Lifeguards, who confirmed he was an employee of the Ovation of the Seas cruise ship, it said.
Lifeguard officials believe he may have fallen overboard at around 02:30, about nine hours before he was discovered.
"It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean," Newport Beach Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told CBS.
Norton credited the man's survival to unusually warm ocean temperatures.
"You have this crazy super El NiÃ±o year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water's 76 degrees," Norton said, which equates to about 24C.
"A different year, no way he makes it," Norton said.
The developing El NiÃ±o climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring the Pacific, with ocean temperatures about 3.05C above average.
In a statement to the BBC, a Royal Caribbean Group spokesperson said: "We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time.
"To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."

The News
Opponents of AI-powered cars have been using artificial intelligence to get their message out in the news media.
Theyâve been waging a kitchen sink campaign, placing op-eds in local news outlets arguing the autonomous taxi company Waymo could cost jobs, endanger riders, deprive the government of information, and block fire trucks. The AI detection service Pangram found that many of the pieces were written with a significant amount of AI input, but none contain labels disclosing AI use.
Several op-eds were drafted by a PR firm, said Ira Goldstein, the former head of New Yorkâs Black Car Fund and the author of an op-ed in the New York Daily News.
âA first draft of this OpEd was prepared by our PR firm at the time, which is standard procedure when working with a PR firm. I reviewed the OpEd, and made some edits. The PR firm then handled placement in the Daily News,â Goldstein told Semafor in a statement.
âWith all that said, I stand by every word in this OpEd and believe that AI being used without my knowledge, to write a first draft of a 700-word opinion piece pales in comparison to the economic and public safety damage that thousands of AI powered robotaxis will inflict on New York City.â
(In the same statement, Goldstein said the PR firm in question later last year also dropped the campaign to work for â¦ Waymo.)
The campaign also included series of op-eds for the Dallas Morning News on autonomous vehicle accidents by local lawyer Amy Witherite, which registered as 95% AI-written and 71% AI written, respectively, on Pangram; a San Francisco Chronicle article warning about how autonomous vehicles could go dormant in public streets during power outages, whose text Pangram reported was 88% generated by AI; another Daily News piece that Pangram said the piece was 68% AI-written; a San Diego Union-Tribune piece arguing that autonomous vehicles would likely displace jobs that registered as 95% likely AI-generated text; and a Times of San Diego piece about how the city should track Waymoâs rollout, 87% of which was likely written with AI assistance.
âLike many, many writers, I use AI tools for research, to sometimes test my arguments, help organize my thinking, and make my writing as clear as possible. These tools are a fact of modern life and modern writing,â said Michael Redmond, the San Francisco Chronicle author. Chronicle editor Matt Fleischer told Semafor that the news organizationâs policies were to ask opinion writers to disclose whether they had used AI.
David Margulies, a spokesperson for Amy Witherite, the author of the Dallas Morning News article, said the firm that runs her communications helps develop, draft, edit and place these pieces, and âsometimes use AI tools to monitor media coverage, develop press lists and to prepare initial drafts, which are then reviewed, edited by our staff, fact-checked and reviewed with Amy or other attorneys in the firm before she gives her comments and final approval.â
âAI is just being used as a shiny object to try to change the subject. It wonât work. Every piece published under Amyâs name reflects her views. They are personally reviewed and approved by her before submission,â he said.
âLimited use of AI for research or polishing doesnât automatically disqualify a submission, but we donât accept pieces generated entirely by AI,â Dallas Morning News commentary editor Ryan Sanders said in an email.
Andrew Julien, executive editor at the Daily News, said in an email the organization aims to create stricter guardrails against AI on the site, given the publicationâs ongoing litigation against Microsoft and OpenAI.
The paper feels âstrongly that our readers deserve original opinions â certainly not machine-generated content created by companies we are suing over billions of dollars they owe us for stealing our content.â
The tokens burned spitting out anti-Waymo opinions are part of a monthslong battle between Waymo and its rivals over whether the autonomous driving company can operate commercially on the streets of several major cities.
The Washington Post reported this month that the Coalition for Accountability and Road Safety, a group of Waymo opponents, spent more than $2.6 million on ads in the DC area in 2026, a greater sum than the winning mayoral candidate spent in the same year. Waymo operates commercially in 15 US cities, but has faced opposition from labor unions, ride-hailing giants such as Uber and Lyft, and various AI-skeptical groups and pedestrian safety advocates.
Maxâs view
AI writing has become a fact of life for billions of people around the world, raising questions within the media and academia about the value of and standards for human-written text.
The realm of authorship in the opinion section has also always been a bit dubious. As Semafor tech reporter JD Capeluto wrote earlier this year: âNewspaper op-eds from big names have long been ghostwritten by junior staffers or outside PR firms â no disclosure necessary, and often watered down and hyper-optimized to be as palatable as possible. In that sense, outsourcing to AI is just replacing one form of slop with another. Just look at LinkedIn, where many cringe human-generated posts have been replaced by AI.â
All that may be true. But for media organizations, allowing the proliferation of AI seems more likely to dilute, rather than enrich, the ultimate product. In a world where chatbots and agents easily answer most generic questions for free, the value of news organizations seeking payment from readers could be to provide a perspective that audiences know has been verified by a human being.
Room for Disagreement
To certain journalists, thereâs little point in distinguishing between AI and human authorship now that many people use AI to research and draft. In a precedent-setting move earlier this year, The Wall Street Journalâs opinion editor declared that AI-generated submissions from notable figures were fine, and didnât need disclosure, so long as they were newsworthy,

The longtime executive producer of 60 Minutes said heâs unimpressed with his successors and disappointed that the show had missed an opportunity to press Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the Iran war.
Bill Owens, who resigned last April in protest of what he saw as editorial overreach that was tilting the show in favor of President Donald Trumpâs administration, argued an interview at Semaforâs New Media & Marketing Playbook event in New York that while 60 Minutes may look and feel the same to many viewers, the quality of the show has declined.
When asked what he thinks now of the show he used to oversee, Owens succinctly replied: âNot a lot.â
âThey own the company, they can do whatever they want,â he said of CBS parent company Skydanceâs new leadership. âBut the ratings are telling.â
âThereâs no doubt that linear television is in decline. But the numbers the other day were less than 6 million people. Itâs like the evening news. 60 Minutes? That would have freaked me out,â he said.
Semafor editor-in-chief Ben Smith noted that the new iteration of 60 Minutes had aired segments on alleged corruption in the Trump administration, and to many viewers the show was nearly indistinguishable from the old version. Owens singled out the news organizationâs recent interview with Hegseth, arguing that what the networkâs journalists didnât ask was notable.
âSome of it is subjective. But other things are just questions that need to be asked,â he said, adding: âThey didnât ask how the war was going. â¦ I would have turned to the producing team and screamed bloody murder.â
Owens, who starts in March as executive producer of the YouTube-native outlet Newpress, acknowledged that his resignation in 2025 hadnât had the intended impact, and may have actually prompted a broader network realignment that has seen many on-air personalities and top producers leave.
âWhen I left, I really hoped that I was going to cause enough of a commotion that they would kind of back off. And the people, my senior team, the correspondents, theyâve tried their best,â he said. âBut itâs just a really difficult circumstance.â

The News
By January 2025, Paulina Mangubat knew the Democratic National Committee needed to change its digital communications approach dramatically.
The organization had been shattered by a second loss to Donald Trump, in which the party had been strategically outmaneuvered by a new alternative media ecosystem that had helped Republicans circumvent traditional gatekeepers. The DNC didnât have an online creator strategy beyond one Signal group chat with about 20 left-leaning creators, where it occasionally shared messaging. Its brand had never quite recovered from the 2016 campaign, when it was thought to have tipped the scales against then-presidential candidate Bernie Sanders.
Voters saw the national party as overly invested in outreach tactics of the past, as exemplified by a widely-mocked February 2025 post in which its official X account shared a long, hard-to-read list of Democratic accomplishments.
That spring, staff met at a weeklong offsite to regroup, and Mangubat, the head of content and creative, opened with a presentation of comments the DNC was getting on social media.
âOur team took a lot of the online criticism to heart,â she recalled Friday.
The committee decided to make a few key changes. Most visibly, it took a more combative and at times personal tone, an approach mirroring the national mood of Democratic voters. It changed the Republican party logo to one labeled âpedo protectors,â invoking Trumpâs connections to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. And after White House senior aide Stephen Miller wrote on X that Texas Democrat James Talarico was the partyâs âfirst transgender Senate candidate,â the DNCâs account replied, âshut up you ugly f*ck.â
The DNC started posting faster, shortening a previously labored back-and-forth approval process to just 15 minutes between drafting and publishing. DNC senior strategist Tim Hogan told Semafor that the committee reoriented its internal leadership structure, empowering its most online staff to make decisions with less oversight from skittish traditional political operatives.
âPut the posters in charge,â Hogan said.
But it also decided to take a more behind-the-scenes approach. The DNCâs toxic brand among some audiences was hampering the reach of its posts. In early 2025, the organization relaunched its rapid response online efforts under a new brand, @FactPostNews, an account intentionally designed to look like an independent news aggregator, not a messaging arm of the party.
âIf you talked to the admins of some accounts, they wouldnât even realize that they were essentially pushing DNC messaging to their audiences who were not explicitly political,â Mangubat said of some users sharing their content.
Mangubat noted that the DNC had hired researchers to monitor and dig up negative material on Republicans, largely in the form of video clips from little-noticed interviews on podcasts or public channels. It needed a better way, though, to seed that information to its audiences and voters online.
So the committee created a clip library, and began to grow its group of unpaid influencers. The DNC would distribute what it saw as embarrassing or damaging clips of Trump or other administration officials to its one-way Signal group chat, which by October had swelled to more than 700 creators. Instead of sharing talking points or bland DNC messaging, the national partyâs communications team decided to simply share clips and let the creators decide whether or how to use them.
Once the primaries were over, the party set up group chats with Democratic campaignsâ digital directors to help them share negative and positive video clips. Jon Ossoffâs campaign, for example, quickly shared highly-produced clips from his rallies to the Signal chat and the partyâs unpaid creators, who helped the Georgia senator become a viral sensation and elevated his profile significantly.
âWe were not really concerned with being credited or receiving attribution,â Mangubat said. âWe were mostly interested in increasing the surface area of our messaging on every single part of the internet.â
While much of its focus was on X, TikTok, and Instagram Reels, the national party also began ramping up production of original longform content for YouTube. Mangubat said the DNC sent its video team out into the country to find farmers and others impacted by Trump administration decisions and created mini documentaries for YouTube, which it then chopped up into clips and distributed across other social platforms.
Maxâs view
A decade of politics that began with Michelle Obamaâs 2016 mantra, âWhen they go low, we go high,â has concluded with âshut up you ugly f*ck.â
For years, the party had struggled to push back against Trumpâs messaging; his bluntness, sensationalism, aggression, and comedic looseness were perfectly suited for the algorithmic-driven online communications environment. Rudeness, when in the spirit of resistance to the partyâs opponents, has clearly proven popular with its base.
But the DNCâs approach may carry more lasting lessons. Clearly, it worked: The clips it distributed to its creator network frequently went viral. The FactPostNews accounts gained millions of new followers and billions of impressions across platforms, and the organization largely avoided becoming a story itself after fumbling the release of its 2024 autopsy report. The party had success whipping up engagement around posts related to food safety issues, which it noticed were performing well, and tried to tie them to Health and Human Services secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
The DNCâs ability to also distance itself from its work by seeding content to seemingly independent creators and accounts is yet another sign that what we see on social media isnât as organic as it may appear at first glance. With 2028 around the corner, expect more political actors to find sneakily creative ways of getting their messaging out.

Dormouse numbers may be recovering in England and Wales after years of decline, offering a rare piece of good news for one of our best-loved mammals.
The animal has disappeared from much of the countryside with conservationists warning of a long-term collapse in its population.
However, new data suggests dormouse numbers increased between 2020-2025, a period that coincided with warmer springs and summers.
Scientists believe these conditions may help dormice survive, by boosting food supplies and reducing the time they spend asleep.
That gives the animals more opportunity to breed and build up fat reserves ahead of winter.
But conservationists caution that many questions remain unanswered, and say protecting the woodlands and hedgerows where dormice live remains essential to their long-term survival.
The only species of dormice in the UK is the hazel dormouse. Once widespread across the country, they are now largely confined to southern England and parts of Wales. They have become much rarer as large areas of woodland are lost and so far native populations have disappeared from around 20 English counties.
The National Dormouse Monitoring Programme, led by the conservation charity People's Trust for Endangered Species (PTES), has been monitoring sites in England and Wales since 1998.
It found that since 2000, dormouse numbers have fallen by almost 60%, equivalent to an average annual decline of 3.5%.
More recently, however, there are signs that trend may be reversing. The data suggests the population increased by almost 10% between 2020 and 2025, although researchers stress there is considerable uncertainty around that estimate.
The apparent improvement coincides with a period of warmer, drier-than-average springs and summers.
Report co-author Ian White of PTES described the "upturn" as "welcome good news" which gives grounds for "cautious optimism".
But he added: "We mustn't lose sight of the bigger picture: populations remain almost 60% lower than they were in 2000."
The hazel dormouse is famous for spending much of the year asleep. It hibernates from around October to May, spending the winter in a nest on the ground.
Even during spring and summer, dormice can go into short periods of deep sleep, known as torpor, when the weather is cold and wet, or food is scarce. This helps the small rodent conserve energy.
Researchers believe warmer summers may be reducing the need for torpor, leaving dormice with more energy for feeding and breeding.
They say more research is needed to understand what longer-term impacts climate change could have on the species.
Dr Charlotte Armitage, an ecologist who worked on the survey, said significant uncertainties remain, including how dormice will respond to warmer, wetter winters.
However, she said warmer summer conditions are likely to give the animals more energy to reproduce and raise additional litters.
"This is good news, but we can't be complacent," she told BBC News.
"We still need to protect their habitat, do more research into the effects of climate change and carry out effective woodland management for the benefit of dormice."
