The Aramco Tower, a skyscraper in the Saudi Arabian capital's central financial district, had been hit by an air attack.
A statement issued via the Houthi-controlled Saba news agency confirmed the group had targeted Riyadh's business zone on Saturday, without mentioning the Aramco Tower by name.
The Saudi energy ministry said the tower had suffered only "minor damage" and no one had been killed or injured.
Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows more extensive damage to the building, with at least one floor appearing to have been badly hit by a missile or drone strike.
Windows on more than one level appear to have been shattered by the strike.
The Houthis also said Riyadh's airport and Aramco oil storage facilities were targeted in separate strikes. Saudi Arabia said its air defences had intercepted and destroyed several missiles.
The strikes were the latest claimed by the Yemen-based armed group against targets deep inside Saudi Arabia, which the Gulf power has struggled to contain in recent months.
It came a day after the Houthis accused a Saudi-led coalition of killing at least 33 people, including women and children, in an air strike on Yemen.
Footage broadcast by Houthi-run television channel Al Masirah showed rescuers pulling bodies from the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.
Saba said 39 people had been injured in the strike. Saudi Arabia has not commented.
A Saudi-led coalition has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government, which has lost control of a large swathe of the country to the rebel group.
Although the conflict had largely been dormant in recent years, fighting has intensified following the outbreak of the Iran war.
An informal ceasefire unravelled in July after the Tehran-backed Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport Saudi Arabia said had been to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing there.
Major fighting has since resumed between Houthi forces and troops aligned with Yemen's Saudi-backed government.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.

5f581f7c6af7.text: By — Susie Blann, Associated Press Susie Blann, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/russia-and-ukraine-exchange-strikes-a-day-before-u-s-brokered-talks-are-scheduled-to-begin Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Russia and Ukraine exchange strikes a day before U.S.-brokered talks are scheduled to begin World Nov 9, 2026 12:19 PM EST KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia battered Ukraine's power grid again and Ukrainian forces hit another of Russia's biggest oil refineries, officials said Monday, hours before delegations from Moscow and Kyiv were due to meet for new U.S.-brokered talks on how to end the fighting. READ MORE: Russian strikes on Ukrainian aid site kill at least 31 people, with dozens still missing Nearly five years after Russia invaded its neighbor, the two countries remain locked in battle with no sign that either side is ready to budge from their demands. The war has already killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians, analysts and humanitarian organizations say. Talks aim to build momentum for settlement, U.S. envoy says The three-way talks between envoys from the U.S., Russia and Ukraine are due to start in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday and last for two days. The previous round of talks was in February. U.S. President Donald Trump said in a "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday that Moscow and Kyiv are "very close" to a deal, despite the "tremendous hatred" between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He said that Ukraine would have "a little bit different shape" under the settlement, but he didn't elaborate. Trump has previously made statements about developments in the war which haven't materialized. Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, who will mediate in the talks with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, said that the priorities will be ending the conflict, finding ways to stop the war reigniting, reviving Ukraine's postwar economy and preparing humanitarian aid. "We hope these discussions will identify areas of common ground, advance practical solutions, and build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations," Kushner said on X Monday. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Monday that Trump's team has placed "collective security," covering not just Russia and Ukraine but also a wider area, at the top of the agenda. Moscow insists that Europe won't be in the 3-way talks The last three-way talks, in Geneva nine months ago, also took place amid continuing attacks. They delivered no significant progress in ending the war, but some circumstances have changed. Trump, whose stance on the war has varied, has to reckon with Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections. They could demand more support for Ukraine. Russian state finances are under heavy strain because of the war, and Ukraine's economy is being choked by the relentless attacks. In Abu Dhabi, the talks will look at what security guarantees would satisfy Russia, which sees NATO as a threat, and Ukraine, which wants to prevent future Russian invasions. Putin has sought to sideline European countries and negotiate Ukraine's future directly with Trump. However, European leaders and Ukraine have insisted that they be included. Moscow says that European representatives won't be directly involved in the Abu Dhabi discussions, but European officials said that representatives will be in the United Arab Emirates. Ukraine's lead negotiator, Rustem Umerov, said that European officials will hold "separate coordination" with the delegation from Kyiv. READ MORE: Zelenskyy pushes for 'clear' postwar security guarantees in Ukraine Kushner said that before the talks in Abu Dhabi begin, he and Witkoff will consult with officials from Ukraine, the European Union, NATO, Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Italy. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Monday that the meeting would focus on trilateral negotiations, with the United States mediating between Russia and Ukraine. "You are aware that the Americans have their own channels of communication with the Europeans, as do the Ukrainians, and it appears they are already establishing their own methods of coordination," Peskov said. "But, to reiterate, this is a matter of trilateral negotiations." Russia hits electrical substations, Ukraine targets a refinery Russian forces targeted four electrical substations in Ukraine's Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Cherkasy and Vinnytsia regions, Russia's Defense Ministry said Monday. The attacks are part of Russia's campaign to deny Ukrainian civilians heating, light and running water during the approaching winter. Zelenskyy said Monday that the European Union had agreed to activate a special emergency mechanism that speeds up funding for power grid repairs. Russia launched 317 drones of various types including 105 jet-powered drones at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine's air force said. Russian aerial attacks have pummeled Ukraine throughout the war, with gruesome consequences. A Russian glide bomb attack last week near the front line in the southern Zaporizhzhia region killed at least 55 people at an aid distribution center. On Monday, Russian forces hit a warehouse in Odesa in southwestern Ukraine containing food supplies for kindergartens and schools, killing three people, local officials said. Meanwhile, an attack by long-range drones developed by Ukraine during the war started a fire at the KINEF oil refinery, one of Russia's largest, close to St. Petersburg and more than 1,200 kilometers (745 miles) from the Ukrainian border, Leningrad Gov. Alexander Drozdenko said Monday. Ukraine said in early October that its long-range strikes had neutralized more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity, hampering Moscow's ability to supply its forces. Ukrainian forces also struck a plant near St. Petersburg, Russia's second-largest city, that produces solid rocket propellant

US President Donald Trump has questioned the legitimacy of the midterm election results in which Republicans suffered sweeping losses - days after saying he would accept the outcome.
"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong?" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.
This appeared to contradict what he told the New York Times on election night that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results.
Democrats retook both chambers of Congress in last week's elections. State and local officials across the US said voting had been mostly problem-free.
Some key races, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi, have yet to be called.
In the Truth Social post, Trump made vague claims about polling, voting "dumps", and "machines" without providing specific evidence of error or wrongdoing.
He has previously attempted to cast doubts on the integrity of elections he has lost, although he himself was not on the ballot in the midterms.
"We would have won easily if I was on the ballot," Trump told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, after it was confirmed his party had lost both the Senate and the House.
As it stands, Democrats have won 54 US Senate seats and 254 US House seats in the midterms, giving them comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress even as counting continues in some races.
The outcome has been clear since election night and Trump told the New York Times then: "We'll, you know, look forward to working with [Democrats]", adding: "We'll probably work something out."
He has also offered his own analysis of why Republicans lost, acknowledging on Fox News that the Iran war had contributed to the defeat.
"People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that," he said.
Vice-President JD Vance has also blamed the Iran war, which began in February and which has severely disrupted global oil and gas supplies - causing costs to soar, as the reason their party lost the election.
In the run-up to the midterms, Trump made claims about widespread voting fraud, despite evidence that it is rare.
He and his allies alleged for months that the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to former President Joe Biden, had been rigged against him. His lawyers and allies spent weeks attempting to litigate the results, but courts repeatedly struck them down.
The justice department during his administration has made unprecedented attempts to exert more federal control over elections - a power the Constitution primarily delegates to individual states.
Days before these midterms, it filed controversial lawsuits in federal courts challenging the count and certification of votes in states like California and Alaska, but judges ruled against them in nearly all instances.
Election law experts, state officials, and local elections offices told the BBC they had spent months preparing for a scenario in which the White House or election sceptics questioned the votes' legitimacy.
Despite the intense focus around election integrity on both sides of the debate, top state and local election officials have reported a mostly smooth process so far for the 2026 midterms.
Extreme weather did force some location closures, and a handful of reported administrative or technical issues slowed the process in some local jurisdictions.

Nine Zimbabweans have been arrested in South Africa after they were caught allegedly trying to leave the country to fight in the war between Russia and the Ukraine, police say.
The group, aged between 20 and 26, were arrested in and around Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team on Sunday evening.
They were caught as they were "preparing to board flights out of the country", authorities added, but their final destination is unclear.
They have been charged with contravening South Africa's Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act, which outlaws mercenary activity without government permission.
Police said five people were arrested at South Africa's biggest airport, OR Tambo, and another four at a hotel in Bruma, east of Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team that involved Interpol.
All nine later appeared in court, according to state prosecutors.
The police statement added that the involvement of Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies indicated that the suspects had also allegedly violated laws in their respective home countries, prompting cooperation with South African authorities.
They have also not said whether the group allegedly intended to fight for Russia or Ukraine nor provided details of the organisations allegedly involved in facilitating their travel.
Citizens of several African countries, including Kenya, Ghana and South Africa, have gone to fight for Russia in Ukraine - some they had been duped and had not realised where they were going.
A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.
Kenya at the time estimated that 252 citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia. In March, Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue.
He said at the time that an agreement had been reached to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.
In March, Zimbabwe said that 15 of its nationals had been killed after being recruited to fight for Russia in Ukraine, with more than 60 still trapped on the frontlines.
The previous month, South Africa secured the return of 17 South Africans who were allegedly tricked into joining the war.
In December last year, South African authorities arrested five people, including a journalist, for allegedly recruiting people to join the war.
Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.

The House convenes at 12 p.m. EDT. Watch the House floor live in the video player above. Newly elected lawmakers arrived on Capitol Hill over the weekend, creating a jumble of split-screen moments reflective of the new political landscape. Dozens of jubilant Democrats, families and suitcases in tow for freshman orientation, appeared emboldened by the party's sweep of power. The trickle of Republicans coming in spoke soberly of the GOP's vast challenges ahead. WATCH: Hegseth speaks at the Naval War College as possible impeachment vote looms "This country sent a clear message from coast to coast, and that message is they've had enough of what's gone on," said Rep.-elect Daniel Biss, D-Ill. "They've had enough of Donald Trump. They've had enough of MAGA. And critically, they are ready to transform who holds power, and what they do with it." Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Republican Rep.-elect Chris Stigall of Missouri said it's clear that voters sent a loud message, "and I hope, as a new member, I can be on the ground level of figuring out how we can reconnect." WATCH: Rep. Garcia says voters gave Democrats a mandate to pursue accountability For starters, he said, the GOP needs to understand that the economy is not where it needs to be. "Six-dollar diesel, I will tell you, for the farmers in my district, that is a tough pill to swallow." But first, it's out with the old before the new Congress takes over in January. Hegseth impeachment vote tops lame-duck agenda The House and Senate are in session for just six short weeks of a lame-duck sprint to finish up the Republican agenda before the GOP majorities come to an end, making way for the change of power on Jan. 3, 2027. Leadership elections and a government funding package are all priorities ahead. READ MORE: After taking control of Congress, Democrats vow major probes into Trump's 'tentacles of corruption' One first order of business is expected to be a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his leadership at the Pentagon. Republican Rep. House Speaker Mike Johnson had tried to prevent a vote on Hegseth's impeachment in September and abruptly halted proceedings by sending lawmakers home early. But it's unclear Johnson, who remains close to Trump, will be able to slow the drive for impeachment now, unless he decides to adjourn the chamber again. Trump defended Hegseth to reporters on Sunday night before he flew back to Washington after spending the weekend at his Florida home. "He's guilty of two things, basically winning two wars," Trump said. "I believe we saved the Middle East and Israel combined. And it's awfully hard to say let's impeach somebody who did that." Democrats are expected to widely support the impeachment resolution and a number of Republicans have signaled they could join them. "I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Sunday on ABC. Jeffries said it's time for Hegseth to go, and that the secretary "has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran." New Congress arrives, as does Trump's new chief of staff The halls of the Capitol are expected to swell this week with the collision of incoming and outgoing lawmakers, as the newcomers attend orientation sessions while the retiring lawmakers start to clear out. At the same time, Trump has tapped top aide Stephen Miller, the hard-right architect of much of the White House's domestic policy agenda, as his new chief of staff. Miller takes the helm Monday in what is expected to be the start of a more direct confrontation with the Congress. Republicans in both the House and Senate are planning to hold their leadership elections this week in closed-door meetings that could end up being blame-casting sessions about what went wrong in the elections. House Republicans are bracing for a contentious leadership battle after Johnson decided to step aside, setting up a showdown between the No. 2 Republican, Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana, and Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, the brawling former wrestling coach allied with the hard-right conservatives. The two men had confronted one another when trying to become House speaker three years ago, but neither was able to win enough support from the Republican rank and file, leading to Johnson's rise. With the House Republican numbers now shrunken, lawmakers could seek wholesale change in leadership. In the Senate, Majority Leader John Thune is expected to retain his job as Republican leader, though in the minority as Democrats flipped Republican-held seats, including milestone wins in Texas and Kansas. Democrats are expected to hold their elections later this month. Men recruited to French gang as children to kill give rare insight into drug underworld
A BBC investigation has found one of Europe's most powerful drug gangs in France is recruiting teenage children from across the country to commit kidnap and murder.
Known as the "DZ Mafia", the gang won a bloody turf war against a rival group in Marseille during 2023, and is now recruiting from further afield.
One member who is in prison awaiting trial after being implicated in several murders told the BBC he was part of a DZ Mafia hit squad.
He agrees the killings he has been charged with were "quite shocking".
"Attempts in broad daylight, in traffic jamsâ¦ it can range from going to hit a guy, slap him to taking him in front of his mother and burning him up in a car. I think I have good composure, I handle it fairly well."
When challenged over whether he feels regret when carrying out such acts of brutality, he says he feels "guilty in-part" but claims to have no regrets.
Like so many teenagers from Marseille, he knew large sums of money could be earned quickly in drug trafficking. Now in his twenties, he admits the environment he entered was a "trap".
The BBC's Paris Correspondent, James Waterhouse, reports from Marseille.

France has accused Iran of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers.
French Foreign Minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot said the attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of Iran.
He said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding that the country would "implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack".
The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up, which spoilt fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Then last week, dozens of supermarkets across seven other European countries were also impacted by a cyber-attack that targeted fridges and freezers. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Iran is yet to respond to Barrot's allegations.
Barrot said of the attack on France's supermarkets: "It marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people."
He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".
France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.
Separately on Monday, the Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as well as his two deputies.
Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.
More than 100 of CoopÃ©rative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from IntermarchÃ© and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.
Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.
In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.
The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.

LONDON (AP) — Russell Brand was sentenced Monday to 10½ years in prison for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others at a time when his bawdy behavior was indulged and celebrated during his rise to stardom. READ MORE: Russell Brand convicted of rape and sexual assault Judge Joel Bennathan denounced Brand's "casual and arrogant disregard" for any woman who said no to him, and castigated him for the series of lies he told in testimony denying assaults that dated back to 2004. "About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous," Bennathan said. "You were clever — and in many people's eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator." Brand showed little emotion during the stinging rebuke. He turned to mouth the words "we'll be OK" to his wife after he stood up and was led away by court officers after the hearing. The 51-year-old actor-comedian, known for outrageous stand-up routines and provocative behavior on television and radio broadcasts, as well as battles with drugs and alcohol, had maintained his innocence and testified that all his encounters were consensual. But a jury of eight men and four women found him guilty of attacking four of six accusers. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault. Prosecutor: Brand used fame to carry out crimes The convictions — years after the #MeToo movement turned a spotlight on sexual abuse by the powerful and famous — raised questions about how Brand's behavior was tolerated by TV and radio stations he worked for, including the BBC, and those around him. "Mr. Brand abused the influence and power that came with his fame," prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said. "He used it to facilitate access to women without which the offending could not have taken place. It also fed his own view that he could commit such offenses with impunity." Brand was supported by his wife, father and fans outside court Brand wore a gray suit and an open collar shirt with a loose white tie. His long, graying hair was pulled back and knotted in a man bun atop his head. He clenched a crucifix in his right hand. Defense lawyer Ian Winter urged the judge to consider Brand's good character, saying his only previous conviction was for marijuana possession in 1995 and that he had performed charitable work and helped others overcome drug and alcohol abuse. He also asked the judge to consider the impact of the sentence on Brand's family, particularly his three young children. Brand was supported in Southwark Crown Court by his wife, Laura, and his father, Ron Brand. Laura entered the courthouse without Brand, who had been in since custody Thursday's verdict. A couple of Brand's supporters, reflecting his recent conversion to Christianity, held a banner bearing crosses with the words: "Russell Brand we stand with you. Christ was crucified for telling the truth. Russell is the truth." Victims tell court it was difficult to see Brand celebrated in public The accusers came forward following a 2023 investigation by The Times and Channel 4 that aired accounts from women who said they had been sexually abused and degraded by Brand. One of the women he was convicted of abusing spoke in court about the trauma the crime caused. The others provided statements read by the prosecutor. A woman whom Brand groped during a birthday party at a London bar in 2004 said that the assault left her in shock and turmoil and made her feel like "damaged goods." "It was impossible to escape seeing him all over the media, being celebrated for his disgusting behavior against women like it was all a joke," she said. READ MORE: Russell Brand denies all charges as he testifies at his rape and sex assault trial Brand stared straight ahead as she spoke from behind a curtain that shielded her from public view to preserve her identity. Bennathan said Brand's entourage may have written off the sexual assault as "laddish," the boorish and obnoxious behavior for which Brand was known and with which he thought he could get away. "It was outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal sexual offense, and as it turns out you haven't got away with it," the judge said. Rape victim felt 'powerless' A former fan he was convicted of anally raping at his home after meeting her backstage at one of his comedy shows in 2009 said that she was left feeling anxious and humiliated and had difficulty eating and sleeping, and went through periods of heavy drinking. She said she spent months fearing that she might have contracted HIV and that it took years for her to speak up. She only came forward after police opened an investigation following the documentary. "I felt that if I reported him, I would not be believed," she said in the statement read by Karmy-Jones. "His fame, wealth and influence created a power imbalance which made me feel powerless." Winter, the defense lawyer, argued that Brand should be "regarded as a man who went too far and overrode consent that had been given" following consensual sex. The judge noted how disrespectfully Brand had treated the woman, including putting her in his phone contacts under "T" for "tart." Russell Brand has managed to move on and even forget," she said. "Over the years, hearing his voice on television, on social media or seeing his image made me jump." At least 39 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) reports.
The interior ministry said one person had been rescued, but the number of people still missing was yet to be established.
The small wooden boat capsized between the capital, Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis, as it headed towards Spain's Canary Islands.
Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026, the highest toll among the routes it monitors.
Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told the AFP news agency that all the bodies recovered by Sunday evening were Senegalese. The nationalities of other people on board was yet to be established, as search operations continued.
Four bodies were recovered on Monday morning in an advanced state of decomposition and buried following a collective funeral prayer organised by the fire service.
Rescue teams are searching along a 25km (15-mile)- stretch of coastline, but operations have been complicated by difficult access and strong ocean currents, which are pushing bodies further south.
Authorities say 24 of the 39 victims have been identified and their bodies returned to their families, while 11 others are still awaiting identification.
President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has expressed his condolences to the victims' families and urged Senegalese nationals not to risk their lives on the dangerous sea crossings.
In a statement posted on X, he pledged to intensify efforts to dismantle the networks organising the journeys.
"We will relentlessly continue the fight against those who organise these crossings and the work that gives our young people reasons to hope here," he said.
The tragedy comes amid renewed concerns over the dangers facing migrant attempting to reach Europe by sea.
Walking Borders estimates that about 21 people died for every 100 who reached the Canary Islands during the period it monitored.
Senegalese authorities said they had intercepted another boat, on Friday, carrying 142 migrants attempting to reach Spain.
Those on board included 23 women, two babies and two other children. Police said the group comprised nationals of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria.
Meanwhile, a state of emergency was declared on the Spanish island of El Hierro on Saturday following a surge in migrant arrivals.
More than 3,300 people have reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of November, according to local authorities.
This amounts to almost a third of the population on the island, one of the main entry points into Europe for migrants arriving from West Africa.
Fernando Clavijo, president of the Canary Islands regional government, described the situation as "absolutely unsustainable," reports the Reuters news agency.
The route has grown in prominence amid tighter controls and increased cooperation between European countries and North African states, which may have diverted some journeys away from the central Mediterranean.
Limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks are among the factors driving people to leave Senegal, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
For many young people, the prospect of finding work and earning more abroad remains a powerful incentive, despite the risks of crossing the Atlantic in overcrowded boat.
Nearly one in four young people in Senegal was unemployed in the second quarter of 2026, according to the country's statistics agency.
The figure highlights the challenge facing President Faye's government as it seeks to create jobs for a predominantly young population that overwhelmingly voted for him in the 2024 elections.
In a statement on Sunday, Senegal's interior ministry said it would continue efforts to combat people-smuggling networks, including by strengthening cooperation with neighbouring countries.

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.
The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.
In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.
Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.
Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.
For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.
Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.
Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.
The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.
The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.
With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

Trump said his deportation policy was part of the reason Republicans lost, telling CBS's "60 Minutes" in an interview that aired on Sunday: "I think it might be too tough, yeah." He added that he thinks he could reach an agreement with the new Democratic majority. "The deal would be we would work something out. And I think it's something -- I think that's something that's actually doable," he said in the interview. Trump did not give specifics about what that deal would look like — and shortly after taping the interview on Friday, Trump named the key architect of his hard-line immigration agenda, Stephen Miller, as his new chief of staff. "Trump says his immigration crackdown went too far," Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer scoffed on social media Sunday after the interview aired. "Apparently, his solution was to put the man responsible for it in charge of the White House. That's not a course correction. That's a promotion." The president's immigration crackdown was a prominent feature of his return to office with major operations in multiple cities sending arrests soaring. Two U.S. citizens — Renee Good and Alex Pretti — were killed by federal officers during protests against the operations. Democrats have said oversight of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security is a priority for the new Congress. Trump said he believes that "killers" and "drug dealers" in the country illegally should be deported, but suggested he was open to the idea of a deal that would let others stay "if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes." Trump says he may stay on the sidelines for the 2028 race On the race among Republicans to succeed him for the 2028 presidential election, Trump hinted at staying neutral. WATCH: Midterm voters rebuke Trump, handing Democrats both chambers of Congress Asked whether he'd endorse a potential successor, the president said "probably, not necessarily." "We have a tremendous bench. I have so many people that I have great relationships with," Trump said in the interview. Asked about possible candidates other than Vice President JD Vance, Trump only named Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is viewed as a possible 2028 contender. "I think Marco's great," Trump said. "But there are many others and I'd rather not mention their names. There's some senators that are excellent. I know 'em all, I like 'em a lot. "So I may or may not get involved. I don't know. Maybe I'm better off not getting involved," Trump said. Trump brushes aside questions about becoming wealthier while in office During the midterms, Democrats sought to make the president's personal wealth a campaign issue. About half of voters nationally said government corruption was "crucial" for their vote for Congress, according to the AP Voter Poll. Asked how his net worth went up by $3 billion since returning to the White House, Trump said he doesn't pay much attention to it and said his sons look after the family business. "I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don't care. I make — I have a lotta money, and far more than I ever thought I'd have. And I guess it's gone up. I don't even know," he said. Trump was asked whether he thinks people from foreign countries investing in the company he co-owns with his sons are trying to buy influence. "I don't know. But that's true — look, every president has a problem," he said. Trump, who survived an assassination attempt while campaigning for reelection in 2024 and has lashed out against his political foes, was asked whether he could forgive his enemies. He said it would be easy to say yes. But he added: "I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies, and I always will." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. f86bf9105d99.text: By — Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/deportation-flight-of-iranians-from-u-s-canceled-at-last-minute-attorney-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Deportation flight of Iranians from U.S. canceled at last minute, attorney says Politics Nov 9, 2026 10:07 AM EST LOS ANGELES (AP) — A U.S. deportation flight of Iranian nationals bound for Iran by way of Pakistan was abruptly canceled Sunday morning, according to an attorney who spoke to some of the detainees slated for repatriation. READ MORE: Trump administration held talks with Iran on deporting Iranians during the war, court documents show At least eight Iranians were loaded onto a plane Sunday morning in Mesa, Arizona, for a deportation flight headed to the country of Georgia, then on to Pakistan, according to Ali Rahnama, an attorney with the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund who filed emergency motions on behalf of some of the Iranian detainees. The flight was canceled without explanation, he said. Court documents unsealed days ago in a civil lawsuit filed by the fund showed the Trump administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians to Iran, even as the war there drags on, via an unnamed third country. The lawsuit was filed in July and alleges that the U.S. government illegally shared confidential information about Iranians seeking asylum in the U.S. with Iranian officials. There were three deportation flights to Iran between September 2025 and January 2026, with over 100 Iranian nationals deported. But the administration's confirmation of the new plans amid the war that began in February highlights its resolve in carrying out its hardline immigration crackdown, which has involved ramping up removals, including to places that critics say could endanger the lives of the returnees. Homeland Security refuses comment In response to questions Sunday from The Associated Press, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that Immigration and Customs Enforcement does not comment on "prospective removal operations, including flight schedules, passenger manifests, destinations, or individual case details," nor would the agency confirm future removal operations. "As promised, the Trump Administration is employing all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history," the statement said. The administration did not specify in the October court records when the deportations would be carried out. But in the past week, roughly a dozen Iranian nationals in immigration detention said they were notified that they were scheduled for an upcoming deportation flight to Pakistan and then to Iran, according to numerous attorneys who have since confirmed those plans with DHS. Advocacy group says detainees have been contacted by Iranian officials According to Rahnama, the eight detainees who boarded the flight on Sunday were visited by a senior official with the Iranian Interests Section — an Iranian representative office in the Pakistani Embassy in Washington that handles consular affairs — and were told that the Iranian government would transport them from Pakistan to Iran. In the litigation brought by the Iranian immigrant advocacy group, at least a dozen Iranian detainees have said they've been contacted by Iranian officials who had knowledge of sensitive information on their asylum claims. U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes, a nominee of President Joe Biden, has not ruled on the claims but ordered the U.S. government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country, and five days' written notice before any such deportation is carried out. In a court filing Sunday, the defense fund laid out what it had learned about plans for a removal flight Sunday and argued that the administration may have violated the judge's directive to give advance notice of deportation plans. Later Sunday, the government filed court documents in the case, but they were sealed and inaccessible to the public. Group says individuals could face persecution The Iranian American Legal Defense Fund has called for a halt to the removal flights, saying in a news release that they would "reportedly mark the first deportation of Iranians to Iran since the U.S.-Iran war began." The group's executive director, Yasmin Chubin, said in a statement Sunday that it was difficult to comprehend why the U.S. would forcibly deport Iranians, including asylum seekers, to Iran, amid ongoing military hostilities. The consequences of removal, Chubin said, "could be irreversible and individuals may face persecution, torture, or death." At least one person who had been part of the scuttled flight volunteered to go back to Iran after nearly two years of detention, Rahnama said, out of desperation to leave what he described as inhumane imprisonment. It's not clear how many other of the deportees may have volunteered to leave. Associated Press reporter Sarah Rankin in Richmond, Virginia, contributed to this report. Resident birds have returned to Broughshane Waterfowl Park after an oil spill which caused the death of 13 of the flock.
The popular attraction in County Antrim was forced to close after a nearby home heating oil tank was vandalised, causing the oil spill into the pond.
In a post on social media, The Waterfowl Pond confirmed that work is still underway to address the oil contamination and that a number of pens remain out of bounds.
More than 20 birds were transported to the USPCA's headquarters for urgent specialist care following the incident.
The park, which was home to 120 birds, has since reopened.
Broughshane Environment Wildfowl and Wildlife Trust's chairman, Gary Hayward, said about 10-12 birds have returned including two black swans and Nenes.
Hayward said they are back safely in their pens and they are lucky to be healthy.
The Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA) was first alerted to the incident on Thursday 22 October and have been involved in removing the oil waste.
The agency said the substance involved had been identified as home heating oil or kerosene.
Police said about 44 gallons (200 litres) of oil had leaked from the tank which had been damaged at a business premise in the Main Street area of Broughshane.
Hayward said that there is very little evidence of the oil left as the NIEA have removed the majority of it.
"They have made problems a lot less than they could have been," he told BBC News NI.
He said there is still some oil around the edges, and once the oil leaves the pens the birds will be moved back into them.
The USPCA has also been a key part of the rescue operation.
They said that all of the birds, including geese, ducks and swans, needed bathed and treated due to the level of contamination they suffered.
Unfortunately some had already ingested too much and died as a result.
The Waterfowl Pond offered thanks to the USPCA for looking after the birds.
"We are truly grateful for everything you have done."
It also paid tribute to the support received from the public.
"It's another positive step forward for our park, and we couldn't have got here without you."
Police have said that enquiries into the incident are ongoing and have appealed to anyone with information to come forward.

68d97c03b26f.text: By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press By — Almudena Calatrava, Associated Press Almudena Calatrava, Associated Press By — Deborah Rey, Associated Press Deborah Rey, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/pope-visits-care-home-in-argentina-for-people-with-disabilities-renewing-call-to-protect-the-vulnerable Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope visits care home in Argentina for people with disabilities, renewing call to protect the vulnerable World Nov 9, 2026 9:41 AM EST BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Pope Leo XIV renewed his call Monday for Argentina to protect its weakest and most vulnerable people as he visited a home for people with disabilities in a symbolically powerful rebuke of President Javier Milei's austerity measures. On his first full day in Argentina, Leo made a pilgrimage to the Cottolengo Don Orione in Claypole, south of Buenos Aires. Founded by an Italian priest in 1935, the institution houses more than 400 people with disabilities on its 123-acre (50-hectare) grounds. READ MORE: Pope Leo arrives in Argentina and tells Milei that people, not the economy, should come first The center, known as the "city of charity," has been hit hard by Milei's austerity measures, which have severely affected healthcare and social services. Milei has taken his signature chain saw to specialized therapy programs that for decades have been a lifeline for many of Argentina's estimated 5 million people with disabilities, freezing payments and dismantling a vital safety net. Some residents and employees wept as Leo arrived Monday and embraced people in wheelchairs. He chatted with them and blessed them and told them their lives were a blessing, not a burden on society. "You can help us to remember the foundation of the dignity of every human being and what is truly important in life," Leo said in the center's chapel. He said he dreamed that Argentines would be inspired to replace the pursuit of economic success and the "cult of outward appearances" with "great works of charity" like the Cottolengo home. "A nation's progress is also measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs," he said. Argentina's Congress overrode Milei's veto last year to pass a law increasing funding for disability care. But his administration has resisted implementing it, citing concerns that it would undermine his hard-won fiscal balance. Care homes such as Cottolengo are still owed hundreds of thousands of dollars. Leo's visit comes days before the Senate is due to consider legislation that would set aside money for disability benefits in next year's budget. Milei opposes the measure. Given the circumstances, it was deeply significant that Leo chose to start his visit to Argentina by meeting with the Cottolengo guests, said Kuyen Rolon Rey, a volunteer at the home. "The people here deserve this grace," Rolon Rey said. "Choosing such a small place, but big if measured with love, makes us very happy." A message to Argentine business and labor The visit kicked off a busy day for Leo in which the American pope, fulfilling the unfinished legacy of Argentine Pope Francis, is emphasizing Catholic social teaching that calls for putting the weakest and most vulnerable at the center of economic policy. Upon arrival Sunday and with Milei at his side, Leo cited Francis' frequent refrain that money must serve and not rule: "The economy must serve the person, not the person the economy," Leo said in his first speech in Argentina. It's a message Leo is expected to repeat later Monday when he meets with business leaders, union representatives and leaders of popular movements at the Catholic University of Argentina. Among those invited are domestic manufacturers battered by cheap imports since Milei scrapped long-standing trade barriers, and members of Argentina's largest labor confederation, who took their worries over job losses and shrinking wages to the Vatican in September. Since Milei took office in late 2023, his austerity agenda has made him an icon of the global conservative backlash against the liberal establishment. Much like its allies in the Trump administration, Milei's government has portrayed the cuts to disability programs as part of a reform process aimed at eliminating fraud and waste in the federal bureaucracy. First papal Mass in nearly 40 years For many Argentines, the day's highlight was to be Leo's late-morning Mass at the Monumento a los Españoles, which was expected to draw as many as 2 million people. The same site hosted the last papal Mass in Argentina, celebrated by St. John Paul II nearly 40 years ago. READ MORE: What to know about Pope Leo XIV's trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru Thousands arrived at midnight to secure a good spot for Leo's first Mass in Argentina. Isabel Martín, 73, came with her parish group from San Andrés Avelino. She said she was praying for Leo to "touch the heart" of Milei, whose spending cuts have also hit pensioners hard. "The pope was very specific in his message yesterday," she said, referring to Leo's inaugural speech to Milei. "The weakest cannot be the ones carrying the burden of the adjustment, especially poor retirees. If anyone can make him reconsider, it's the pope." Argentina's minimum pension is approximately $300, about a quarter of what an older adult needs to cover medicine, housing and food. Leo's message was also resonating with younger Argentines, who have shown the sharpest decline in Catholic practice of any age group. Margarita Lanús celebrated her 16th birthday Monday while waiting for Leo's Mass, sharing a cake on the sidewalk with her large family. "I really like that he says things as they are; he goes straight to the point," she said. Leo has been welcomed by huge and adoring crowds in Buenos Aires, the second stop of his three-nation tour of South America that ends later this week in his second homeland of Pe

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.
A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.
Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.
We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.
Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.
The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.
It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.
And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

Alexisâs view
Nigeriaâs Federal High Court invalidating the election candidacy of President Bola Tinubuâs leading challenger was unexpected â but not entirely surprising.
Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, runner-up in the last election, has fewer than 100 days to secure a reversal on appeal ahead of the January vote. But the broader danger is that last weekâs legal curveball further erodes trust in Africaâs biggest democratic exercise.
The ruling is consistent with a recent pattern of late interventions ahead of Nigerian elections. In 2019, the countryâs then most senior judge was suspended weeks before the vote, prompting speculation that he was dismissed because he couldnât be relied upon to back the incumbent if courts weighed in on a close result. And Nigeriaâs central bank wreaked havoc four years ago when it issued new bank notes in a move widely seen as an attempt to disadvantage some politicians and favor others. Each intervention raised questions about the independence of key institutions.
Tinubu was already the frontrunner, even before Atikuâs legal headache. Peter Obi, the other main opponent, should not be underestimated. But the failure of the opposition to unify behind a single candidate has weakened the challenge to Tinubu, despite widespread anger over the rising cost of living, which many blame on the presidentâs removal of the countryâs fuel subsidy.
The smart money is on the ruling against Atiku being overturned before the election. The danger for Tinubu is that suspicion that the judiciary undermined a rival â one who vowed to restore the fuel subsidy â turns Atiku into a lightning rod for public frustration.
The more deep-rooted threat is apathy. Tinubu won in 2023 with just 27% voter turnout â the lowest since the return to civilian rule in 1999. Any sense that courts, rather than the ballot box, will sway the election could dampen interest further, handing the victor an even slimmer mandate to govern Africaâs most populous country. Under such circumstances, a Tinubu victory could soon feel Pyrrhic.
Notable
- South Africaâs biggest party, the ANC, faced intense campaigns ahead of the local elections, which involved politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and wading through giant-sized potholes.

An 80 cent âmaternal drapeâ is saving womenâs lives in Kano, Nigeria â the country where more women die in childbirth than anywhere else in the world. The drape measures blood loss during childbirth; once the level passes 300ml, midwives use massage, oxytocin, tranexamic acid, and IV fluids to encourage the uterus to contract.
Hadiza Galadanci, an obstetrics and gynecology professor at Bayero University, was initially skeptical that anything could reduce the mortality rate from postpartum hemorrhage â experienced by 10% of women who give birth and the biggest risk to new mothers â when she was approached by researchers. But the drastic reduction in deaths since the drapeâs implementation spurred her to persuade Nigeriaâs health minister to introduce it as a national standard of care. Suppliers in Kano now produce them for Nigeria and neighboring countries.

- Published
At least 13 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of the Greek island of Crete.
The coastguard said it had rescued 18 people, all of whom were Sudanese nationals. Four of the survivors were taken to hospital, including a toddler.
Authorities said it was not immediately clear what caused the deaths, but they believe the boat had been at sea for days and had struggled to reach shore due to strong winds.
Crete remains one of several key gateways for migrants attempting to reach Europe from the Middle East and North Africa, with more than 22,000 of the 86,400 sea arrivals so far this year landing in Crete alone.
One unnamed coastguard official who spoke to news agency Reuters on condition of anonymity said the survivors were "shivering from the cold".
The migrants' boat was spotted by a Moroccan-flagged container ship about 15 nautical miles (28km) off Crete's coast.
The Greek coastguard rescued another 187 people in three separate incidents off the coast of Greece on Monday.
More than 37,000 migrants have arrived in Greece so far this year, UN figures show, already surpassing the number who arrived in the entirety of 2025.
The Greek government has announced plans to deal with the influx, including opening a temporary housing complex near the Cretan capital, Heraklion.
Greece was at the heart of Europe's migration crisis in 2015-16, when nearly a million people arrived on its islands, mostly from Turkey.
Arrivals later fell as border controls tightened, but crossings from Libya have surged in recent years, particularly among people fleeing conflict in Sudan and seeking better economic opportunities from countries including Bangladesh.

Under the proposed tie-up, Shoprite, which built its retail empire by partly borrowing from Walmartâs mass market playbook, will use Investecâs banking backbone and regulatory framework to expand financial services to millions of its customers. African sovereigns are flooding back into global debt markets, accepting some of the worldâs highest borrowing costs and adding to the debate about how investors price risk just as the continentâs new credit agency begins operations.
External debt owed by low- and middle-income countries climbed 5.5% to a record $9.4 trillion in 2025, the fastest pace since 2021, according to the World Bankâs International Debt Report. Africaâs poorest borrowers, which are eligible for the World Bankâs cheapest financing, paid 9.8% interest on new bonds in 2025, nearly double the 5.5% paid by middle-income borrowers, whose rates fell.
âAccess to international finance has improved, but the price of that finance has not,â World Bank Chief Statistician Haishan Fu said. The report comes almost a month after the launch of the Africa Credit Rating Agency, the African Unionâs most concrete answer yet to longstanding complaints that global rating agencies unfairly attach risk premiums that eat up an estimated $75 billion in additional annual interest fees.

The African National Congress suffered its worst-ever result in local elections, potentially shifting the balance of power in South Africaâs coalition government.
The ANC, which led the country out of apartheid, won 31% of the vote nationwide, just over six percentage points ahead of the Democratic Alliance, a historically white-led movement. The performance extends the decline that cost the ANC its national parliamentary majority in 2024 and sets up a battle over the direction of economic policy as the once-dominant party prepares to choose a new leader next year. It also means the biggest cities, key drivers of growth in Africaâs largest economy, will mostly be governed by coalitions.
The DA emerged as the largest party in three metropolitan municipalities in Gauteng, the economic heartland, including in the commercial hub of Johannesburg. That outcome is likely to boost its bargaining power nationally and in talks to form municipal governments where no party won a majority. But some warned the new political reality has drawbacks: âUnstable coalitions with precarious leadership teams cannot deliver,â said Busi Mavuso, CEO of lobby group Business Leadership South Africa.

c65ed8e83606.text: By — Huizhong Wu, Associated Press Huizhong Wu, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/china-dismisses-claims-of-spy-plot-involving-nvidia-ceo-huang-as-a-smear-campaign Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter China dismisses claims of spy plot involving Nvidia CEO Huang as a smear campaign World Nov 9, 2026 8:31 AM EST BANGKOK (AP) — China denied on Monday it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, saying the spying allegations were unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing. Huang has acknowledged he had been intimate with a business executive, issuing an apology to his wife and to the company in an open letter posted on Nvidia's website. He did not name the woman. READ MORE: Nvidia investigates whether CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese spy when he had affair Nvidia announced Sunday it was conducting an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined that the woman was gathering information for Beijing. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security," Huang said in his letter. In a routine news briefing Monday, a Chinese spokesperson rejected claims it used the woman as a spy. READ MORE: Nvidia announced a software tool to stop rogue AI. How would it work? "The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday. Beijing earlier had dismissed The New York Times report saying Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, who ran a company that last year faced claims it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China. Nvidia shares dropped roughly 5% in pre-market trading early Monday. The New York Times said Alice Huang was a former executive of a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed International, whose website prominently touts its partnership with Nvidia. READ MORE: Taiwan charges 9 over illegal AI server exports to China, including Nvidia and Super Micro staffers Many offices in Singapore were closed on Monday for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment. Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies, alongside Apple and Microsoft. Its sales of computer chips to China have at times been targeted by U.S. regulators seeking to limit Beijing's access to such technology. "The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised," said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy. "Those questions require evidence rather than speculation," he added in a text message to reporters. Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China in recent years, winning U.S. President Donald Trump's approval for selling its H200 chips this year. It's unclear if Beijing would allow Chinese companies to buy those chips in large quantities. Nvidia said in a regulatory filing in August that it has sold only a small amount to China as such sales are restricted by the Chinese government. The H200 chips are not Nvidia's most cutting-edge models, but they are still advanced. Previously, Huang also lobbied Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia's less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China. Chinese media have largely focused on Huang admitting to the affair and state media outlets have mainly echoed the official government line. Some have said the New York Times report was aimed at destabilizing U.S.-China relations. "Whenever China-US relations begin to improve, there are often those firing shots from the shadows," the state-owned Global Times said. Associated Press Business Writer Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 699f2cc5c934.text:
Lizâs view
This feels like the beginning of the end of the AI trade. Itâs going to have wider consequences than we think.
The geyser of money is starting to sputter, affecting high-flying stocks and zapping debt deals. OpenAI set out to raise $30 billion, money it could have put together in its sleep a few months ago, and appears likely to fall far short. Lenders are treating SpaceX, an investment-grade giant, like a flier bet on a junk-rated startup.
Those companies will likely find the money somewhere. But the canât-lose trade powered by a combination of FOMO and the greater-fool theory of investing is evaporating, replaced by a tinder pile ready to ignite. The spark could come from almost anywhere. A data-center delay sets off a hyperscaler guarantee fight, a swarm of rogue agents hacking into a major cityâs electric grid, Nvidiaâs CEO admitting he slept with a Chinese spy, pick your poison.
The market is sobering up and going back to doing its job of separating winners from losers. Some of those losers are likely to be household names with 12-figure valuations.
And because the AI boom pulled in companies far outside Silicon Valley, the unwind will, too. Glassmaker Corningâs stock doubled in the first six months of the year after a $6 billion deal to outfit Metaâs data centers; it has now given up almost all of those gains. Modine, a maker of car radiators, is now trading lower than before it announced the spinoff of that business in January to become âa pure-play climate solutions company focused on the high-growth data centerâ market. Paint supplier Sherwin-Williams and HVAC-maker Carrier are in the middle of their own pivots to AI.
The boom reached far beyond Silicon Valley. So will the hangover.
Notable
- A Bloomberg analysis of corporate and regulatory filings and credit deals showed that marketsâ dependency on tech â which, these days, is mostly AI â has grown to record levels. Technology also now makes up more than 50% of the S&P 500âs market cap.

468510e660eb.text: By — Rio Yamat, Associated Press Rio Yamat, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/nvidia-investigates-whether-ceo-jensen-huang-was-targeted-by-chinese-spy-when-he-had-affair Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Nvidia investigates whether CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese spy when he had affair World Nov 9, 2026 8:08 AM EST Nvidia is opening an investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort," the company's board of directors said Sunday. The announcement came after Huang acknowledged to the board that he had been intimate with a business executive whom, according to The New York Times, U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for Beijing. READ MORE: Nvidia announced a software tool to stop rogue AI. How would it work? In a letter to Nvidia employees obtained by The Associated Press, Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologized to his family and colleagues. He said he took "full responsibility" for his actions. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News "Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life," Huang wrote. "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility." Nvidia's board said it has "no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information. Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it," the board said. READ MORE: Taiwan charges 9 over illegal AI server exports to China, including Nvidia and Super Micro staffers Huang, 63, will remain CEO during the investigation. "Today's news will not slow Nvidia," company spokesperson John Rizzo said in a statement. "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." Nvidia has become a central player in the global race to develop artificial intelligence, with its chips powering many of the data centers and computing systems used to train and run AI models. Its advanced processors have also been a focus of U.S. export restrictions aimed at limiting China's access to cutting-edge semiconductor technology. The Times reported last month that U.S. intelligence agencies had discovered that Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and chip buyer, and determined that she was feeding information directly to Beijing. The two are not related, according to the Times. Alice Huang was previously a television reporter in China before becoming a top executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which has become one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to the Times. The Nvidia CEO's letter to employees did not name Alice Huang or address her apparent ties to Beijing. He did, however, refer to the national security concerns raised in news reports and said he supported the board's investigation and would cooperate fully. "I love our country and our company," Jensen Huang said. "I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security." President Donald Trump said Sunday he hasn't spoken to Huang about the latest development and praised him. "I hope everything's fine then. He's done such an incredible job," Trump said, speaking to reporters before returning to the White House. Asked whether he wished he had acted on intelligence when he was briefed about spying, Trump again praised Huang: "I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. He's done an amazing job for our country." As to whether he'd take the CEO with him on his trip to Asia next week, Trump said he was open to it. "I don't know, but I'd certainly take him," he said of Huang, who serves on the president's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday as he was departing the U.S. for a G7 meeting in Paris that he could not address the situation with Huang. "I just can't comment because of the nature of it," he told reporters. "And I also can't comment on an internal corporate matter that's going on with Nvidia." Nvidia, the world's most valuable company, has regularly surpassed Wall Street's earnings expectations in the past three years since its high-end chips emerged as AI's best building blocks. The Santa Clara, California-based company reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion in August. Associated Press writer Michelle L. Price contributed to this report from West Palm Beach, Florida. 2178bfc4756d.text:
The News
The Democratsâ historic sweep in US elections has been setting markets askew, as investors guess at what it could mean for economic policy or the billions of dollars being poured into AI infrastructure. One thing seems clear: All signs point to disinflation, according to Thierry Wizman, global rates and FX strategist at Macquarie Group.
For much of the last half of the year, the cost of capital has only been going up â yields on sovereign debt and corporate bonds alike have been rising, as hyperscalers loaded up on debt and the data center buildout faced pushback on the ground. The Fed raised rates. And the cost to buy insurance against hyperscalers defaulting on their debts has spiked.
But if President Donald Trump retreats from the Iran war and oil prices fall, or tariffs are rolled back, Wizman said, yields will come down. âUltimately the view on yields has to be linked to the view on inflation. So, most of whatâs happened overnight as a result of the election feels disinflationary.â
Q&A
This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.
Ellen DiMauro: European sovereigns have been under pressure. At what point do those yields get interesting?
Thierry Wizman: Well, they are interesting. Because theyâve been very volatile.
If youâre thinking of jumping into France, Iâd be somewhat cautious. It really depends on how the events are going to transpire over the next few months. But if youâre not the gambling sort, you would want to wait until thereâs clarity on the election in France next year.
And if thereâs any clarity on any trajectory towards debt sustainability, the budget thatâs going to have to be passed by the end of the year is a part of that, but itâs not going to be the thing that determines ultimately what Franceâs long-term debt trajectory is. Thatâll be determined after the election. If thereâs an austerity program thatâs put in place, itâs not a question of what the yields are, itâs a question of, âwhat do I need to see happen?â The yields are already very high and theyâre already attractive.
Are the hyperscalers crowding out Treasuries and competing with governments for cash?
Theyâre definitely competing with governments for cash. Itâs one reason why the US Treasury is considering reducing the issuance of 20- and 30-year bonds. It doesnât want to crowd out the issuance of the bonds that are used to finance the expansion of the AI infrastructure economy.
Itâs one reason why bond yields have been higher all year. Itâs evident in the data on how much issuance thereâs been by corporations and itâs slated to continue potentially for another two years based on the CapEx intentions that the hyperscalers have divulged to investors already. So, thereâs no doubt there. The answer is yes.
Where are we seeing investors get scared?
Itâs not just that the hyperscalers may have over-invested, itâs also that the turn in the political atmosphere in the US is going to turn against the hyperscalers. Politically, not just economics. State and local legislatures [are turning] against data-center construction.
Are prediction markets a better way to play at rates and foreign exchange markets? Are they a way to hedge?
Not if youâre an institutional investor. Because thereâs just not that much liquidity in these prediction markets. There are people who are trying to bring liquidity to the prediction markets by entering them and making markets. But the amount of capital thatâs being devoted to them is not great enough yet for institutional-size bets.
Itâs difficult to look at the price of a prediction market and be assured that if you try to come into that market and buy or sell contracts that you wonât move the price. So, itâs not an easy way to hedge.
It looked like the US Treasuries rallied on news of the Blue Tsunami. Whatâs your take on that?
Well, there is the possibility that thereâll be less inflation in the US. So thereâs three ways that could happen. One way is if the data-center construction slows down. That would depress the economy somewhat because the economyâs been very dependent on data-center construction.
Bond yields could come down simply because the market thinks the economy will slow down a bit under a Democratic victory. Some of the tariffs might be rolled back and that would be disinflationary, something that helps bring down yields. And the final thing is the fact that oil prices are down on the premise that heâs not going to tempt the fates with an attack on Iran. Itâs globally disinflationary.
The unemployment rate has ticked up very slightly. How do you see that factoring into moves by the Fed and potential rate hikes?
Weâre still at a very low unemployment rate. The Fed is not really concerned about the labor market based on what theyâve said themselves. Theyâre much more concerned about inflation and inflation expectations right now.
What else are you looking out for post-midterms?
The Democratic agenda is going to be largely about reducing the cost of living. I donât think they will succeed, but there may be people in the market who think that they will. So if thereâs enough people who believe that and itâs in conjunction with maybe Trump reducing some tariffs here and there, the narrative around disinflation can continue.
